choices.text: To permit the tumor to re-enter its log-linear growth phase

explanation.summary: Cycling therapy balances tumor cell kill with recovery of the patient's healthy, rapidly dividing tissues.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chemotherapy must balance killing malignant cells with sparing enough of the patient's healthy, rapidly dividing cells. Treatment is therefore given in cycles: an intensive dose reduces tumor burden, then a recovery period allows normal tissues to regenerate before the next cycle resumes the process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cycling is scheduled for normal tissue recovery, not to screen for resistant clones between doses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The interval is a drug-free recovery window, not a period for building tumor drug concentrations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hormone responsiveness is a property of certain tumors and is not induced by a treatment interval.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Allowing tumor regrowth is an unwanted consequence of delay, not the purpose of the interval.

questions.stem: On a tumor growth curve, an untreated cancer approaching a 1-kg mass flattens out of its log-linear growth phase and enters the plateau growth phase. Compared with the log-linear phase, the plateau phase is characterized by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A higher growth fraction with a shorter doubling time

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lower growth fraction with a longer tumor-doubling time

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tumor burden that is clinically undetectable

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complete absence of cell division within the tumor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the ability to seed micrometastatic disease

explanation.summary: The plateau growth phase has a lower growth fraction and longer tumor-doubling times than the log-linear phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The tumor growth curve labels the late, flattening portion as the plateau growth phase, defined by a lower growth fraction and longer tumor-doubling times. The earlier log-linear phase is the one with a high growth fraction and a short doubling time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high growth fraction with a short doubling time describes the log-linear growth phase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The clinically undetectable range lies at very low cell numbers, far below a 1-kg tumor mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cells continue to divide in the plateau phase; the growth fraction is lower, not zero.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The micrometastatic disease area refers to a low-burden region of the curve, not a property lost at plateau.

questions.stem: A patient's disease has been reduced from a bulky mass to a micrometastatic burden by surgery followed by multiple-course intensive chemotherapy. On the tumor growth curve, this low-cell-number region is identified as the setting in which which of the following is of greatest benefit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endocrine blockade of tumor hormone receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irradiation of the primary tumor site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surgical debulking of the tumor mass

explanation.summary: Immunotherapy is of greatest benefit in the micrometastatic disease area of the tumor growth curve.
explanation.whyCorrect: The tumor growth curve marks immunotherapy as being of greatest benefit in the micrometastatic disease area, where the residual cell number is low. Bulk tumor reduction by surgery, irradiation, and multiple-course intensive chemotherapy is what is needed first, at high tumor burden.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endocrine blockade applies to hormone-responsive cancers and is not the modality identified for this region of the curve.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irradiation is listed among the methods for bulk tumor reduction at high burden.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple-course intensive chemotherapy is also a bulk reduction strategy and has already been given.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Surgery is a bulk tumor reduction measure and has already been performed here.

questions.stem: A tumor that initially responded to a single agent progresses after several months. Sequencing of the resistant cells shows a new mutation in the drug's receptor target that prevents the drug from binding. This observation is the central argument for which of the following treatment principles?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adding an agent that blocks hormone receptors on the tumor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combining drugs so a second agent can kill clones that survive the first

choices.label: C
choices.text: Escalating the dose of the single agent until the target is saturated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lengthening the recovery period between successive cycles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replacing cycled dosing with one maximally intensive dose

explanation.summary: Because a mutation in a receptor target or enzyme can prevent drug binding, drug combinations are used to combat resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA mutations are a particularly common mode of resistance: a mutation in a receptor target or enzyme may prevent a drug from binding. Drug combinations combat this, because even if a cancer cell develops resistance to one drug, another drug may still be able to kill it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hormone receptor blockade applies only to hormone-responsive cancers, not to this resistance mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: If the mutated target no longer binds the drug, a higher dose of that same drug does not restore its effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The recovery interval exists to let normal tissues regenerate and does not address target mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single treatment rarely eradicates all cells, and intensity does not overcome a binding-site mutation.

questions.stem: Tumor cells from a progressing cancer accumulate very little drug intracellularly. Testing shows that efflux activity is normal and the membrane protein that carries the drug into the cell has stopped working. Which resistance mechanism is present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Altered DNA methylation of the cancer cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inactivation of the drug by intracellular glutathione

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased efflux by the multiple drug-resistance protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resistance to uptake of the drug

explanation.summary: Cancer cells may resist uptake of a drug when the protein that transports it across the cell membrane stops working.
explanation.whyCorrect: One listed mechanism of resistance is that cancer cells resist uptake of the drug because the protein that transports the drug across the cell membrane stops working. The normal efflux activity in this case excludes an MDR-mediated mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Altered methylation confers decreased drug sensitivity without blocking transport into the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutathione reacts with and inactivates drug that has already entered the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MDR-mediated efflux pumps drug out as fast as it enters, but efflux activity here is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: DNA-repair upregulation corrects drug-induced breaks and does not limit drug entry.

questions.stem: A drug kills tumor cells by inducing breaks in their DNA. In a resistant subclone, drug entry and intracellular drug concentrations are normal, but the breaks the drug produces are corrected shortly after they form. Which mechanism best explains this resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Efflux through the multiple drug-resistance protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin 6 production by the tumor cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resistance to uptake of the drug across the membrane

explanation.summary: Cancer cells can resist DNA-damaging drugs by upregulating DNA-repair enzymes that correct the breaks the drug induces.
explanation.whyCorrect: One listed resistance mechanism is that cancer cells upregulate DNA-repair enzymes, correcting the breaks induced by the drug. Normal drug entry and intracellular levels exclude transport-based mechanisms, and the repair of induced breaks is the defining finding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MDR efflux would also lower intracellular drug levels rather than repair DNA damage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glutathione reacts with and inactivates the drug rather than correcting DNA breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin 6 produced by tumor cells acts by inducing MDR expression, an efflux mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired uptake would reduce intracellular drug concentrations, which are normal here.

questions.stem: Resistant tumor cells are found to contain normal intracellular concentrations of an active drug, but the drug is chemically inactivated in the cytoplasm by a molecule that these cells now express at increased levels. Which of the following is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Increased intracellular glutathione allows it to react with chemotherapy drugs and inactivate them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased intracellular expression of glutathione allows it to react with chemotherapy drugs, inactivating them within the cell. This fits a cell with normal intracellular drug levels in which the drug is nonetheless chemically neutralized.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA-repair enzymes correct drug-induced breaks rather than chemically inactivating the drug.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin 6 produced by tumor cells induces MDR expression rather than inactivating drug directly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The inward transport protein carries drug into the cell; its failure reduces uptake instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The MDR protein shuttles drugs out of the cell and would lower intracellular drug levels.

questions.stem: A tumor progresses on therapy. Studies show normal drug uptake and efflux, intracellular glutathione that is not elevated, and unchanged DNA-repair activity. Karyotyping of the tumor cells demonstrates rapid chromosomal rearrangement. Which of the following best accounts for the diminished drug effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amplification or deletion of genes from the rearrangement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhanced correction of drug-induced DNA breaks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin 6-induced expression of the MDR transporter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of function of the inward drug transport protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reaction of the drug with intracellular glutathione

explanation.summary: Rapid chromosomal rearrangement leads to amplification or deletion of genes, which can diminish a drug's effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cells may undergo rapid chromosomal rearrangement, leading to amplification or deletion of genes, and this may diminish the drug's effect. Every other listed mechanism is explicitly excluded by the transport, glutathione, and repair findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Upregulated DNA repair is excluded because repair activity is unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MDR-mediated efflux is excluded because efflux is normal in these cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired uptake is excluded because drug entry is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glutathione-mediated inactivation is excluded because glutathione levels are not elevated.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with acute leukemia receives cytarabine. Like methotrexate, this agent belongs to the antimetabolite class. At which point in the cell cycle do these agents exert their cytotoxic effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: G2, at the double-check repair step

choices.label: B
choices.text: Independently of the cell cycle phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: M phase, at the mitotic spindle

explanation.summary: Antimetabolites such as cytarabine and methotrexate act in S phase, during DNA synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: On the cell cycle map of anticancer drugs, the antimetabolites cytarabine and methotrexate are placed at the DNA synthesis step of interphase, meaning they act during S phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin is placed at the G2 double-check repair step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cell cycle-independent action characterizes the platinum and alkylating agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mitotic spindle in M phase is the target of the microtubule inhibitors, the taxanes and vinca alkaloids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The G1 restriction point is modulated by Rb and p53 rather than by antimetabolites.

questions.stem: An oncologist selects an agent whose cytotoxicity does not depend on which phase of the cell cycle a tumor cell happens to occupy. Which of the following agents fits this description?

explanation.summary: Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide, along with the platinum agents, act independently of the cell cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cell cycle map lists the cell cycle-independent drugs as the platinum agents (cisplatin, carboplatin) and the alkylating agents, which include busulfan, cyclophosphamide, nitrosoureas, and the anthracyclines such as doxorubicin. Cyclophosphamide is therefore the agent that acts regardless of cell cycle phase.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytarabine is an antimetabolite acting during DNA synthesis in S phase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irinotecan is a topoisomerase inhibitor acting at a defined point in the cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paclitaxel is a taxane, a microtubule inhibitor acting at mitosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine is a vinca alkaloid, also a microtubule inhibitor acting at mitosis.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is started on irinotecan and is counseled about the risk of severe acute and delayed diarrhea. Consistent with its drug class, irinotecan produces its antitumor effect by inhibiting which of the following?

explanation.summary: Irinotecan is the topoisomerase inhibitor on the cell cycle map and is associated with severe acute and delayed diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Irinotecan is listed as the example topoisomerase inhibitor among the cell cycle-specific anticancer drugs, and the adverse-effect map links irinotecan to severe acute and delayed diarrhea, matching the counseling described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibition of an abnormal tumor kinase describes molecularly targeted therapy such as imatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Microtubule assembly is inhibited by the taxanes and vinca alkaloids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Estrogen receptor signaling is the target of endocrine therapy such as tamoxifen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nucleotide synthesis in S phase is blocked by the antimetabolites cytarabine and methotrexate.

questions.stem: A patient's chemotherapy regimen includes a nitrosourea. Which of the following adverse effects is most characteristically associated with this agent?

explanation.summary: Nitrosoureas are characteristically associated with neurotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ChemoMan adverse-effect map pairs the nitrosoureas with neurotoxicity, which is the expected toxicity to counsel about with these agents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemorrhagic cystitis is characteristic of cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Keratitis, with conjunctivitis, is characteristic of cytarabine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ototoxicity is characteristic of cisplatin and carboplatin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary fibrosis is characteristic of bleomycin and busulfan.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for leukemia develops bilateral eye pain, redness, and photophobia. Examination shows corneal inflammation with conjunctivitis. Which agent in his regimen is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Keratitis and conjunctivitis are the characteristic adverse effects of cytarabine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ChemoMan adverse-effect map links cytarabine to keratitis and conjunctivitis, matching the corneal inflammation with conjunctivitis described here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin is associated with pulmonary fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxorubicin, an anthracycline, is associated with cardiotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate is associated with myelosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine, a vinca alkaloid, is associated with peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: A woman receiving a monoclonal antibody for her cancer notes that she has had far fewer side effects than a friend treated with a traditional cytotoxic regimen. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytotoxic drugs act only on tumor cells that are in the plateau growth phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytotoxic drugs spare the bone marrow but injure only the gastric mucosa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monoclonal antibodies kill tumor cells without ever entering the circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: More specific agents act in a more targeted way, so adverse effects are fewer and less intense

choices.label: E
choices.text: Targeted agents are effective only after cytotoxic therapy has already failed

explanation.summary: More specific agents such as monoclonal antibodies and small molecule inhibitors act in a more targeted way, reducing the number and intensity of adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Traditional cytotoxic drugs target any rapidly dividing cell, not just cancer cells, so they also kill normal cells that turn over rapidly. More specific agents like monoclonal antibodies and small molecule inhibitors act in a more targeted way, which reduces the number and intensity of adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic drugs act on rapidly dividing cells, and the plateau phase is the low-growth-fraction portion of the growth curve.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytotoxic drugs affect both tissues: gastric mucosa injury causes nausea and vomiting, and bone marrow injury causes myelosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Systemic therapies reach tumor cells through the circulation; this is not why toxicity differs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Treatment reserved for failure of preferred therapies is salvage therapy, which is a timing category rather than a toxicity explanation.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the office with 3 weeks of fatigue, decreased activity, and easy bruising. Examination shows pallor and scattered petechiae. A complete blood count reveals an elevated white blood cell count, low hemoglobin, and a very low platelet count. A peripheral blood smear shows numerous lymphoblasts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia with Auer rods

explanation.summary: A child with cytopenias and circulating lymphoblasts has acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma until proven otherwise.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ALL, malignant lymphoblasts proliferate in and replace the marrow, crowding out normal precursors and producing anemia and thrombocytopenia while lymphoblasts spill into the blood. ALL is the most common childhood malignancy, so a child presenting with an acute leukemia is assumed to have ALL until proven otherwise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute myeloid leukemia produces myeloblasts (often with Auer rods) rather than lymphoblasts and is far less common in children.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow and does not produce circulating blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura causes isolated thrombocytopenia without anemia or circulating blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infectious mononucleosis produces reactive atypical lymphocytes, which are mature cells, not lymphoblasts.

questions.stem: A pediatrician explains that a child who presents with an acute leukemia should be assumed to have a particular disease until proven otherwise, and that this disease is also the most common malignancy of childhood, accounting for about 25% of childhood cancers. Which of the following is this disease?

explanation.summary: ALL is the most common malignancy of childhood and the default assumption for a child with acute leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALL is much more common in children than adults and is the most common childhood malignancy overall (about 40 cases per million children), accounting for roughly 25% of childhood cancers. In children it also carries a good prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute myeloid leukemia occurs in children but is much less common than ALL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic myeloid leukemia is largely an adult disease and is rare in children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hodgkin lymphoma typically affects older adolescents and adults and is not the most common childhood malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuroblastoma is a common childhood solid tumor but is not a leukemia and is not the most common childhood malignancy overall.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with cough, dyspnea, and facial swelling. A chest radiograph reveals a large anterior mediastinal mass. A complete blood count shows lymphoblasts, and biopsy confirms a lymphoblastic malignancy whose cells express CD2, CD3, and CD7. Which of the following is the most likely subtype?

explanation.summary: T-cell ALL commonly presents as an anterior mediastinal mass and expresses T-cell markers such as CD2, CD3, and CD7.
explanation.whyCorrect: T-cell ALL frequently presents with lymph node or mediastinal involvement, and an anterior mediastinal mass can cause cardiorespiratory compromise. T-cell ALL is usually positive for CD2, CD3, CD4, CD7, and CD8, matching this immunophenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B-cell ALL is usually positive for CD19, CD22, and CD79a and is less associated with a mediastinal mass.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia is a myeloid disorder and does not present as a lymphoblastic mediastinal mass.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Follicular lymphoma is a mature B-cell lymphoma of adults, not a lymphoblastic malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hodgkin lymphoma is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells, not lymphoblasts expressing TdT and T-cell CD markers.

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews marrow blasts from a newly diagnosed acute leukemia. The cells show fine chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and scant bluish cytoplasm, and no Auer rods are identified. Absence of Auer rods is most useful in distinguishing this leukemia from which of the following?

explanation.summary: Auer rods are seen in myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome but not in the lymphoblasts of ALL.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike the myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, ALL lymphoblasts do not contain Auer rods (crystalline cytoplasmic inclusions). Their absence therefore helps distinguish ALL from a myeloid leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicular lymphoma is a mature B-cell lymphoma and is not evaluated by the presence of Auer rods.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is not a blastic malignancy, so Auer rods are not part of its differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm and does not present with Auer rod-containing blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Auer rods do not distinguish B-cell from T-cell ALL because lymphoblasts of both subtypes lack them.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia is found on cytogenetic testing to have the t(9;22) translocation (Philadelphia chromosome). Addition of which of the following agents to his chemotherapy regimen is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL is treated with the addition of a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as dasatinib.
explanation.whyCorrect: The t(9;22) translocation produces the BCR-ABL fusion gene and its constitutively active tyrosine kinase. In Ph-positive ALL a tyrosine kinase inhibitor is added, and long-term dasatinib-based therapy has shown better outcomes than imatinib.

whyWrongByChoice.B: L-asparaginase is a standard chemotherapeutic and has no relation to the Philadelphia chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prednisone is a glucocorticoid backbone agent and does not specifically target the t(9;22) kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rasburicase is used to treat hyperuricemia in tumor lysis syndrome, not to target BCR-ABL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine is a standard component of induction but is not targeted to the BCR-ABL kinase.

questions.stem: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia and a high white blood cell count is about to begin induction chemotherapy. To prevent uric acid precipitation in the renal tubules and resulting acute renal failure, which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Packed red blood cell transfusion daily

explanation.summary: IV hydration and allopurinol are given to prevent tumor lysis syndrome and its uric acid nephropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor lysis syndrome releases potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids that are catabolized to uric acid, which can precipitate in the renal tubules and cause acute renal failure. IV hydration and allopurinol, which blocks uric acid production, are given to prevent this.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Broad-spectrum antibiotics treat infection, which does not prevent uric acid precipitation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intrathecal methotrexate is given for CNS prophylaxis, not for tumor lysis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Packed red blood cells correct anemia and have no role in preventing tumor lysis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion addresses thrombocytopenic bleeding, not uric acid nephropathy.

questions.stem: A patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia develops tumor lysis syndrome and has a markedly elevated uric acid level despite allopurinol. Rasburicase is administered. Rasburicase lowers the uric acid level by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking xanthine oxidase to reduce uric acid production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing renal reabsorption of uric acid

explanation.summary: Rasburicase is a recombinant urate-oxidase enzyme that converts existing uric acid to allantoin.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the uric acid level is already elevated, rasburicase is administered. It is a recombinant urate-oxidase enzyme that converts uric acid to allantoin, an inactive and soluble metabolite, thereby lowering the existing uric acid burden.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urinary alkalinization is a separate supportive measure and is not how rasburicase acts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking xanthine oxidase to reduce uric acid production describes allopurinol, which prevents formation rather than degrading existing uric acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rasburicase lowers uric acid; it does not increase its renal reabsorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting purine synthesis is not the mechanism of rasburicase.

questions.stem: One agent in a pediatric ALL induction regimen is an enzyme derived from bacteria that deprives leukemic cells of an amino acid they are unable to synthesize because they lack the necessary synthetase. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this agent?

explanation.summary: Asparaginase depletes circulating asparagine, starving leukemic cells that cannot synthesize it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Asparaginase catalyzes conversion of L-asparagine into aspartic acid and ammonia, reducing circulating asparagine. Leukemic cells lack asparagine synthetase activity and cannot make their own, so depriving them of an exogenous source leads to cell death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cross-linking DNA describes an alkylating agent such as cyclophosphamide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase describes tyrosine kinase inhibitors used in Ph-positive ALL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase is the mechanism of methotrexate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting microtubule assembly is the mechanism of vincristine, not asparaginase.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old receiving induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia develops paresthesias, loss of deep tendon reflexes, and constipation. Which chemotherapeutic agent, acting by inhibition of microtubule function, is most likely responsible for these findings?

explanation.summary: Vincristine inhibits microtubule function and causes dose-related peripheral neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vincristine acts by inhibition of microtubule function, and its use is associated with dose-related peripheral neuropathy that can cause paresthesia, loss of reflexes, weakness, and autonomic effects including vocal cord paralysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytarabine causes myelosuppression and megaloblastic anemia, not this neuropathic pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Daunorubicin inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis and causes cumulative cardiomyopathy, not peripheral neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L-asparaginase causes pancreatitis, coagulopathy, and hepatic toxicity rather than neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisone causes steroid-associated effects such as fractures and mood changes, not peripheral neuropathy.

questions.stem: Prior to starting systemic therapy, a child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia undergoes a lumbar puncture through which chemotherapy is delivered into the subarachnoid space. What is the primary rationale for delivering chemotherapy by this route?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The CNS is a sanctuary site

choices.label: D
choices.text: To obtain a bone marrow sample

explanation.summary: Intrathecal chemotherapy is used because the CNS is a sanctuary site with barriers that resist systemic chemotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALL has a high propensity to disseminate to the CNS, which is concerning because the CNS has built-in barriers that make it resistant to some systemic chemotherapy. Intrathecal chemotherapy delivered into the subarachnoid space, along with prophylactic dosing, targets this sanctuary site.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperuricemia is managed with hydration, allopurinol, or rasburicase, not intrathecal therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mediastinal disease is evaluated with imaging such as a chest radiograph, not a lumbar puncture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A bone marrow sample is obtained by bone marrow biopsy/aspirate, not by intrathecal drug delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenic bleeding is managed with platelet support, not intrathecal chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A teenager treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia is monitored for cumulative dose-related cardiac toxicity during therapy. Which agent in the induction regimen is most associated with cardiomyopathy?

explanation.summary: Daunorubicin causes cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy that can progress to heart failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Daunorubicin inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis, and its characteristic toxicity is cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy, which can also lead to heart failure, so cardiac function is monitored during therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytarabine causes myelosuppression and megaloblastic anemia rather than cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L-asparaginase causes pancreatitis, coagulopathy, and hepatic toxicity rather than cardiac toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate causes myelosuppression, nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, and mucositis, not cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy, not cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry of a child's marrow blasts shows expression of CD19, CD22, and CD79a, and the nuclear enzyme terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is positive. These findings best support which of the following diagnoses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia with myeloid markers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia, a mature B-cell tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multiple myeloma, a plasma cell neoplasm

explanation.summary: CD19, CD22, and CD79a with nuclear TdT positivity identify B-cell ALL.
explanation.whyCorrect: B-cell ALL is usually positive for CD19, CD22, and CD79a. TdT is expressed in the nucleus of lymphoblasts and disappears as the cell matures, so its presence supports a lymphoblastic malignancy; together these findings indicate B-cell ALL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myeloid leukemia expresses myeloid markers and does not express this B-lymphoid, TdT-positive profile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a mature B-cell disorder and is TdT negative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm and does not express a TdT-positive lymphoblast profile.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T-cell ALL is usually positive for CD2, CD3, CD4, CD7, and CD8 rather than the B-cell markers shown.

questions.stem: A hematopathologist reviews the lineage of consecutive new diagnoses of acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. Precursor B-cell disease accounts for approximately what proportion of all cases of ALL?

explanation.summary: B-cell ALL is the most common form, accounting for about 85% of cases, while T-cell ALL accounts for 15-20%.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALL can arise from either T- or B-cell precursor cells. The B-cell type is the most common, making up about 85% of cases, and it also has a better prognosis. The two types are treated differently, so establishing lineage matters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5% understates B-cell disease; it is closer to the share of childhood cases that are Philadelphia chromosome-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 15% corresponds to the T-cell type, which accounts for 15-20% of ALL cases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The two lineages are not evenly split; B-cell disease clearly predominates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T-cell ALL is a well-recognized subtype, so B-cell cases do not approach 99%.

questions.stem: Leukemias begin in the bone marrow and lymphomas begin in lymph nodes, yet acute lymphoblastic leukemia and lymphoblastic lymphoma are grouped as one disease. Which of the following best explains why they are considered the same entity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are defined by the Philadelphia chromosome and respond to dasatinib

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both are mature lymphoid neoplasms that have lost nuclear TdT expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both arise from myeloid precursors that later mature along a lymphoid line

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both remain confined to lymph nodes until the terminal phase of illness

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cells mark alike, share a prognosis, and eventually involve all three sites

explanation.summary: Lymphoblastic leukemia and lymphoblastic lymphoma share markers, prognosis, and eventual involvement of marrow, nodes, and blood, so they are lumped together.
explanation.whyCorrect: Study of many cases showed that the cells 'mark' the same (similar cell surface and nuclear markers), have the same prognosis, and will eventually progress to involve all three sites: bone marrow, lymph nodes, and blood. For that reason the two are no longer separated, similar to the approach used in low-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Philadelphia chromosome occurs in only a minority of ALL cases and does not define the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphoblasts express nuclear TdT, which is lost as the cell matures; these are precursor, not mature, neoplasms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ALL is a lymphoid neoplasm derived from lymphocyte precursors, not from myeloid precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Disease at either site eventually involves marrow, nodes, and blood, which is precisely why they are combined.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the office because of 2 weeks of limping and diffuse pain in the legs; he now refuses to walk. A complete blood count shows anemia, thrombocytopenia, and circulating lymphoblasts. Which of the following best explains his bone pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bleeding into the joint spaces due to thrombocytopenia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expansion of the blast population within the bone marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis within the spleen and liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leukemic deposits within the subarachnoid space and meninges

choices.label: E
choices.text: Precipitation of uric acid crystals within the joint spaces

explanation.summary: Bone and joint pain in ALL results from the expanding blast population filling the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the common signs and symptoms of ALL, bone/joint pain is attributed to the expanding blast population in the bone marrow. Fatigue and pallor reflect anemia, petechiae and bruising reflect thrombocytopenia, and fever reflects infection or cytokines from the leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thrombocytopenic bleeding in ALL most often involves skin and mucous membranes rather than joints.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis produces hepatosplenomegaly and abdominal fullness, not bone pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Subarachnoid leukemic deposits cause headache, vomiting, lethargy, and neck rigidity rather than limb pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uric acid precipitation is a feature of tumor lysis syndrome after therapy begins and threatens the renal tubules.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma reports abdominal fullness, and the liver and spleen are both palpable well below the costal margins. Apart from direct organ infiltration by neoplastic cells, which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of uric acid within the hepatic and splenic parenchyma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis in the liver and spleen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Portal venous congestion produced by an anterior mediastinal mass

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequestration of circulating platelets within an enlarged spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subcapsular hemorrhage resulting from severe thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Hepatosplenomegaly in ALL results from direct organ infiltration or from extramedullary hematopoiesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Abdominal fullness in ALL is due to an enlarged spleen and/or liver. These can be due to direct organ infiltration by neoplastic cells or to extramedullary hematopoiesis, the manufacture of blood cells in the liver and spleen when the bone marrow has been replaced by leukemic cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uric acid generated in tumor lysis syndrome precipitates in renal tubules, not in the liver and spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A mediastinal mass causes cardiorespiratory compromise from local pressure, not portal congestion with organomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet sequestration would be a consequence of splenomegaly rather than a cause of the enlarged organs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subcapsular hemorrhage is not the described mechanism of organ enlargement in ALL.

questions.stem: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is the most common leukemia associated with which of the following chromosomal disorders?

explanation.summary: ALL is the most common leukemia associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21).
explanation.whyCorrect: Although most cases of ALL have no known cause, a few associations are recognized, including concurrent genetic syndromes such as Down syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, Fanconi anemia, and ataxia-telangiectasia. ALL is specifically described as the most common leukemia associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Trisomy 18 is not a recognized association with ALL.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klinefelter syndrome is not listed among the syndromes that predispose to ALL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trisomy 13 is not a recognized association with ALL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Turner syndrome is not among the genetic syndromes linked to ALL.

questions.stem: An 8-month-old infant is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. Cytogenetic analysis shows a t(4;11) translocation, a finding present in roughly 60% of infant cases. This translocation confers which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A favorable outcome, as with hyperdiploidy of more than 50 chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: A favorable outcome, as with the t(12;21) translocation

choices.label: C
choices.text: A neutral effect, with outcome determined only by age at diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: A poor outcome, worse than hyperdiploidy or t(9;22)

choices.label: E
choices.text: An intermediate outcome, as with the t(9;22) translocation

explanation.summary: t(4;11) occurs in about 60% of infant ALL and carries a poor prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the important mutations in ALL, t(4;11) occurs in 60% of infant ALL and about 5% of other ALL, and its prognosis is poor. By comparison, hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes, 25% of cases) and t(12;21) (16-22%) carry a good prognosis, and t(9;22) is intermediate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperdiploidy with gain of more than 50 chromosomes carries a good prognosis, unlike t(4;11).
whyWrongByChoice.B: t(12;21) is a favorable abnormality, whereas t(4;11) is unfavorable.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These mutations are identified precisely because they affect treatment and prognosis independently.
whyWrongByChoice.E: t(9;22) confers an intermediate prognosis, which is better than that of t(4;11).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man and a 6-year-old girl are each newly diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. The oncologist explains that the man's expected outcome is considerably worse. Which of the following best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adults more often carry the favorable t(12;21) translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adults more often carry unfavorable mutations such as t(9;22)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adults more often have hyperdiploidy with more than 50 chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adults more often present with fewer than 20% blasts in the marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Adults more often tolerate only reduced doses of intrathecal therapy

explanation.summary: Adults with ALL fare worse largely because they carry unfavorable cytogenetics such as t(9;22), while children carry favorable ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prognosis in adult ALL is worse than in children. One of the reasons is that children are more likely to have the favorable genetic mutations, whereas adults are more likely to have unfavorable mutations such as t(9;22), which occurs in about 20% of adult ALL versus 3-5% of childhood cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: t(12;21) is a favorable abnormality that is characteristic of pediatric rather than adult disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperdiploidy is a favorable abnormality and would predict a better, not worse, outcome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A diagnosis of leukemia generally requires 20% or more blasts, and blast percentage is not what separates adult from childhood outcomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intrathecal therapy is given to both groups and is not cited as the reason adults do worse.

questions.stem: Cytogenetic testing on an adult with acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma demonstrates a t(9;22) translocation. The same translocation is characteristically found in which other hematologic malignancy, in which the breakpoint region on chromosome 22 differs?

explanation.summary: t(9;22) also produces the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukemia, but with a different chromosome 22 breakpoint.
explanation.whyCorrect: The t(9;22) translocation that generates the Philadelphia chromosome is also seen in chronic myeloid leukemia. In CML, however, the translocation occurs at a different breakpoint region on chromosome 22 than it does in ALL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myeloid leukemia is characterized by myeloblasts with Auer rods and is not defined by t(9;22).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Burkitt lymphoma is a high-grade mature B-cell neoplasm and is not a Philadelphia chromosome disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hairy cell leukemia is a low-grade mature B-cell neoplasm unrelated to t(9;22).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm without this translocation.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is examined. Which of the following sets of features best describes the neoplastic lymphoblasts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abundant granular cytoplasm containing crystalline Auer rods

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bilobed nuclei with coarse, brightly eosinophilic cytoplasmic granules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coarse clumped chromatin with abundant clear, vacuolated cytoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Large nucleoli, fine chromatin, and a small amount of bluish cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small condensed nuclei with prominent perinuclear clearing

explanation.summary: ALL lymphoblasts show large nucleoli, fine chromatin, and scant bluish cytoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: In ALL, the lymph nodes and bone marrow fill with neoplastic lymphoblasts that demonstrate large nucleoli, fine chromatin, and sometimes a small amount of bluish cytoplasm that may appear somewhat granular. These blasts may also be seen in the peripheral circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Auer rods are crystalline cytoplasmic inclusions of myeloblasts and are not present in ALL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bilobed nuclei with eosinophilic granules describe eosinophils, not lymphoblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coarse, clumped chromatin indicates a mature lymphocyte rather than a blast with fine chromatin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blasts have prominent nucleoli and open chromatin rather than small condensed nuclei.

questions.stem: A pediatric oncology team counsels a family about the risks of therapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. Which of the following is the most common cause of treatment-related mortality in these patients?

explanation.summary: Infections are the most common cause of treatment-related mortality in ALL.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with ALL are susceptible to systemic bacterial, fungal, and viral infections because of functional neutropenia and lymphopenia at diagnosis and further myelosuppression caused by chemotherapy. Infection is the leading cause of treatment-related death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiomyopathy from daunorubicin is a cumulative dose-related toxicity rather than the leading cause of death on therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bleeding is usually from skin or mucous membranes; significant visceral or intracranial bleeding is rare.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Second malignancies such as brain tumors are a late risk, not the usual cause of treatment-related mortality.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor lysis syndrome is an oncologic emergency but is largely preventable with hydration and allopurinol.

questions.stem: A child undergoing therapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma has bleeding from the gums and scattered petechiae. Risk of hemorrhage is greatest once the platelet count falls below which of the following values?

explanation.summary: Patients with platelet counts below 10,000 are at greatest risk of hemorrhage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemorrhage in ALL is typically caused by thrombocytopenia, and patients with platelet counts under 10,000 are at greatest risk. Bleeding from skin or mucous membranes is most common, while significant visceral or intracranial bleeding is rare.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Although low, 20,000 is above the level identified as conferring the greatest risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Counts around 50,000 may allow minor bruising but are not the stated threshold for greatest risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Counts near 100,000 are reduced but well above the level of greatest hemorrhagic risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A count of 150,000 is at the lower end of the normal range and is not the high-risk threshold.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl receiving therapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma develops headache, vomiting, lethargy, and neck rigidity. She is afebrile. Lumbar puncture yields cerebrospinal fluid containing lymphoblasts. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autonomic and peripheral neuropathy caused by vincristine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Central nervous system involvement by leukemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intracranial hemorrhage caused by severe thrombocytopenia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mucositis and encephalopathy caused by methotrexate

explanation.summary: Headache, vomiting, lethargy, and neck rigidity with blasts in the CSF indicate CNS involvement by leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: ALL has a high propensity to disseminate to the CNS. Symptoms of CNS involvement by leukemia include headache, vomiting, lethargy, and/or neck rigidity, and blasts can be identified in the cerebrospinal fluid obtained at lumbar puncture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vincristine neuropathy causes paresthesia, loss of reflexes, weakness, and autonomic paralysis, not meningeal signs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacterial meningitis would be expected to produce fever and organisms rather than lymphoblasts in the CSF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intracranial hemorrhage is a rare bleeding complication and would not deposit lymphoblasts in the CSF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methotrexate toxicity manifests as myelosuppression, nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, and mucositis.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy being treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is found to have painless enlargement of the right testis, and biopsy shows deposition of lymphoblasts. In addition to systemic chemotherapy, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this site of disease?

explanation.summary: Disease in the CNS or testicles is treated with radiotherapy in addition to systemic chemotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Testicular deposition of lymphoblasts poses the same problem as CNS disease: the site resists some systemic chemotherapy. Treatment of ALL includes systemic chemotherapy as well as radiotherapy if there is disease in the CNS or testicles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Exchange transfusion has no role in eradicating testicular leukemic deposits.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet transfusion addresses thrombocytopenic bleeding rather than leukemic infiltration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rasburicase lowers an elevated uric acid level in tumor lysis syndrome and does not treat local disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is not part of the management of ALL, even when the spleen is enlarged.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with a very high blast count begins induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. Two days later he develops nausea, vomiting, lethargy, muscle cramps, and cardiac arrhythmias. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Tumor lysis syndrome releases potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids, and the resulting hyperkalemia drives arrhythmias.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor lysis syndrome is caused by lysis of tumor cells that releases large amounts of potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids into the circulation. Its symptoms are largely the result of these metabolic abnormalities and include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, hematuria, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, muscle cramps, syncope, and possible sudden death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catabolism of released nucleic acids to uric acid produces hyperuricemia, not a decreased level.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium is not among the substances released by lysing tumor cells in this syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Potassium is released from lysed cells, so the level rises rather than falls.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phosphate is also released from lysed tumor cells, producing an elevated rather than a low level.

questions.stem: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma is found to have CNS infiltration, and triple therapy is delivered directly into the subarachnoid space by lumbar puncture. Which of the following combinations of agents is used?

explanation.summary: Triple intrathecal therapy for CNS infiltration consists of methotrexate, cytarabine, and hydrocortisone.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the case of CNS infiltration, triple therapy is administered directly into the subarachnoid space with a lumbar puncture. The agents used are methotrexate, which competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; cytarabine, a pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA polymerase; and hydrocortisone, a glucocorticoid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cyclophosphamide and 6-mercaptopurine are consolidation agents given systemically.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dasatinib is an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor reserved for Philadelphia chromosome-positive disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate is used intrathecally, but vincristine and dexamethasone belong to the systemic regimens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This combination resembles systemic induction therapy rather than the intrathecal regimen.

questions.stem: A bone marrow aspirate is reviewed in a patient with pancytopenia and circulating blasts. A diagnosis of leukemia generally requires blasts to make up at least what percentage of cells in the blood or bone marrow?

explanation.summary: A diagnosis of leukemia generally requires 20% or more blasts in the blood or bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: A diagnosis of leukemia generally requires 20% or more blasts in the blood or bone marrow, although some exceptions exist. In ALL the marrow is largely replaced by sheets of lymphoblasts, with decreased numbers of the other cell lines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A blast fraction of 1% may be seen in reactive marrow and is far below the diagnostic threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 5% blasts falls short of the percentage generally required to call a process leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 10% blasts is still below the accepted diagnostic cutoff.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 15% blasts is elevated but does not meet the stated requirement.

questions.stem: Marrow cells from a patient with suspected acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma are sent for a study that detects surface and nuclear markers on the malignant cells. Which of the following studies is being performed?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum LDH and uric acid measurement

explanation.summary: Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry detects the surface and nuclear markers of leukemic cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cells obtained at biopsy are studied histologically, sent for genetic analysis, and also studied by immunophenotyping (flow cytometry), which detects surface and nuclear markers on the malignant cells. These markers include the CD profiles of B- and T-cell ALL and nuclear TdT.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chest radiography looks for distant spread such as mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A coagulation profile assesses PT, PTT, and fibrinogen for bleeding risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytogenetic testing looks for translocations such as t(9;22) rather than cell-surface markers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LDH and uric acid are chemistries used to evaluate for tumor lysis syndrome.

questions.stem: The parents of a newly diagnosed 5-year-old with acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma ask how long treatment will continue. Most of the therapy is given on an outpatient basis and lasts approximately how long in total?

explanation.summary: Treatment of ALL is mostly outpatient and lasts about 2.5 years in total.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment includes systemic chemotherapy as well as radiotherapy if there is disease in the CNS or testicles. The majority of the therapy is done on an outpatient basis and lasts 2.5 years, spanning induction, consolidation, and maintenance phases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 4 to 8 months is the approximate duration of consolidation therapy alone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 4 to 8 weeks is the average duration of the induction phase alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 5 years refers to the duration of remission most children achieve, not the treatment course.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No phase of ALL therapy extends to a decade.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma begins a 6-week regimen of a glucocorticoid, vincristine, daunorubicin, and L-asparaginase. Which of the following best states the goal of this phase of therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eradicating residual blasts sequestered in the testes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inducing complete remission and restoring normal hematopoiesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Limiting the cumulative anthracycline dose to protect the heart

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preventing tumor lysis syndrome before cytotoxic therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sustaining an existing remission for at least 2 years

explanation.summary: Induction therapy aims to induce complete remission and restore normal hematopoiesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first goal of therapy is to induce complete remission and to restore normal hematopoiesis. A typical induction regimen for children combines a glucocorticoid (prednisone, prednisolone, or dexamethasone), vincristine, daunorubicin, and L-asparaginase, and induction lasts on average 4-8 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Testicular disease is addressed with radiotherapy to that site rather than being the aim of induction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Limiting anthracycline exposure is a toxicity consideration, not the goal of the phase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor lysis prophylaxis is supportive care with hydration and allopurinol, not the purpose of the regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sustaining remission for at least 2 years describes maintenance therapy, which follows later.

questions.stem: An oncologist selects dexamethasone rather than prednisone as the glucocorticoid in an induction regimen for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. Which of the following best supports this choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It avoids the mood and behavior problems seen with steroids

choices.label: B
choices.text: It causes fewer fractures and less osteonecrosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has a longer half-life and penetrates the CNS better

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces less myelosuppression than other glucocorticoids

choices.label: E
choices.text: It removes the need for intrathecal chemotherapy

explanation.summary: Dexamethasone has a longer half-life and better CNS penetration than prednisone, at the cost of more steroid toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dexamethasone has a longer half-life and penetrates the CNS better than prednisone. Its long-term use, however, can cause steroid-associated adverse effects such as fractures, osteonecrosis, infections, and mood or behavior problems.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mood and behavior problems are among the recognized adverse effects of dexamethasone use.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Long-term dexamethasone is specifically associated with fractures and osteonecrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myelosuppression is not the distinguishing feature between these two glucocorticoids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intrathecal therapy is still required because the CNS is a sanctuary site for lymphoblasts.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old receiving induction therapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma develops severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with vomiting and a markedly elevated serum lipase. Which agent in his regimen most likely caused this complication?

explanation.summary: Asparaginase causes acute pancreatitis in about 4% of patients, along with infusion reactions, coagulopathy, and hepatic toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Asparaginase derived from Erwinia chrysanthemi can cause infusion reactions (>10%), allergic reactions, coagulopathies, acute pancreatitis (4%), and hepatic toxicity (>10%). Epigastric pain radiating to the back with an elevated lipase fits its pancreatitis risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytarabine causes myelosuppression and megaloblastic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Daunorubicin causes cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy that can progress to heart failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methotrexate causes myelosuppression, nephrotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, and mucositis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine causes dose-related peripheral neuropathy with paresthesia, areflexia, and autonomic paralysis.

questions.stem: A consolidation regimen for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma includes glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, cytarabine, vincristine, asparaginase, and 6-mercaptopurine. Which of these agents acts as a purine antagonist?

explanation.summary: 6-mercaptopurine is the purine antagonist in the consolidation regimen, which lasts about 4-8 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Consolidation therapy for ALL lasts about 4-8 months, and a typical regimen includes glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide (an alkylating agent), cytarabine, vincristine, asparaginase, and 6-mercaptopurine, which is the purine antagonist.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Asparaginase is an enzyme that depletes circulating asparagine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyclophosphamide is the alkylating agent of the regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytarabine is a pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA polymerase function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vincristine acts by inhibition of microtubule function.

questions.stem: After completing consolidation, a child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma enters a phase of therapy that continues for at least 2 years. Which of the following combinations is typically used during this phase?

explanation.summary: Maintenance therapy lasts at least 2 years and uses methotrexate, vincristine, and glucocorticoids.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maintenance therapy continues for at least 2 years and includes the use of methotrexate, vincristine, and glucocorticoids. Doses, schedules, and duration of therapy can vary based on the patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 6-mercaptopurine and asparaginase appear in the consolidation regimen, not in this phase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These agents belong to the consolidation regimen rather than to maintenance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dasatinib is added only for Philadelphia chromosome-positive disease, and hydrocortisone is used intrathecally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Daunorubicin is an induction agent whose cumulative dose is limited by cardiac toxicity.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman treated successfully for acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma in childhood presents with fatigue and pancytopenia. A bone marrow biopsy shows sheets of blasts containing Auer rods. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Late relapse of her original lymphoblastic disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marrow aplasia from cumulative intrathecal chemotherapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marrow infiltration by a metastatic primary brain tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secondary acute myelogenous leukemia from prior chemotherapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transformation to chronic myeloid leukemia via t(9;22)

explanation.summary: Survivors of ALL are at increased risk for second malignancies, particularly brain tumors and acute myelogenous leukemia, secondary to their chemotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both children and adult patients with ALL are at increased risk for a second malignancy, particularly brain tumors and acute myelogenous leukemia, secondary to the chemotherapy treatment. Auer rods are crystalline cytoplasmic inclusions of myeloblasts and are not present in ALL, so this marrow indicates a myeloid rather than a lymphoblastic process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Relapsed ALL would show lymphoblasts, which lack Auer rods.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aplasia is characterized by a hypocellular marrow without sheets of blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Brain tumors are a recognized second malignancy in survivors, but they do not fill the marrow with myeloblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic myeloid leukemia is a chronic myeloproliferative disorder, not a marrow packed with Auer rod-containing blasts.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis is hospitalized for a flare and treated with high-dose corticosteroids. She now feels well, and her temperature has been normal throughout admission with an unremarkable physical examination. Morning laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 16,000/mm3 with 92% mature segmented neutrophils. Which of the following best explains her elevated neutrophil count?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Occult bacterial infection with left shift

explanation.summary: Corticosteroids cause a benign mature neutrophilia by driving marginated neutrophils into the circulating pool (demargination).
explanation.whyCorrect: In the absence of signs or symptoms of infection, an elevated count of mature segmented neutrophils in a patient on high-dose steroids reflects benign leukocytosis. Steroids and stress cause marginated neutrophils pressed against the vessel wall to enter the bloodstream, a process called demargination; because roughly half of the body's neutrophils are normally marginated, this can significantly raise the count without any increase in marrow production. It is not a serious concern and requires no further testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia produces circulating lymphoblasts with dangerously low normal WBCs, not a predominance of mature neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia typically produces a markedly high WBC count and is often accompanied by basophilia, not a modest steroid-associated rise in mature neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A leukoerythroblastic reaction shows immature neutrophils and nucleated red blood cells, which are not present here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There are no signs or symptoms of infection by history or physical examination, and the cells are all mature without a left shift.

questions.stem: A hematologist defines a laboratory finding as an elevated white blood cell count in the peripheral blood, greater than 11,000 cells/mm3, that is caused by something other than a neoplasm. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Benign leukocytosis is an elevated peripheral WBC count (>11,000/mm3) caused by something other than neoplasms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukocytosis means the WBC count is above the normal range; benign leukocytosis specifically denotes an elevation greater than 11,000 cells/mm3 that is not due to a hematopoietic neoplasm. The most common cause is infection, and other causes include drugs, inflammatory diseases, and stress.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A leukoerythroblastic reaction is one specific pattern of immature neutrophilia, not the general term for a non-neoplastic elevated count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukopenia is a decreased WBC count, the opposite of leukocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neoplastic leukocytosis is caused by bone marrow neoplasms and is often associated with very high WBC counts of 100,000/mm3 or more.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutropenia refers to a depletion of neutrophils, not an elevated total WBC count.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with fever, sweating, and fatigue. Her complete blood count shows a WBC count of 18,000/mm3 with 60% neutrophils. The blood smear reveals occasional bands, metamyelocytes, and promyelocytes, along with many mature segmented neutrophils containing dark cytoplasmic granules. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her findings?

explanation.summary: Neutrophilia with a left shift and toxic granulation is characteristic of a leukemoid reaction to bacterial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has neutrophilia with a left shift (immature neutrophil forms such as bands, metamyelocytes, and promyelocytes), characteristic of a leukemoid reaction due to infection or inflammation. The dark granules represent toxic granulation, which is most consistent with a bacterial infection and accounts for her fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute leukemia would show numerous circulating blast cells rather than a maturing left shift with toxic granulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia typically shows a markedly high WBC count, usually more than 100,000/mm3.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parasitic infection is typically associated with eosinophilia, not neutrophilia with toxic changes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactive lymphocytosis involves a proliferation of reactive lymphocytes, not neutrophils with a left shift.

questions.stem: A patient admitted to the hospital has a blood smear showing a left shift. Which of the following cell types is most likely to be present in increased numbers?

explanation.summary: A left shift refers to the presence of immature neutrophils (bands, metamyelocytes, promyelocytes) in the peripheral blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally only mature segmented neutrophils are seen in the blood. A left shift means neutrophil precursors are present in the circulation, most commonly as a response to infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils are elevated in allergies, myeloproliferative disorders, hypothyroidism, and certain infections, not in a left shift.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils are elevated in allergies, drug reactions, asthma, and parasitic worm infections.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes are occasionally elevated in conditions such as chronic infection or inflammation but do not define a left shift.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive lymphocytes are seen primarily in viral infections, not in a neutrophil left shift.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic patient has a routine complete blood count showing a total leukocyte count of 10,000 cells/mm3. The differential shows 50% neutrophils, 45% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes, 1% eosinophils, and 1% basophils. The blood smear reveals normal-appearing cells. Which of the following disorders is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: A normal total WBC count with an elevated absolute lymphocyte count (>4000/mm3) indicates lymphocytosis, and normal-appearing cells make it a non-reactive lymphocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The total leukocyte count is normal at 10,000/mm3, but 45% lymphocytes yields an absolute lymphocyte count of 4500, above the normal upper limit of about 4000. This is lymphocytosis. Because the cells appear normal under the microscope, it is not a reactive lymphocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The absolute neutrophil count (5000) is normal (below 7700), so immature neutrophilia is not present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The absolute neutrophil count is normal, so mature neutrophilia is not present either.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The monocyte count is normal, making monocytosis incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive lymphocytosis would show abnormal reactive lymphocyte forms, whereas the cells here appear normal.

questions.stem: A neutrophil on a blood smear from a septic patient contains numerous small, clear, membrane-bound bubbles in its cytoplasm. This toxic change occurs by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Degranulation of lysosomes within the neutrophil

choices.label: C
choices.text: Demargination of neutrophils from the vessel wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of nucleated red blood cells from the marrow

explanation.summary: Cytoplasmic vacuolization results from degranulation of lysosomes within neutrophils and is typically seen in sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A vacuole is a membrane-bound vesicle in the cytoplasm. Cytoplasmic vacuolization occurs due to degranulation of lysosomes within the neutrophils, appearing as small clear bubbles. The process usually occurs in cases of sepsis, when there is widespread destruction of pathogens inside the neutrophils.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum remnants describe Dohle bodies, not vacuolization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Demargination raises the mature neutrophil count but does not create cytoplasmic vacuoles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased primary granules containing peroxidases and hydrolases describe toxic granulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Release of nucleated red blood cells is characteristic of a leukoerythroblastic reaction, not vacuolization.

questions.stem: A blood smear from a patient with a bacterial infection shows neutrophils containing small blue-gray oval inclusions located at the periphery of the cytoplasm. These inclusions are composed of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crystalline aggregates of fused azurophilic granules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fragments of nucleated red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peroxidases and hydrolases within primary granules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum

explanation.summary: Dohle bodies are blue-gray peripheral cytoplasmic inclusions made of ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dohle bodies are small circular or oval blue-gray cytoplasmic inclusions usually located at the periphery of the neutrophil. They consist of ribosomes and remnants of rough endoplasmic reticulum and are often a manifestation of the increased protein production in neutrophils responding to a bacterial infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crystalline granule aggregates (Auer rods) are seen in myeloid blasts, not as Dohle bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nucleated red blood cell fragments are not the composition of Dohle bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Membrane-bound vesicles from lysosomal degranulation describe cytoplasmic vacuolization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peroxidases and hydrolases in primary granules describe toxic granulation, not Dohle bodies.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with fever, sore throat, and cervical lymphadenopathy. A blood smear shows an increased number of large lymphocytes with abundant, agranular cytoplasm and a fried-egg appearance that molds around adjacent red blood cells. These cells are most characteristic of infection with which of the following?

explanation.summary: Downey type II reactive lymphocytes are most commonly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (infectious mononucleosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: Downey cells are a specific type of reactive lymphocyte. Downey type II cells are the most common type and are often associated with Epstein-Barr virus. They are larger cells, often with a fried-egg appearance, and have abundant agranular cytoplasm that abuts or molds around adjacent erythrocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bordetella pertussis causes lymphocytosis with normal-appearing lymphocytes, not reactive Downey cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coxsackievirus causes infectious lymphocytosis with normal-appearing lymphocytes, typically in children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause lymphocytosis but is not the classic cause of Downey type II cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staphylococcus aureus causes a neutrophilic response with toxic changes, not reactive lymphocytosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a history of asthma and seasonal allergies is evaluated for an elevated white blood cell count, and his differential shows an increased eosinophil count. Besides allergies, asthma, and drug reactions, which of the following is most classically associated with eosinophilia?

explanation.summary: Eosinophilia (>500/mm3) is classically associated with allergies, drug reactions, asthma, and helminthic (parasitic worm) infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: An elevated eosinophil count is fairly common and is associated with many conditions, including allergies, drug reactions, asthma, and helminthic (parasitic worm) infections. Of the options, parasitic worm infection is the classic infectious cause of eosinophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial infection classically causes neutrophilia, not eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute stress causes neutrophilia via demargination or a transient lymphocytosis, not eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viral infection classically raises the lymphocyte count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypothyroidism is a classic cause of basophilia, not eosinophilia.

questions.stem: A previously healthy man is found to have persistent basophilia on repeated complete blood counts, with no evidence of allergy, hypothyroidism, or recent infection. This finding is classically associated with which of the following neoplastic disorders?

explanation.summary: Basophilia is the least common benign leukocytosis but is classically seen in myeloproliferative disorders, particularly chronic myeloid leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Basophilia (>300/mm3) is the least common type of benign leukocytosis, with benign causes including allergies, hypothyroidism, and certain infections. There are also neoplastic diseases (myeloproliferative disorders) that classically show basophilia, particularly chronic myeloid leukemia and, to a lesser extent, polycythemia vera.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia produces circulating lymphoblasts, not a characteristic basophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Follicular lymphoma is a mature B-cell lymphoma and is not associated with basophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infectious mononucleosis causes a reactive lymphocytosis, not basophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm and does not classically cause basophilia.

questions.stem: A patient with severe anemia has a blood smear showing both immature neutrophils and nucleated (immature) red blood cells in the peripheral blood. Which of the following best describes this pattern of benign immature neutrophilia?

explanation.summary: A leukoerythroblastic reaction is defined by immature neutrophils together with nucleated red blood cells in the peripheral blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a leukoerythroblastic reaction (sometimes called a myelophthisic process), there are two kinds of immature cells in the blood: immature neutrophils and immature (nucleated) red blood cells. This can represent a normal bone marrow response, most often in severe anemia when the marrow is operating at high speed, but it can also occur when a neoplasm or fibrosis fills the marrow so cells leave early.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A leukemoid reaction includes immature neutrophils and their precursors but not nucleated red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Benign mature neutrophilia shows only normal mature segmented neutrophils, with no immature forms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Demargination shifts existing mature neutrophils into the circulation and does not release nucleated red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive lymphocytosis involves reactive lymphocytes, not immature neutrophils and nucleated red cells.

questions.stem: A clinician notes that in most conditions, relying only on differential percentages can be misleading, and that a particular value is generally most important in diagnosing conditions. Which of the following is generally most important?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The absolute counts of the individual WBC types

choices.label: B
choices.text: The morphology of the red blood cells on the smear

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes reported

choices.label: D
choices.text: The relative percentages of the individual WBC types

choices.label: E
choices.text: The total WBC count without the differential

explanation.summary: Absolute counts, not percentages, are generally most important in diagnosing most conditions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although differential percentages are important and easy to use, they can sometimes lead you astray if you do not pay attention to the absolute values. In general, the absolute counts, not the percentages, are most important in diagnosing most conditions. The absolute count is obtained by multiplying the total WBC count by the percentage of each type.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cell morphology is not the WBC value used to interpret the differential.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio is not the value the brick emphasizes for diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Percentages alone can be misleading because a normal percentage can correspond to an abnormal absolute number and vice versa.
