questions.stem: A lymph node removed adjacent to a resected carcinoma contains no tumor cells, but the paracortex is markedly expanded. Which of the following best explains this histologic finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A paracortical hyperplasia reaction to the nearby malignancy

choices.label: B
choices.text: B-cell proliferation forming enlarged germinal centers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct infiltration of the node by carcinoma cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Granuloma formation from sarcoidosis involving the node

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune complex deposition from a serum-sickness-like drug reaction

explanation.summary: A paracortical hyperplasia reaction pattern can be provoked by a nearby malignancy even when the node contains no tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Causes of a paracortical hyperplasia reaction pattern include responses to viral infection, responses to vaccination, reaction to a nearby malignancy, and autoimmune disease. A tumor-free node beside a carcinoma showing an expanded paracortex fits the reactive pattern rather than metastatic involvement.

whyWrongByChoice.B: B-cell proliferation produces follicular hyperplasia with germinal centers, not paracortical expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct infiltration is excluded because the node contains no tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease that classically produces hilar adenopathy rather than this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A serum-sickness-like drug reaction causes generalized adenopathy and is not suggested in this patient.

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy from a patient with adenopathy shows both enlarged germinal centers within the follicles and expansion of the paracortex. Which of the following is the best interpretation of these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single node may demonstrate more than one reaction pattern

choices.label: B
choices.text: The combination is diagnostic of one specific infectious organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: The germinal center change alone indicates a neoplastic process

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paracortical change alone indicates a neoplastic process

choices.label: E
choices.text: The two patterns are mutually exclusive, so the specimen is inadequate

explanation.summary: Lymph node specimens may demonstrate more than one benign reaction pattern at the same time.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymph node specimens may demonstrate more than one pattern, so follicular hyperplasia driven by B-cell proliferation and paracortical hyperplasia driven by T-cell proliferation can coexist in the same node. Finding both patterns together does not by itself indicate neoplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither reaction pattern is specific enough to identify a particular organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enlarged germinal centers reflect benign follicular hyperplasia in response to an immune stimulus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paracortical expansion reflects a benign T-cell response to stimuli such as viral infection or vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patterns are not mutually exclusive, so their coexistence does not make the specimen inadequate.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man develops generalized lymphadenopathy approximately two weeks after receiving an immunization. Vaccine-associated generalized adenopathy occurs most often after administration of which of the following types of vaccine?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Live vaccines such as measles and BCG

choices.label: C
choices.text: mRNA vaccines such as COVID-19 vaccines

explanation.summary: Generalized adenopathy after vaccination occurs most often with live vaccines such as measles vaccine and BCG.
explanation.whyCorrect: Generalized adenopathy occurs most often with live vaccines, such as the measles vaccine and BCG vaccine for tuberculosis. Other vaccine types may also produce adenopathy, but live vaccines are the most frequent trigger.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inactivated whole-organism vaccines are not the type most often associated with generalized adenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adenopathy may follow COVID-19 vaccination, but live vaccines remain the most common vaccine trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polysaccharide conjugate vaccines are not the leading vaccine-related cause of generalized adenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoid vaccines are not singled out as a frequent cause of generalized node enlargement.

questions.stem: Most drugs that cause generalized lymphadenopathy do so through a serum-sickness-like, type 3 hypersensitivity reaction. Which of the following drugs instead produces generalized adenopathy by a mechanism that is not understood?

explanation.summary: Phenytoin causes generalized adenopathy through unknown mechanisms rather than by a type 3 hypersensitivity reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Generalized adenopathy can occur via unknown mechanisms with phenytoin, or via a serum-sickness-like hypersensitivity reaction of type 3 for most other implicated drugs. Phenytoin is therefore the agent whose mechanism is singled out as not understood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allopurinol is listed among the drugs producing adenopathy by type 3 hypersensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbamazepine is an antiseizure drug that causes adenopathy through the type 3 hypersensitivity mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydralazine is a cardiovascular drug acting through the same type 3 hypersensitivity mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin is an antibiotic that causes generalized adenopathy through type 3 hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old wildlife biologist presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of sudden high fever, chills, and a painful swelling in his right groin. He works outdoors in rural New Mexico and reports handling a dead prairie dog without gloves several days ago. On examination he appears acutely ill and has a tender, markedly enlarged inguinal lymph node. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?

explanation.summary: Sudden fever with a tender bubo after rodent exposure in the western US is classic bubonic plague.
explanation.whyCorrect: Y. pestis is endemic in the western United States, where rodents, prairie dogs, and squirrels are natural reservoirs and the flea is the main vector. Bubonic plague, the most common form, follows a flea bite or contact with an infected animal or carcass and produces a massively enlarged, tender lymph node (bubo) with sudden fever and chills.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B. henselae causes milder lymphadenopathy after a cat scratch or bite, not an acute febrile bubo after rodent contact.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. trachomatis L1-L3 causes lymphogranuloma venereum, a sexually transmitted infection with buboes, not a zoonotic exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: F. tularensis typically produces an ulcer at the inoculation site and is found predominantly in the Ozarks after rabbit or tick exposure, not prairie dog handling in the western US.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Human herpesvirus-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, not an acute febrile lymphadenopathy after rodent contact.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A patient with suspected plague has an aspirate taken from an enlarged inguinal lymph node. The sample is sent for staining. Which of the following staining patterns would most strongly support a diagnosis of Yersinia pestis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gram-positive cocci arranged in long chains

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gram-positive cocci arranged in grapelike clusters

explanation.summary: Y. pestis is a gram-negative bacillus that shows a distinctive bipolar 'safety-pin' staining pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: Y. pestis is a non-motile, gram-negative facultative anaerobe. With select stains, the dye concentrates at the ends of the bacillus, giving a bipolar appearance that resembles a safety pin. Patient samples such as bubo aspirates, blood, or sputum are examined for this pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acid-fast bacilli suggest mycobacteria; Y. pestis is not acid-fast.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gram-negative diplococci suggest organisms such as Neisseria, not the bipolar bacillus of plague.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gram-positive cocci in chains suggest Streptococcus species, not Y. pestis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gram-positive cocci in clusters suggest Staphylococcus species, not a gram-negative plague bacillus.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 40 cells/uL presents with fever and multiple red-purple, dome-shaped skin nodules on his trunk and arms that have gradually increased over the past month. The lesions are tender and bleed easily. Biopsy stain reveals small gram-negative bacilli, and histology shows neutrophilic infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?

explanation.summary: Vascular skin nodules in a severely immunocompromised host caused by a gram-negative bacillus indicate bacillary angiomatosis from B. henselae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacillary angiomatosis is seen only in severely immunocompromised patients, such as HIV patients with T-cell counts below 100 cells/uL. It presents with multiple disseminated bright red or purple vascular skin nodules. B. henselae lesions are tender, bleed easily, and show neutrophilic infiltrates, distinguishing them from Kaposi sarcoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C. trachomatis L1-L3 causes lymphogranuloma venereum with genital ulcers and buboes, not vascular skin nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: F. tularensis causes ulceroglandular, pneumonic, or typhoidal disease, not disseminated vascular nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which resembles bacillary angiomatosis but is caused by a virus (not a gram-negative bacillus); its lesions are usually painless, do not bleed, and show lymphocytic infiltrates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Y. pestis causes plague with buboes and pneumonia, not chronic vascular skin nodules.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 45-year-old hunter in Arkansas presents with fever, chills, and a painful swollen lymph node in his right axilla. A few days earlier he skinned a wild rabbit and later noticed a small ulcer with an erythematous base on the dorsum of his right hand. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?

explanation.summary: A skin ulcer at the inoculation site plus regional lymphadenopathy after rabbit exposure in the Ozarks is classic ulceroglandular tularemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: F. tularensis is transmitted by direct contact with rabbits or by tick and deer fly bites, and skinning a rabbit can aerosolize or inoculate the bacteria. Ulceroglandular disease is the most common form (75-85%) and uniquely causes ulceration at the inoculation site with enlarged regional lymph nodes. Most US cases occur in the Ozarks (Arkansas and Missouri).

whyWrongByChoice.A: B. henselae follows a cat scratch or bite, not rabbit skinning, and causes milder lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. trachomatis L1-L3 is sexually transmitted and causes genital ulcers, not a hand ulcer from rabbit contact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus can cause skin infection and lymphadenopathy but does not fit the rabbit exposure and classic ulceroglandular pattern in an endemic area.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Y. pestis causes a bubo but classically does not ulcerate at the inoculation site and is found in the western US after rodent exposure.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: The F1 antigen capsule is an important virulence factor of Yersinia pestis. Which of the following best describes a distinguishing property of this capsule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enhances phagocytosis of the bacterium by neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is composed of lipopolysaccharide endotoxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is composed predominantly of protein rather than polysaccharide

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is encoded on the bacterial chromosome rather than a plasmid

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is produced at 25 degrees C within the flea vector

explanation.summary: Unlike most encapsulated bacteria, the Y. pestis capsule is protein-based, built predominantly from the F1 antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: What distinguishes the Y. pestis capsule from most other bacterial capsules is that it is protein-based, constructed predominantly from the F1 antigen (a protein), rather than the polysaccharide typical of most encapsulated bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The capsule is anti-phagocytic and conceals surface antigens, providing early immune evasion, not enhanced phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LPS is a separate gram-negative endotoxin; the capsule is made from the F1 antigen protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The capsule is encoded on a plasmid, not the chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsule is only produced at 37 degrees C, not at the flea's 25 degrees C body temperature, allowing the bacterium to conserve energy.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is diagnosed with septicemic plague and is critically ill with hypotension and evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line antibiotic for this severe infection?

explanation.summary: Severe or systemic plague is treated first-line with an intravenous aminoglycoside such as gentamicin.
explanation.whyCorrect: For severe disease presentations such as septicemic or pneumonic plague, the first-line therapy is intravenous aminoglycosides, typically gentamicin, which provide reliable bactericidal activity in life-threatening infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin is a first-line agent for cat scratch disease, not for severe plague.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone) is an option for mild, stable cases, not the preferred agent for severe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is effective for plague but is reserved for mild, non-severe cases or when other options are contraindicated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillin V is a beta-lactam that does not provide coverage against plague.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: Yersinia pestis is a facultative intracellular pathogen that can survive attacks by phagocytes in the lymph nodes. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how Y. pestis directly delivers immunosuppressive effector proteins into host phagocytes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A type III secretion system that injects Yops into host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of a biofilm that physically excludes neutrophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Production of an exotoxin that ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of coagulase that forms a protective fibrin clot

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of a polysaccharide capsule that lyses phagocytes

explanation.summary: Y. pestis uses a syringe-like type III secretion system to inject Yersinia outer proteins (Yops) into phagocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Yops are delivered to host cells via type III secretion systems (T3SS), transmembrane protein complexes that function like a syringe. As phagocytes approach, Y. pestis uses the T3SS to inject Yops into those cells, effectively neutralizing them, which is why the bacterium can fight the immune system from within the lymph nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Biofilm exclusion of neutrophils is not the described mechanism; Yops are actively injected via the T3SS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The article does not attribute plague virulence to an EF-2-inactivating exotoxin; effectors are delivered by the T3SS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Coagulase and fibrin clot formation are not the described mechanism for Yop delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsule is anti-phagocytic and conceals antigens, but it does not lyse phagocytes or deliver effector proteins.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A laboratory attempts to culture Francisella tularensis from a patient with suspected tularemia. Which of the following is a specific requirement for successful growth of this organism in culture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anaerobic incubation with added vitamin K and hemin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Charcoal-yeast extract agar with iron and cysteine at 42 degrees C for Legionella

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chocolate agar supplemented with factors V and X

choices.label: D
choices.text: Media supplemented with cysteine, often charcoal agar

explanation.summary: F. tularensis culture requires cysteine, often on charcoal agar, and must be handled carefully because of its low infectious dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because infection can occur with a very small inoculum, culture of F. tularensis is dangerous and must be done with cysteine, often in charcoal agar; this is a requirement for the organism to grow. F. tularensis is a BSL3 pathogen, so labs must be alerted when it is suspected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaerobic incubation with vitamin K and hemin is used for organisms such as Bacteroides, not F. tularensis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick specifies cysteine and charcoal agar for F. tularensis and does not describe a Legionella-specific protocol as the requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chocolate agar with factors V and X supports Haemophilus influenzae, not F. tularensis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tellurite agar is used for Corynebacterium diphtheriae, not tularemia.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A patient develops severe pneumonia with a productive cough and bloody sputum after close contact with another person who had plague pneumonia. Which of the following best explains why pneumonic plague, unlike pneumonic tularemia, is a major public health concern for person-to-person spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Once Y. pestis actively replicates in the lungs, it spreads person-to-person

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pneumonic plague is transmitted exclusively by flea bites indoors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pneumonic tularemia spreads more efficiently between people than pneumonic plague

choices.label: D
choices.text: Y. pestis is transmitted person-to-person only through contaminated blood products

choices.label: E
choices.text: Y. pestis requires an arthropod vector to move between human hosts

explanation.summary: Pneumonic plague can spread directly between people by respiratory droplets, making prompt treatment critical.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once Y. pestis is actively replicating in the lungs, it can spread person-to-person via respiratory droplets. Pneumonic plague causes severe pneumonia with necrotization of lung tissue and a productive cough with bloody sputum (hemoptysis), and prompt treatment is critical to prevent spread.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumonic plague is acquired by aerosolized droplets or blood spread to the lungs, not exclusively indoor flea bites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unlike pneumonic plague, there is no significant person-to-person transmission of tularemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transmission is via respiratory droplets from active lung infection, not exclusively contaminated blood products.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Respiratory droplet spread does not require an arthropod vector between human hosts.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl presents with a low-grade fever and a tender, enlarged lymph node in her right axilla. Two weeks earlier she developed a small papule on her right forearm after playing with a new kitten. She is otherwise healthy. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three months of doxycycline plus erythromycin

explanation.summary: Cat scratch disease in an immunocompetent patient is treated first-line with the macrolide azithromycin.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is cat scratch disease from B. henselae, presenting with a low-grade fever, an inoculation papule (3-10 days), and regional lymphadenopathy (1-3 weeks) in an axillary node after a kitten scratch. In otherwise healthy individuals, first-line therapy is a short course of the macrolide azithromycin, which helps accelerate resolution of the lymphadenitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Intravenous gentamicin is reserved for severe plague and tularemia, not uncomplicated cat scratch disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymph node aspiration is not recommended for cases of cat scratch disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin V does not provide appropriate coverage for B. henselae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolonged doxycycline or erythromycin is used for bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, not cat scratch disease in a healthy child.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: Public health officials list Francisella tularensis as a potential agent of bioterrorism. Which of the following properties of F. tularensis most contributes to this concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An extremely low infectious dose, as few as 10-50 bacteria

choices.label: B
choices.text: An infectious dose of 1000-2000 organisms, similar to influenza A

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resistance to all aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones

explanation.summary: F. tularensis can infect with a very small inoculum and can be aerosolized, making it a bioterrorism concern.
explanation.whyCorrect: A very small number of F. tularensis bacteria are needed to cause infection, as low as 10-50 bacteria. It can be aerosolized (for example, by skinning a rabbit) and could be aerosolized for weaponization, which is why it is considered an agent of bioterrorism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An infectious dose of 1000-2000 organisms describes influenza A virus (ID50), not F. tularensis, whose dose is far lower.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Unlike pneumonic plague, there is no significant person-to-person transmission of tularemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: F. tularensis can readily be aerosolized, which is precisely part of the weaponization concern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: F. tularensis is treatable with aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones; it is not pan-resistant.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A pathologist is asked to distinguish bacillary angiomatosis from Kaposi sarcoma in an immunocompromised patient with red-purple skin lesions. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor bacillary angiomatosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of any identifiable bacteria on tissue stains

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lesions that occur only in immunocompetent hosts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Painless lesions that do not bleed with lymphocytic infiltrates

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tender lesions that bleed easily with neutrophilic infiltrates

explanation.summary: Bacillary angiomatosis lesions are tender, bleed easily, and show neutrophilic infiltrates, unlike Kaposi sarcoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The skin nodules of bacillary angiomatosis can resemble Kaposi sarcoma, but they are distinguished by their lesions: BA lesions are tender, bleed easily, and have neutrophilic infiltrates. BA is caused by the gram-negative bacillus B. henselae.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BA is caused by a gram-negative bacillus that can be demonstrated in tissue; absence of bacteria would argue against it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both bacillary angiomatosis and Kaposi sarcoma occur in severely immunocompromised patients, so this does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Painless lesions that do not bleed and show lymphocytic infiltrates describe Kaposi sarcoma, not bacillary angiomatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-8 positivity indicates Kaposi sarcoma, which is caused by that virus rather than B. henselae.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A public health team investigates a cluster of human plague cases in a rural western county that follows a large die-off of prairie dogs. To reduce further human risk, the team plans a control program directed at the arthropod that transmits the organism between rodents and people. Which of the following should be targeted?

explanation.summary: Fleas carried by rodents are the main vector of Y. pestis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unsanitary conditions in medieval cities led to a large influx of rats, which carried the main vector for Y. pestis: fleas. Bubonic plague usually follows a bite from an infected flea or contact with an infected animal or carcass, so vector control is aimed at fleas on the rodent reservoir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deer flies transmit F. tularensis, not Y. pestis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mosquitoes are not described as a vector for Y. pestis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sand flies are not a vector for plague in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ticks transmit F. tularensis, not Y. pestis.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man in New Mexico is diagnosed with bubonic plague after developing sudden fever, chills, and a tender inguinal bubo. His family asks what would happen if he refused antibiotics. Which of the following best compares the mortality of untreated and treated bubonic plague?

explanation.summary: Untreated bubonic plague kills 50-60% of patients; treatment drops mortality below 10%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bubonic plague is characterized by a bubo plus sudden fever, chills, and malaise. Without treatment, mortality is 50-60%; with treatment, mortality is less than 10%, which is why prompt antibiotics matter so much in this form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These figures understate bubonic plague, which is lethal in the majority of untreated patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 30-50% treated mortality describes septicemic plague, not the bubonic form.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Near-100% untreated with 30-50% treated mortality describes septicemic plague.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Near-100% untreated with 5-15% treated mortality describes pneumonic plague.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A markedly enlarged inguinal lymph node is excised from a patient with plague and examined microscopically. Which of the following sets of findings is most likely within the node?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulated neutrophils, necrotic cells, hemorrhage, and edema

choices.label: C
choices.text: Non-caseating granulomas containing multinucleated giant cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sheets of monomorphic lymphoblasts effacing the nodal architecture

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spindle-cell vascular proliferation with lymphocytic infiltrates

explanation.summary: The bubo is the product of a severe acute inflammatory response with neutrophils, necrosis, hemorrhage, and edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: After a flea bite, Y. pestis replicates in the skin and travels to the draining lymph nodes, where a severe inflammatory response produces accumulation of neutrophils, necrotic cells, hemorrhage, and edema. The resulting massively enlarged node is the bubo, and the swelling can be severe enough that the node ruptures.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli indicate mycobacterial lymphadenitis, not plague.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Non-caseating granulomas with giant cells are not the described response in a plague bubo.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sheets of lymphoblasts indicate a lymphoid malignancy, not an infectious bubo.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spindle-cell vascular proliferation with lymphocytic infiltrates describes Kaposi sarcoma, not a bubo.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man presents with painful, tender, unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy that has begun to suppurate. He recalls a small painless genital ulcer several weeks earlier that he had barely noticed and that resolved on its own. He has no animal, rodent, or arthropod exposures. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bartonella henselae from a cat scratch

choices.label: C
choices.text: Francisella tularensis from a tick bite

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yersinia pestis from a flea bite

explanation.summary: A painless genital ulcer followed by tender, suppurating inguinal buboes is lymphogranuloma venereum.
explanation.whyCorrect: C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum, a sexually transmitted infection characterized by an initial small, painless genital ulcer or papule that often goes unnoticed. This is followed by painful, tender inguinal and/or femoral lymphadenopathy, often unilateral, that may suppurate and form buboes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B. henselae follows a cat scratch or bite and begins with an inoculation papule or pustule, not a painless genital ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tularemia follows rabbit, tick, or deer fly exposure and its inoculation ulcer is at the site of contact rather than genital.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular skin lesion, not genital ulceration with suppurating buboes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plague buboes follow flea bites or contact with infected animals and begin with sudden high fever, not a preceding painless genital ulcer.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A patient with septicemic plague becomes hypotensive and develops laboratory evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Over the next several days his fingers and toes turn black and necrotic. Which of the following best explains this finding, from which the disease took its historical nickname?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arterial embolization of infected vegetations from the heart valves

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial synthesis of a melanin-like pigment within the epidermis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clotting and necrosis in the extremities during widespread coagulopathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dermal hemosiderin deposition from ongoing intravascular hemolysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasculitis mediated by antibodies directed against endothelial cells

explanation.summary: Acral gangrene in septicemic plague results from clotting and necrosis in the extremities during DIC.
explanation.whyCorrect: In septicemic plague, the immune response to PAMPs generates a cytokine storm, systemic inflammation, and vasodilation that can lead to shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and organ failure. Clotting and necrosis in the extremities is common in septicemic plague and is how the disease earned the nickname the Black Death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Septic emboli from endocarditis are not the described mechanism of extremity necrosis in plague.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Y. pestis is not described as producing a pigment that darkens the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemosiderin deposition from hemolysis is not the mechanism of acral gangrene in plague.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An anti-endothelial antibody vasculitis is not the mechanism described for septicemic plague.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A patient hospitalized with untreated bubonic plague develops severe pneumonia on hospital day 4. He has been in a private room and has had no contact with anyone who has respiratory illness. Which of the following best explains how Y. pestis reached his lungs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions colonized with the organism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct extension into the lung from an adjacent axillary bubo

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dissemination of the infection from the bloodstream to the lungs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhalation of aerosolized bacteria while skinning an infected animal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhalation of respiratory droplets from a person with pneumonic plague

explanation.summary: Pneumonic plague can arise either from inhaled droplets or from hematogenous spread of an existing infection to the lungs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pneumonic plague can be acquired in two ways: through dissemination of the infection from the blood to the lungs, or via aerosolized droplets from a patient with pneumonic plague. With no respiratory exposure and an untreated bubonic infection already present, blood-borne dissemination to the lungs is the explanation here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aspiration of colonized oropharyngeal secretions is not a described route of acquiring pneumonic plague.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Buboes form in the inguinal, axillary, or cervical nodes near the bite site and do not extend directly into lung tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aerosolization while handling a carcass is a described exposure for tularemia and would have preceded the hospitalization, not caused pneumonia on day 4.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Droplet transmission requires a contact with active pneumonic plague, which this patient did not have.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonic plague begins antibiotics 5 days after the onset of fever and productive cough rather than on the first day of symptoms. Which of the following statements about pneumonic plague outcomes is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Treated mortality is 30-50%, and the delay before therapy does not change outcomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Treated mortality is 5-15%, and longer delays before therapy worsen the prognosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Treated mortality is below 1%, regardless of how long therapy is delayed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Untreated mortality is 30-50%, and early therapy provides little added benefit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Untreated mortality is 50-60%, and the delay before therapy does not change outcomes

explanation.summary: Pneumonic plague is near-uniformly fatal untreated; treatment lowers mortality to 5-15%, and delays worsen prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mortality of pneumonic plague is near 100% without treatment. Even with treatment, mortality ranges from 5% to 15%, with worse prognoses for patients who have larger delays between the onset of symptoms and the beginning of treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 30-50% treated mortality describes septicemic plague, and delay does affect pneumonic plague outcomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mortality below 1% overstates the effectiveness of therapy in pneumonic plague.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Untreated pneumonic plague approaches 100% mortality, and prompt therapy substantially improves survival.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 50-60% untreated mortality describes bubonic plague; untreated pneumonic plague approaches 100%.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A laboratory scientist who will begin working with live Y. pestis cultures asks whether she can be vaccinated before starting. Which of the following best describes the status of plague vaccination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A conjugate polysaccharide vaccine is recommended before travel to endemic regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: A killed whole-cell vaccine was developed but is not currently available in the US

choices.label: C
choices.text: A live attenuated vaccine is routinely given to residents of endemic western states

choices.label: D
choices.text: A toxoid vaccine directed at the plague exotoxin is given to laboratory workers

choices.label: E
choices.text: An mRNA vaccine encoding the F1 antigen is the standard for high-risk groups

explanation.summary: A killed whole-cell plague vaccine was developed but is not currently available in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: A vaccine was developed for Y. pestis because of concerns about its use as an agent of bioterrorism. That vaccine was a killed whole-cell vaccine and is currently unavailable in the United States, although alternative vaccines are being developed for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel working with plague research and for counter-terrorism purposes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vaccine that was developed was a killed whole-cell preparation, not a conjugate polysaccharide vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No live attenuated plague vaccine is given routinely to residents of endemic areas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plague virulence is attributed to the capsule, Yops, T3SS, and LPS rather than a toxin targeted by a toxoid vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alternative vaccines are still in development; no mRNA F1 vaccine is the current standard.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: One of the Yersinia outer proteins injected into host cells functions as an acetyltransferase. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this protein's activity inside the host cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of MAPK and NF-kB signaling, inhibiting cytokine production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of Rho GTPases, further inhibiting cytoskeletal dynamics

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dephosphorylation of host signaling proteins, blocking phagocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: GTPase-activating inactivation of Rho GTPases, disrupting actin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pore formation in the host membrane, enabling protein translocation

explanation.summary: The acetyltransferase Yop blocks MAPK and NF-kB signaling, suppressing host cytokine production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Y. pestis produces multiple Yops that inhibit the host immune response through a variety of mechanisms. The Yop with acetyltransferase activity (YopJ/P) blocks MAPK and NF-kB signaling, thereby inhibiting cytokine production by the host cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleaving Rho GTPases is the action of the cysteine protease Yop (YopT), not the acetyltransferase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dephosphorylating host signaling proteins to block phagocytosis is the action of the tyrosine phosphatase Yop (YopH).
whyWrongByChoice.D: GTPase-activating inactivation of Rho GTPases is the action of YopE, not the acetyltransferase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pore formation to enable translocation is performed by YopB/D, which are translocators rather than true effectors.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: Y. pestis residing in the gut of a flea, whose body temperature is 25 degrees C, displays no capsule, yet the organism is abundantly encapsulated once it enters a human host. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capsule assembly requires host transferrin, available only in humans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flea digestive enzymes strip the capsule as quickly as it is assembled

choices.label: C
choices.text: The capsule is produced only at 37 degrees C, conserving energy in the flea

choices.label: D
choices.text: The capsule is required for attachment to the flea and shed in the host

choices.label: E
choices.text: The plasmid carrying the capsule genes is lost at cooler temperatures

explanation.summary: The F1 capsule is temperature-regulated and made only at 37 degrees C, so it is not produced in the flea.
explanation.whyCorrect: The capsule of Y. pestis is encoded on a plasmid and is only produced at 37 degrees C. It is not produced in the flea, which has a body temperature of 25 degrees C. This allows Y. pestis to conserve energy by producing the capsule only when there is a host immune response to evade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capsule production is not described as requiring a host iron-binding protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Degradation by flea enzymes is not the described reason the capsule is absent in the vector.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The capsule provides anti-phagocytic immune evasion in the host; it is not an attachment factor for the flea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The plasmid is retained; capsule expression is regulated by temperature rather than lost.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A rapid antigen detection test is performed at the bedside on a bubo aspirate from a patient with suspected plague. Which of the following does this test identify?

explanation.summary: Rapid antigen detection testing for plague identifies the F1 protein in patient samples.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnosis of plague combines staining, culture, and serological testing. A rapid antigen detection test has been developed to identify F1 protein in patient samples, and serology may additionally be used to detect rises in anti-F1 antibodies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nucleic acid amplification is a separate modality; the rapid antigen test detects the F1 protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serologic testing looks for rises in anti-F1 antibodies, not antibodies to the T3SS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LPS contributes to tissue damage in high doses but is not the target of the rapid antigen test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Yops are injected into host cells and are not the analyte for the rapid test.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: In 1911, investigators in Tulare County, California studied an outbreak whose clinical presentation resembled bubonic plague but that was not caused by Y. pestis. Dr. Edward Francis characterized the novel organism and traced its source back to rabbits. Which of the following organisms was named for both that county and that investigator?

explanation.summary: Francisella tularensis takes its name from Tulare County and from Dr. Edward Francis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 1911 Tulare County outbreak resembled bubonic plague but was not caused by Y. pestis. Extensive studies by Dr. Edward Francis characterized the novel bacteria and traced the source to rabbits, and the organism was named after both the county where it was first identified and the scientist who characterized it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B. henselae is the agent of cat scratch disease and bacillary angiomatosis, linked to cats rather than rabbits.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum, a sexually transmitted infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C. burnetii is not one of the organisms characterized in the Tulare County investigation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Y. pestis is precisely the organism that this outbreak was shown not to involve.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman in rural Missouri is diagnosed with tularemia. She owns no pets, has not hunted or skinned an animal, and no one in her household has been ill. She spends most of her free time clearing brush on her property. Which of the following exposures most likely caused her infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bite from an infected household contact during an illness

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tick or deer fly bite sustained while working outdoors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drinking well water contaminated with human sewage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhalation of respiratory droplets coughed by an infected relative

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sexual contact with a recently infected partner

explanation.summary: Besides direct rabbit contact, tularemia is transmitted by bites from ticks, deer flies, and other insects.
explanation.whyCorrect: F. tularensis is transmitted by direct contact with rabbits or by bites from ticks, deer flies, and other insects. Rabbit-borne infection can also occur through skin contact or eating undercooked meat, but with no animal handling reported, an arthropod bite acquired outdoors in the Ozarks is the most likely route.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unlike pneumonic plague, there is no significant person-to-person transmission of tularemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sewage-contaminated drinking water is not a described route of tularemia transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tularemia does not spread person-to-person by respiratory droplets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tularemia is a zoonosis and is not sexually transmitted.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 45-year-old Arkansas man who handles wild rabbits develops fever, chills, malaise, and a tender, enlarged right axillary lymph node. A careful head-to-toe skin examination reveals no ulcer, papule, or other lesion at any site. Which of the following best describes his presentation?

explanation.summary: Glandular tularemia has the same features as ulceroglandular disease but without an ulcer at the inoculation site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ulceroglandular tularemia produces enlarged local lymph nodes with fever, chills, and malaise, and uniquely the inoculation site ulcerates. With glandular tularemia, the same symptoms are present but there is no ulcer at the inoculation site, which is exactly this patient's picture.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Oculoglandular disease follows eye exposure and presents with conjunctival erythema plus local node enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oropharyngeal disease follows ingestion and presents with sore throat, neck swelling, and cervical adenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pneumonic tularemia presents as an atypical pneumonia with cough, chest pain, and difficulty breathing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Typhoidal tularemia is a systemic febrile illness without clear localizing signs or lymphadenopathy, whereas this patient has a prominent axillary node.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 60-year-old Missouri farmer develops fever, chest pain, and difficulty breathing with a dry, non-productive cough. Chest imaging shows an atypical pneumonia. Three days earlier he mowed over a rabbit carcass in tall grass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Pneumonic tularemia follows inhalation of aerosolized bacteria and causes an atypical pneumonia with a dry cough.
explanation.whyCorrect: Roughly 5-15% of tularemia cases present as an atypical pneumonia with a dry, non-productive cough, along with fever, chest pain, and difficulty breathing. This pneumonia is acquired by inhalation of aerosolized bacteria, which is exactly what mowing over a rabbit carcass in the Ozarks would produce.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oropharyngeal tularemia follows ingestion and presents with sore throat and cervical adenopathy, not pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumonic plague causes a productive cough with bloody sputum and follows rodent exposure in the western US or droplet contact with a plague patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Septicemic plague is dominated by sepsis, shock, and DIC rather than an isolated atypical pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Typhoidal tularemia is a systemic febrile illness without clear localizing signs and with an unclear source.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 74-year-old Arkansas man with several chronic medical conditions has 10 days of fever, chills, anorexia, headache, sore throat, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. He is dehydrated with mild abdominal tenderness. There is no skin ulcer and no palpable lymphadenopathy, and no source of exposure can be identified. Which of the following forms of tularemia is most likely?

explanation.summary: Typhoidal tularemia is a systemic febrile illness without localizing signs or lymphadenopathy, often in older adults with chronic conditions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typhoidal tularemia is a systemic febrile illness without clear localizing signs or lymphadenopathy and was the most common form in Arkansas during 2009-2013, especially in older adults. It often occurs in patients with chronic conditions, the source of infection is usually unclear, and symptoms include fever, chills, anorexia, headache, sore throat, abdominal pain, and diarrhea with possible dehydration and abdominal tenderness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glandular disease still features enlarged regional lymph nodes, which this patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oculoglandular disease presents with conjunctival erythema and local node enlargement after eye exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pneumonic tularemia presents with cough, chest pain, and difficulty breathing rather than this gastrointestinal-predominant illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulceroglandular disease requires an ulcer at the inoculation site with enlarged regional nodes, neither of which is present.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A wildlife technician who power-washed animal enclosures without eye protection develops unilateral conjunctival erythema with tender enlargement of the nearby lymph nodes. She is afebrile otherwise well and has no skin lesions. Which of the following forms of tularemia does she most likely have?

explanation.summary: Portal of entry shapes the syndrome: eye exposure to aerosolized bacteria produces oculoglandular tularemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oculoglandular disease results from exposing the eyes to aerosolized bacteria and presents with conjunctival erythema, often unilateral, together with local lymph node enlargement and tenderness. This illustrates the broader principle that the portal of entry determines which form of tularemia develops.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glandular disease presents with regional lymphadenopathy after skin inoculation, without conjunctival findings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oropharyngeal disease results from ingestion and produces sore throat, neck swelling, and cervical adenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Typhoidal disease is a systemic febrile illness without clear localizing signs or lymphadenopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulceroglandular disease requires an ulcer at a skin inoculation site with regional node enlargement.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: After F. tularensis is phagocytized by a host macrophage, the organism secretes effector proteins. Which of the following best describes what happens next inside that cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It escapes the phagosome and replicates in the cytosol until the cell dies

choices.label: B
choices.text: It forms a replicative vacuole that fuses with the endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is killed by reactive oxygen species, releasing LPS as the cell lyses

choices.label: D
choices.text: It propels itself into adjacent cells using actin-based intracellular motility

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stays within the phagosome and prevents its fusion with the lysosome

explanation.summary: F. tularensis escapes the phagosome, multiplies in the cytosol, and is released when the host cell undergoes apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: If F. tularensis is phagocytized, it secretes effector proteins that allow it to escape the phagosome and replicate in the cytosol. As the bacterium replicates, the host cell undergoes apoptosis, releasing the bacteria to repeat the cycle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Replication occurs free in the cytosol, not inside an ER-associated vacuole.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The organism survives within the phagocyte rather than being killed by the oxidative burst.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Release occurs by host cell apoptosis rather than by actin-based spread to adjacent cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: F. tularensis does not remain in the phagosome; it breaks out into the cytosol.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A student compares the capsules of the two zoonotic gram-negative organisms that cause bubo-like lymphadenopathy. Which of the following correctly characterizes the capsule of F. tularensis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is absent; this organism has no capsule and relies on LPS instead

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is composed of lipopolysaccharide and serves as the organism's endotoxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is expressed only at 37 degrees C and is absent in arthropod vectors

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is polysaccharide, as in most other encapsulated bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is protein-based, constructed predominantly from the F1 antigen

explanation.summary: F. tularensis has a conventional polysaccharide capsule, unlike the protein capsule of Y. pestis.
explanation.whyCorrect: F. tularensis has a polysaccharide capsule. This contrasts with Y. pestis, whose capsule is distinctive precisely because it is protein-based and constructed predominantly from the F1 antigen rather than the polysaccharide typical of most encapsulated bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: F. tularensis does possess a capsule, and it separately has LPS that contributes to tissue damage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LPS is a distinct gram-negative cell wall component; it is not what the capsule is made of.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Temperature-dependent capsule production at 37 degrees C describes the Y. pestis capsule and its absence in the flea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A protein capsule built from the F1 antigen is the hallmark of Y. pestis, not F. tularensis.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory receives a specimen from a patient with strongly suspected tularemia. The Gram stain is essentially unrevealing, showing no clear organisms. Which of the following best explains this result and the appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The organism is acid-fast, so a Ziehl-Neelsen stain should be performed

choices.label: B
choices.text: The organism is gram-positive and obscured, so a spore stain is indicated

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism is obligately intracellular and cannot be stained at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism stains very poorly on Gram stain, so immunofluorescence is used

choices.label: E
choices.text: The specimen was fixed improperly, so the Gram stain should be repeated

explanation.summary: F. tularensis stains very poorly with Gram stain, and immunofluorescence gives better visualization.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staining, serology, culture, and PCR in combination are the options for diagnosing tularemia. F. tularensis stains very poorly with the Gram stain, and immunofluorescence can be used for better visualization of the organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: F. tularensis is a gram-negative bacterium, not an acid-fast organism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: F. tularensis is gram-negative and does not form spores.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The organism can be visualized with the right technique; poor Gram staining is not the same as being unstainable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Poor Gram staining is an intrinsic property of this organism rather than a technical failure to be repeated.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: The parents of a child recently diagnosed with cat scratch disease ask how their indoor cat could have been carrying the bacterium. Which of the following best describes the reservoir and transmission of B. henselae?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adult cats carry it more often than kittens, and only a deep bite transmits it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cats acquire it from infected rodents, and transmission requires ingestion of saliva

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cats are incidental hosts, and the true reservoir is the wild rabbit population

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is shed in cat feces and acquired by inhaling aerosolized litter dust

choices.label: E
choices.text: Kittens carry it more often than adult cats, and grooming spreads it to mouth and paws

explanation.summary: Cats are the reservoir for B. henselae, kittens carry it at a higher rate, and grooming moves it to the mouth and paws.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cats are the main reservoir for B. henselae, and the carry rate is higher in kittens than in adult cats. When cats groom themselves, they introduce the bacterium to their mouths and paws, so a scratch or a bite from a cat can cause infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The carry rate is higher in kittens than adult cats, and a scratch as well as a bite can transmit infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rodents are the reservoir for Y. pestis; cats themselves are the main reservoir for B. henselae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rabbits are the classic source for F. tularensis; cats are the true reservoir for B. henselae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fecal shedding with inhalation of litter dust is not the described route of transmission.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A lymph node is biopsied from an immunocompetent 8-year-old with cat scratch disease. Which of the following histologic findings would be most characteristic at both the inoculation site and the affected node?

explanation.summary: In cat scratch disease, both the inoculation site and the involved lymph nodes may form necrotizing granulomas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cat scratch disease presents with low-grade fever, a papule or pustule at the inoculation site 3-10 days after infection, and regional lymphadenopathy 1-3 weeks after infection. Both the site of inoculation and the affected lymph nodes may form necrotizing granulomas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli indicate mycobacterial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reed-Sternberg cells indicate Hodgkin lymphoma, not an infectious lymphadenitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spindle cells with lymphocytic infiltrates describe Kaposi sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vascular proliferation with neutrophilic infiltrates describes the lesions of bacillary angiomatosis, the other B. henselae syndrome, which occurs in severely immunocompromised patients.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 44-year-old kidney transplant recipient on maintenance immunosuppression is diagnosed with bacillary angiomatosis after developing multiple bright red vascular skin nodules. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgical excision of the nodules without antibiotics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Three months of oral doxycycline or erythromycin

explanation.summary: Bacillary angiomatosis requires prolonged, roughly 3-month, therapy with doxycycline or erythromycin.
explanation.whyCorrect: In immunocompromised patients, bacillary angiomatosis is a more serious manifestation of Bartonella infection, and the recommended first-line treatment is prolonged therapy, about 3 months, with either doxycycline or erythromycin. Severe cases may be given intravenously, and the underlying source of immunosuppression must also be addressed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intravenous gentamicin is first-line for severe plague and tularemia, not for bacillary angiomatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A short macrolide course is first-line for cat scratch disease in immunocompetent hosts, not for bacillary angiomatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-lactams such as penicillin are not the recommended therapy for Bartonella infections.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bacillary angiomatosis is a disseminated bacterial infection that can be fatal untreated; excision alone is inadequate.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has a new cat scratch on his forearm and tender axillary lymphadenopathy. A B. henselae IgG titer returns elevated. His chart documents an episode of cat scratch disease four years ago that resolved with treatment. Which of the following best describes the value of this serologic result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It adds little, since the assay cross-reacts with anti-F1 antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: It adds little, since titers can stay high for years after an infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: It confirms active infection, since IgG appears only during acute illness

choices.label: D
choices.text: It confirms active infection, since titers fall within weeks of recovery

choices.label: E
choices.text: It excludes B. henselae, since IgG would be negative on reinfection

explanation.summary: Bartonella antibody titers can remain elevated for years, so serology is not useful in a patient with prior infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serology, along with a patient history confirming suspicion, is a common way to confirm a diagnosis of Bartonella infection. However, these antibody titers can be high for years after an infection, so serology will not be useful if the patient has a previous history of Bartonella infections, as this patient does.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The limitation described is persistence of titers after prior Bartonella infection, not cross-reaction with plague serology.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A positive titer cannot distinguish active infection from the patient's documented prior episode.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Titers do not reliably fall within weeks; they can remain high for years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A negative result is not expected; prior infection tends to leave titers elevated rather than absent.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularensis, and B. henselae

questions.stem: A public health officer is counseling residents of a flood-affected tropical region on how to reduce their risk of acquiring Leptospira infection. Which of the following measures is most effective in preventing human infection?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Practicing safe sex with barrier protection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets at night

choices.label: D
choices.text: Using insect repellent on exposed skin regularly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wearing gloves when handling raw poultry and meat

explanation.summary: Leptospira spreads through water, soil, or food contaminated with the urine of infected animals, so avoiding contaminated freshwater is the key preventive measure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transmission occurs when people are exposed directly or indirectly to the urine or body fluids of infected animals, often via contaminated water during flooding. The bacteria enter through skin, small cuts, or mucous membranes, so avoiding potentially contaminated freshwater (and wearing shoes) is the most effective prevention.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Person-to-person transmission of Leptospira is rare, so safe sex is not a relevant preventive measure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bed nets prevent mosquito-borne disease such as lymphatic filariasis, not water-borne leptospirosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leptospirosis is not insect-borne, so insect repellent does not prevent it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Handling poultry is not a described route of transmission for Leptospira.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man returns from a camping trip during which he waded through a flooded river. He presents with sudden onset of high fever, severe myalgia especially in the calves, headache, and red eyes without discharge. Laboratory tests reveal mild jaundice and elevated liver enzymes. Which of the following infections is most consistent with this presentation?

explanation.summary: Acute febrile illness with calf myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, and jaundice after freshwater exposure points to leptospirosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leptospirosis follows exposure to contaminated freshwater and produces fever, myalgia (especially in the calves and lower back), headache, and photophobia with conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without purulent discharge). Progression to jaundice and hepatic involvement reflects more severe disease, and L. interrogans causes the majority of clinical cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chikungunya is an arbovirus causing acute fever with prominent arthralgia, not calf myalgia with jaundice and freshwater exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dengue is an arbovirus causing febrile illness with rash and should be considered in the differential, but it does not classically cause conjunctival suffusion with jaundice from freshwater exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: W. bancrofti causes chronic lymphedema rather than an acute febrile illness with jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zika is an arbovirus causing a mild febrile illness with rash, not this waterborne hepatic picture.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man from a tropical endemic region presents with chronic swelling of his right leg and recurrent episodes of fever. On examination, the leg shows non-pitting edema and markedly thickened skin. Which of the following infections is most consistent with this clinical presentation?

explanation.summary: Chronic lymphedema with skin thickening (elephantiasis) and recurrent fevers in an endemic region is characteristic of lymphatic filariasis from W. bancrofti.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adult W. bancrofti worms live in the lymphatic vessels and, with the host immune response, cause dilation, blockage, and destruction of lymphatics. Chronic disease from repeated infection produces lymphedema and elephantiasis (thickening and fibrosis of the skin and subcutaneous tissue), often with recurrent acute inflammatory episodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chikungunya is an arbovirus causing acute fever and arthralgia, not chronic lymphedema.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dengue is an arbovirus causing acute febrile illness, not chronic limb swelling with thickened skin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leptospira causes acute febrile illness with myalgia and jaundice, not chronic elephantiasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zika is an arbovirus causing a mild acute febrile illness, not progressive lymphatic damage.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman is hospitalized with severe leptospirosis complicated by jaundice and acute kidney injury. Which of the following is the drug of choice for her treatment?

explanation.summary: Doxycycline remains the drug of choice for severe, hospitalized leptospirosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibiotics shorten disease duration, reduce urinary shedding, and prevent complications. For hospitalized patients with severe disease, doxycycline is still the drug of choice, with penicillin or ceftriaxone as alternatives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azithromycin is an alternative for outpatients with mild disease, not the drug of choice for severe leptospirosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ceftriaxone is also only an alternative to doxycycline in severe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diethylcarbamazine treats lymphatic filariasis (W. bancrofti), not leptospirosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penicillin is listed only as an alternative to doxycycline in severe disease.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is diagnosed with early lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti. Which of the following medications is preferred for early treatment?

explanation.summary: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the preferred medication for early treatment of W. bancrofti.
explanation.whyCorrect: DEC, a piperazine derivative, is a potent microfilaricidal and macrofilaricidal agent active against W. bancrofti and is the preferred medication for early treatment. Because early lymphatic changes may be reversible, all patients with lymphatic filariasis are treated regardless of symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albendazole is an alternative agent and is used for advanced cases, not the preferred early treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Doxycycline is an alternative regimen and is not typically used for early treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ivermectin is used, often yearly with albendazole, to manage advanced disease rather than as preferred early treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Praziquantel is not effective against W. bancrofti.

questions.stem: A microbiology instructor describes a bacterium that causes a waterborne febrile illness and whose curved organism resembles a question mark under electron microscopy. Which of the following morphologies best describes Leptospira spp.?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gram-negative curved rods with a single polar flagellum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thin, tightly coiled spirochetes with hooked ends

explanation.summary: Leptospira are thin, tightly coiled, highly motile spirochetes with hooked ends.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leptospira spp. are coiled, thin, highly motile spirochetes with hooked ends and two periplasmic flagella, giving a question mark-like appearance. Although they have an outer membrane and are considered gram-negative, they stain poorly with Gram stain and are difficult to visualize with light microscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gram-negative curved rods with polar flagella describes organisms such as Vibrio, not Leptospira.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gram-negative diplococci describes organisms such as Neisseria, not a coiled spirochete.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gram-positive cocci in clusters describes staphylococci, not a spirochete.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spore-forming gram-positive rods describe organisms such as Clostridium or Bacillus, not Leptospira.

questions.stem: A physician suspects lymphatic filariasis and orders a peripheral blood smear to detect microfilariae of Wuchereria bancrofti. To maximize the yield of the smear, when should the blood sample be collected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At any time of day, since timing does not matter

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the early morning while fasting

explanation.summary: Microfilariae of W. bancrofti are nocturnal, so blood for a smear should be collected at night (10 PM to 2 AM).
explanation.whyCorrect: The most straightforward way to identify W. bancrofti is a peripheral blood smear stained with Giemsa or hematoxylin-and-eosin. Because the microfilariae are nocturnal and enter the blood predominantly at night, collecting the sample between 10 PM and 2 AM yields better results.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Timing does matter for the blood smear; only antigen detection can be collected any time because antigens circulate throughout the day.
whyWrongByChoice.B: At midday the microfilariae are not at their peak in the blood, lowering smear yield.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Timing sampling to a mosquito bite is not how microfilaremia is detected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Early-morning fasting collection does not coincide with the nocturnal peak of microfilariae.

questions.stem: An elderly man with leptospirosis deteriorates and develops jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage. This severe icterohemorrhagic form of leptospirosis is best known by which of the following names?

explanation.summary: Severe leptospirosis with jaundice, kidney injury, and hemorrhage is called Weil disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe leptospirosis is sometimes referred to as Weil disease or icterohemorrhagic leptospirosis and is associated with children, the elderly, and patients with pre-existing conditions. Shock, hemorrhage, jaundice, and acute kidney injury are common in severe cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conjunctival suffusion is a mild sign of leptospirosis, not the severe icterohemorrhagic form.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elephantiasis is a chronic complication of lymphatic filariasis, not severe leptospirosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The filarial dance sign is an ultrasound finding of moving worms in filariasis, not a leptospirosis syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is a hypersensitivity reaction seen in lymphatic filariasis, not a form of leptospirosis.

questions.stem: A patient in a region where dengue and chikungunya are endemic presents with an undifferentiated febrile illness, and leptospirosis is suspected. Given the difficulty of culturing the organism and the limitations of serology, which of the following is the preferred method to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Light microscopy of a wet mount

explanation.summary: PCR is the preferred confirmatory test for leptospirosis because culture is difficult and serology is limited.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cultures of Leptospira are time consuming and difficult and are not used for routine diagnosis, and serology has limitations. Because of these constraints, PCR (nucleic acid amplification) is the preferred method of confirming a diagnosis, and leptospirosis should always be considered in the differential in arbovirus-endemic areas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A single antibody titer is limited; titers take up to 2 weeks to rise and prior exposure can elevate them, so paired titers are needed rather than one acute sample.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cultures of Leptospira are time consuming and difficult and are not employed in routine diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leptospira stain poorly with Gram stain and are difficult to visualize, so Gram stain is not confirmatory.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thin cells are difficult to visualize under a light microscope, making wet-mount microscopy unreliable.

questions.stem: A patient with lymphatic filariasis develops a cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath resembling asthma. Laboratory studies show marked eosinophilia and elevated IgE levels. Which of the following best explains this presentation?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute kidney injury from the parasitic infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secondary bacterial cellulitis of the limb

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weil disease with jaundice and renal failure

explanation.summary: Asthma-like symptoms with eosinophilia and elevated IgE in filariasis reflect tropical pulmonary eosinophilia, a hypersensitivity reaction to microfilariae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some patients in the acute phase develop a hypersensitivity reaction to microfilariae in the blood known as tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE). This produces asthma-like symptoms including coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath, with laboratory findings of eosinophilia and elevated IgE.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute kidney injury is a feature of severe leptospirosis, not this eosinophilic respiratory reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydrocele is scrotal swelling from chronic lymphatic obstruction, not a pulmonary hypersensitivity syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secondary bacterial cellulitis complicates chronic lymphedema but does not cause asthma-like symptoms with eosinophilia and elevated IgE.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weil disease is a severe form of leptospirosis, not a manifestation of lymphatic filariasis.

questions.stem: A patient with mild leptospirosis is treated as an outpatient with doxycycline. By which of the following mechanisms does doxycycline exert its antibacterial effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis

explanation.summary: Doxycycline is a tetracycline that inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit.
explanation.whyCorrect: For outpatients with mild leptospirosis, treatment is similar to that for rickettsia, and doxycycline (a tetracycline and 30S protein synthesis inhibitor) is the go-to agent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cell wall synthesis inhibition describes beta-lactams such as penicillin, not a tetracycline.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA gyrase inhibition describes fluoroquinolones, not doxycycline.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Folate synthesis inhibition describes sulfonamides, not doxycycline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibition of the 50S subunit describes macrolides such as azithromycin, the alternative agent, not doxycycline.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing how Wuchereria bancrofti is transmitted to humans. Through which of the following vectors is W. bancrofti predominantly transmitted?

explanation.summary: W. bancrofti is a nematode transmitted by the bites of female mosquitoes.
explanation.whyCorrect: W. bancrofti is a nematode (roundworm) transmitted via the bites of female mosquitoes; depending on the region it is predominantly carried by Culex, Anopheles, or Aedes spp. Mosquito control with treated bed nets, repellents, and insecticide spraying reduces transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blackflies transmit Onchocerca, a different filarial nematode, not W. bancrofti.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ixodes ticks transmit spirochetes such as Borrelia, not W. bancrofti.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sandflies transmit other pathogens (such as Leishmania), not W. bancrofti.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tsetse flies transmit African trypanosomes, not W. bancrofti.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man hospitalized with fever and calf myalgia after a rafting trip has marked redness of both conjunctivae. There is no discharge, and his visual acuity is normal. This finding, conjunctival suffusion, is distinguished from bacterial conjunctivitis by which of the following features?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A thick mucopurulent discharge that crusts the lashes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corneal ulceration with a layered hypopyon

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dense subconjunctival hemorrhage with scleral thinning

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diffuse conjunctival injection without purulent discharge or exudate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Painful vesicles clustered along the eyelid margin

explanation.summary: Conjunctival suffusion is redness of the conjunctiva without the purulent discharge or exudate typical of bacterial eye infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Photophobia with conjunctival suffusion is listed among the common symptoms of mild leptospirosis. Suffusion refers to conjunctival redness that lacks the purulent discharge or exudate commonly seen with other bacterial infections of the eye, which is what makes it a useful clue in a febrile traveler.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Purulent, crusting discharge points to a bacterial conjunctivitis and is precisely what suffusion lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Corneal ulceration with hypopyon is a sight-threatening keratitis finding, not a feature of conjunctival suffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Suffusion is diffuse conjunctival redness, not a discrete hemorrhage with scleral thinning.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vesicles along the lid margin suggest a vesicular viral eruption rather than the diffuse redness of suffusion.

questions.stem: A veterinarian investigating a cluster of human leptospirosis cases traces the exposures to a single farm stream. Which of the following best describes how Leptospira spp. reach the water in which these people became infected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aerosolized respiratory droplets coughed out by infected farm workers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bites of infected ticks that had fed on grazing livestock

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larval forms released into the water by freshwater snails

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sexual transmission between infected people who then bathe in the stream

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urine shed into the water by infected rodents and farm animals

explanation.summary: Leptospira spp. are shed in the urine of infected animals and contaminate water, soil, and food.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bacteria circulate between wild and domestic animals, including rodents, cattle, pigs, horses, and dogs, and are shed in their waste. Humans are infected by direct or indirect exposure to the urine or other body fluids of these animals, most often through contaminated water or soil.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leptospirosis is not spread by respiratory droplets; person-to-person spread of any kind is rare.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leptospira is not tick-borne; it is acquired from animal urine in water, soil, or food.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leptospira are free-living spirochetes in contaminated water, not larval parasites released from snails.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Person-to-person transmission of Leptospira, including sexual transmission, is rare and is not how outbreaks arise.

questions.stem: Between 100 and 200 cases of leptospirosis are reported in the United States each year. About half of these reported cases occur in which of the following states?

explanation.summary: About 50% of reported U.S. leptospirosis cases occur in Hawaii.
