Staging tests follow only after tissue diagnosis is made.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A chest x-ray may reveal a mediastinal mass but cannot provide a definitive diagnosis of HL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A complete blood count may suggest marrow infiltration but does not establish the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An elevated ESR is used during staging to reflect cell turnover but is not diagnostic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PET/CT is used to stage the lymphoma after diagnosis, not to make the initial tissue diagnosis.

questions.stem: Infection with which of the following organisms has been identified in as many as 40% of Hodgkin lymphoma cases, with its DNA isolated from some malignant cells?

explanation.summary: Epstein-Barr virus is the infection most strongly associated with Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that Epstein-Barr virus infection has been identified in as many as 40% of HL cases and that Epstein-Barr DNA has been isolated from some malignant cells. HIV infection is also associated with HL, and most of those patients are also EBV-positive.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicobacter pylori is linked to MALT lymphoma and gastric ulcers, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Human herpesvirus-8 is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Human papillomavirus is linked to cervical and oropharyngeal cancers, not HL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, not Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy from a patient with classic Hodgkin lymphoma is sent for immunophenotyping of the large, binucleated malignant cells. Which of the following marker patterns is most characteristic of these Reed-Sternberg cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Positive for CD15 and CD30; negative for CD45 and CD20

choices.label: B
choices.text: Positive for CD19 and CD20; negative for CD30

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive for CD3 and CD4; negative for CD15

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive for CD45 and CD20; negative for CD15 and CD30

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive for CD45 and CD30; negative for CD15 and CD20

explanation.summary: Classic Reed-Sternberg cells are CD15- and CD30-positive but CD45- and CD20-negative.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that Reed-Sternberg cells arise from germinal or post-germinal B cells with defective immunoglobulin genes and have therefore lost many B-cell markers. They are negative for CD45 and CD20 but positive for CD15 and CD30.

whyWrongByChoice.B: RS cells have lost B-cell markers such as CD20 and are not CD19/CD20 positive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RS cells derive from B cells, not T cells, so a CD3/CD4 T-cell pattern is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This is the pattern of 'popcorn' cells in nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease, not classic RS cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RS cells are negative, not positive, for CD45, and are positive for CD15.

questions.stem: A pathologist describes the malignant cells in a Hodgkin lymphoma specimen as large and binucleated, with centrally located nucleoli that give the cells an 'owl's eye' appearance. This description refers to which of the following?

explanation.summary: The binucleated 'owl's eye' cell is the classic Reed-Sternberg cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes classic Reed-Sternberg cells as binucleated with centrally located nucleoli, giving them an 'owl's eye' appearance. The RS cell is the most distinct morphologic feature of Hodgkin lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lacunar cells are RS variants surrounded by clear space seen in nodular sclerosis, not defined by an owl's eye appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Popcorn cells are large cells with convoluted nuclei seen in nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease, not the owl's eye morphology.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sezary cells are circulating cerebriform T cells of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, unrelated to RS cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Smudge cells are fragile lymphocytes seen in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, not Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with the most common type of Hodgkin lymphoma in the United States. Her biopsy shows fibrous bands dividing the lymph node into nodules, along with giant cell variants surrounded by clear space. Which of the following subtypes does she most likely have?

explanation.summary: Nodular sclerosis is the most common HL subtype and features fibrous bands and lacunar cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states nodular sclerosis is the most common type of HL in the US (about 70-75% of cases), with fibrous bands dividing the lymph nodes into nodules and lacunar cell variants (giant cells surrounded by clear space). It most commonly occurs in young adults and has an excellent prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphocyte-depleted HL shows abundant classic RS cells with few reactive lymphocytes, not fibrous nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocyte-rich HL has abundant reactive lymphocytes with few classic RS cells and no fibrous banding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mixed cellularity is the second most common subtype and lacks the defining fibrous bands.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease is characterized by popcorn cells, not lacunar cells or fibrous bands.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has localized cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows a nodular growth pattern with a background of small lymphocytes and occasional large cells with convoluted nuclei ('popcorn' cells). Immunostaining shows these large cells are positive for CD45 and CD20 and negative for CD15 and CD30. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Popcorn cells that are CD45/CD20 positive and CD15/CD30 negative define nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes this uncommon tumor as occurring in young males with localized disease and showing popcorn cells that, in contrast to Reed-Sternberg cells, are positive for CD45 and CD20 and negative for CD15 and CD30. Because of its opposite immunophenotype and different genetics, it is now labeled nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphocyte-depleted disease has abundant classic RS cells, which are CD15/CD30 positive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocyte-rich HL still contains classic RS cells that are CD15/CD30 positive, not CD20 positive popcorn cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mixed cellularity contains classic CD15/CD30-positive RS cells with a reactive inflammatory infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nodular sclerosis is defined by fibrous bands and lacunar cells, with classic CD15/CD30-positive RS cells.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with Hodgkin lymphoma is treated with the ABVD regimen. Several months into therapy she develops progressive dyspnea, a dry cough, and imaging consistent with severe pulmonary fibrosis. Which component of ABVD is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Bleomycin is the ABVD agent most associated with severe pulmonary fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that bleomycin is a metal-chelating chemotherapy antibiotic whose adverse effects include fever, hypersensitivity reactions, skin changes, and severe pulmonary fibrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Brentuximab is a salvage anti-CD30 antibody and is not part of the ABVD regimen described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dacarbazine causes nausea, vomiting, and bone marrow suppression, not pulmonary fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Doxorubicin causes cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy and heart failure, not pulmonary fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vinblastine causes peripheral neuropathy, not pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma develops a decline in cardiac function with new heart failure. His oncologist attributes this to the cumulative dose of one of his agents, which acts by inhibiting DNA and RNA synthesis. Which drug is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Doxorubicin causes cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy and inhibits DNA/RNA synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that doxorubicin (Adriamycin, the 'A' in ABVD) acts by inhibition of DNA/RNA synthesis and that cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy can occur, which can also cause heart failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bleomycin fragments DNA chains and causes pulmonary fibrosis, not cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dacarbazine inhibits DNA polymerase and causes nausea and marrow suppression, not cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pembrolizumab is a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor used as salvage therapy, not the cardiotoxic ABVD agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vinblastine inhibits microtubule function and causes peripheral neuropathy, not heart failure.

questions.stem: During staging of a patient with Hodgkin lymphoma, PET/CT reveals involved lymph node chains in the neck and in the para-aortic region below the diaphragm, without organ involvement. Which of the following stages best describes this distribution?

explanation.summary: Nodal disease on both sides of the diaphragm defines stage III.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that staging considers the number and location of affected nodes. Stage III is the stage in which lymph node involvement is first seen on both sides of the diaphragm, matching this patient's cervical and para-aortic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stage I is localized disease confined to a single lymph node region on one side of the diaphragm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Stage II involves two or more nodal regions but all on the same side of the diaphragm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stage IIB would require all nodes on one side of the diaphragm plus B symptoms, not disease on both sides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stage IV is widespread disease involving multiple organs, which this patient does not have.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with a large mediastinal mass from Hodgkin lymphoma develops facial swelling and erythema, distended veins over the face and upper chest, and headache. Which of the following best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: A mediastinal mass compressing the superior vena cava produces SVC syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that massive mediastinal lymphadenopathy may cause superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome, in which SVC compression leads to facial erythema, distended veins in the face, upper chest, and upper limbs, and headache.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Airway compression causes respiratory distress and stridor, not facial swelling and distended neck veins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow infiltration causes pancytopenia on CBC, not facial plethora and distended veins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hodgkin lymphoma rarely spreads extranodally, and liver involvement would not cause SVC-type findings.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick links increased cell turnover to elevated potassium, LDH, and ESR, not to this venous congestion syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient with relapsed classic Hodgkin lymphoma is started on a targeted salvage agent that is a monoclonal antibody directed against a cell-surface receptor highly expressed on classic Reed-Sternberg cells. Which of the following is this agent's target?

explanation.summary: Brentuximab is a monoclonal antibody directed against CD30 on classic Reed-Sternberg cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that brentuximab is a monoclonal antibody directed against CD30 cell-surface receptors that are highly expressed on classic Hodgkin lymphoma Reed-Sternberg cells, and it is used as salvage therapy in refractory or relapsed disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PD-1 is the target of pembrolizumab, a checkpoint inhibitor, not the anti-CD30 antibody described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Although RS cells are CD15 positive, the brick identifies the antibody's target as CD30.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Classic Reed-Sternberg cells are negative for CD20, so it is not the target of this agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reed-Sternberg cells are negative for CD45, so it cannot be the target of this therapy.

questions.stem: A hematology instructor contrasts Hodgkin lymphoma with non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Which of the following features is most characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single peak of incidence limited to adults older than 65 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Common extranodal presentation in the liver and marrow at diagnosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frequent involvement of mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer's ring at onset

choices.label: D
choices.text: Noncontiguous spread to distant, unrelated nodal groups early on

choices.label: E
choices.text: Orderly, contiguous spread involving central and axial lymph nodes

explanation.summary: Hodgkin lymphoma typically spreads in an orderly, contiguous fashion through central and axial nodes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that, in contrast to non-Hodgkin lymphoma, HL typically demonstrates orderly, contiguous lymph node spread, involves more central and axial lymph nodes, seldom involves mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer's ring, and rarely has an extranodal presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HL has a bimodal age distribution, peaking in young adults and again after age 65, not a single older-adult peak.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HL rarely has an extranodal presentation, unlike many non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick specifies that HL seldom involves mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer's ring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HL spreads contiguously, not by noncontiguous jumps to unrelated nodal groups.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma. His family is surprised, because they had read that this cancer affects mainly young people. Which of the following best describes the age-related incidence of Hodgkin lymphoma in the United States?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Incidence is essentially confined to adults between 20 and 40 years of age

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incidence is highest in children younger than 10 years and declines steadily thereafter

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incidence is uniform across all age groups after puberty

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incidence peaks in adolescents and young adults and rises again after age 65 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: Incidence rises steadily from childhood and peaks in the ninth decade of life

explanation.summary: Hodgkin lymphoma has two peak age groups: adolescents/young adults and adults older than 65 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that HL is a rare cancer affecting fewer than 10,000 people in the United States each year, with an average age at diagnosis of 35 years. Looking closer, there are two peak age groups: it is one of the most common cancers of adolescents and young adults, and it peaks again in patients older than 65 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Older adults are a second peak group, so incidence is not confined to ages 20 to 40 years.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Young children have a very low incidence of HL; the first peak is in adolescence and young adulthood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incidence is clearly age-dependent rather than uniform, with a trough in middle age between two peaks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Incidence does not rise steadily with age; there is a distinct early peak in adolescents and young adults.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman with newly diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma undergoes PET/CT, which shows involvement of the right cervical and right supraclavicular lymph node regions. There is no disease below the diaphragm and no organ involvement. She reports no fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Which of the following is the most appropriate stage designation?

explanation.summary: Two nodal regions on the same side of the diaphragm without B symptoms is stage IIA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two or more involved lymph node regions on one side of the diaphragm define stage II. The brick teaches that HL staging is further modified by the presence or absence of B symptoms: stage II without B symptoms is stage IIA, and stage II with B symptoms is stage IIB. This patient has two nodal regions above the diaphragm and no B symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stage I is localized disease involving a single lymph node region, but two regions are involved here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In addition to understating the nodal extent, the B designation requires fever, night sweats, or weight loss, which she denies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The B modifier is applied only when B symptoms are present, and this patient has none.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stage III requires nodal involvement on both sides of the diaphragm, and she has no disease below it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common physical examination finding in patients with Hodgkin lymphoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A firm, enlarged spleen palpable below the left costal margin

choices.label: B
choices.text: A nodular, enlarged liver palpable below the right costal margin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Firm, nontender subcutaneous nodules scattered over the trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multiple large, hard, fixed lymph nodes in one or more body regions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scattered petechiae and ecchymoses over the lower extremities

explanation.summary: Lymphadenopathy with large, hard, fixed nodes is the most common examination finding in HL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the most common physical exam finding in HL is lymphadenopathy, characterized by multiple large, hard, fixed lymph nodes in one or more body regions. Many patients are otherwise asymptomatic, and the disease is found when the clinician feels this adenopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Splenic enlargement may occur with disease spread but is not the most common examination finding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Liver involvement is considered in staging but is not the usual presenting physical finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HL rarely has an extranodal presentation, so cutaneous nodules would be a very unusual finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Petechiae reflect thrombocytopenia from marrow infiltration or therapy rather than the typical presentation.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has fever, weight loss, and widespread lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows classic Reed-Sternberg cells scattered within an abundant reactive inflammatory infiltrate containing neutrophils, lymphocytes, basophils, eosinophils, and macrophages. No fibrous bands are present, and Epstein-Barr virus studies are positive. Which of the following subtypes is most likely?

explanation.summary: Classic RS cells in an abundant mixed inflammatory infiltrate without fibrous bands indicate mixed cellularity HL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes mixed cellularity as the second most common type of HL in the United States (approximately 20% of cases), containing classic RS cells and a reactive inflammatory infiltrate but lacking fibrous bands. It tends to occur in older patients, can present with more advanced disease, and is more often associated with EBV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphocyte-depleted disease shows abundant classic RS cells with few reactive cells, not an abundant infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocyte-rich disease has abundant reactive mature lymphocytes rather than a mixed inflammatory infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease contains popcorn cells rather than classic Reed-Sternberg cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nodular sclerosis is defined by fibrous bands dividing the node into nodules, which are absent here.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus infection presents with advanced lymphoma. Lymph node biopsy shows abundant classic Reed-Sternberg cells that are CD15 and CD30 positive, with only sparse reactive lymphocytes and no collagen banding. Which of the following subtypes is most likely?

explanation.summary: Abundant classic RS cells with few reactive lymphocytes in an HIV-positive patient indicates lymphocyte-depleted HL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies lymphocyte-depleted HL as a less common classic subtype containing abundant classic RS cells but few reactive lymphocytes, and notes it is more often associated with EBV and HIV infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocyte-rich disease has more reactive mature lymphocytes than classic RS cells, the opposite of this picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mixed cellularity contains an abundant reactive inflammatory infiltrate rather than sparse reactive cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease has CD15- and CD30-negative popcorn cells in a nodular lymphocytic background.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nodular sclerosis requires fibrous bands dividing the node into nodules, which are absent in this specimen.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with nodular lymphocyte-predominant B-cell lymphoma has had an indolent course with long survival over 8 years of follow-up. He now develops rapidly enlarging adenopathy, and repeat biopsy shows a higher-grade lymphoma. Transformation to which of the following is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma of T-cell origin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Burkitt lymphoma with a MYC translocation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia with CD5 expression

explanation.summary: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease may transform into T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that patients with nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease typically experience an indolent clinical course with long survival; however, they may transform into a higher-grade lymphoma such as T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma arises from T cells, whereas this tumor is of B-cell origin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Burkitt lymphoma is not the higher-grade lymphoma this tumor is described as transforming into.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a distinct small B-cell leukemia and is not the described transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease has a different immunophenotype and genetics and does not evolve into classic HL.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has an isolated enlarged cervical lymph node. Biopsy shows abundant reactive mature lymphocytes with only scattered classic Reed-Sternberg cells that stain positive for CD15 and CD30. There are no collagen bands and no popcorn cells. Which of the following subtypes is most likely?

explanation.summary: Abundant reactive mature lymphocytes with few classic RS cells characterizes lymphocyte-rich classic HL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists lymphocyte-rich HL as one of the two less-common types of classic HL, defined by having more reactive mature lymphocytes than classic RS cells. The RS cells present retain the classic CD15- and CD30-positive immunophenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphocyte-depleted disease has abundant classic RS cells with few reactive lymphocytes, the reverse of this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mixed cellularity contains an abundant mixed inflammatory infiltrate including eosinophils and macrophages, not purely mature lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease contains CD15- and CD30-negative popcorn cells, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nodular sclerosis is characterized by fibrous bands and lacunar cell variants, neither of which is described.

questions.stem: Reed-Sternberg cells in classic Hodgkin lymphoma fail to express CD45 and CD20. Which of the following best explains the loss of these markers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They arise from follicular dendritic cells within the germinal center

choices.label: B
choices.text: They arise from germinal or post-germinal B cells with defective immunoglobulin genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: They arise from hematopoietic stem cells that bypass lymphoid commitment

choices.label: D
choices.text: They arise from monocyte-macrophage precursors recruited into the involved node

choices.label: E
choices.text: They arise from thymic T-cell precursors that never express B-cell antigens

explanation.summary: RS cells are B-cell derived but have defective immunoglobulin genes and lose many B-cell markers.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that Reed-Sternberg cells stem from germinal or post-germinal B cells with defective immunoglobulin genes, so they have lost many of their B-cell markers. As a result they are negative for CD45 and CD20 while remaining positive for CD15 and CD30.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Follicular dendritic cells are stromal cells of the germinal center and are not the RS cell of origin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The loss of markers reflects defective immunoglobulin genes in a committed B cell, not bypassed lymphoid commitment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophages are part of the reactive background infiltrate, not the origin of the malignant RS cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RS cells are of B-cell rather than T-cell origin, so a thymic T-cell precursor does not explain the findings.

questions.stem: A lymph node involved by classic Hodgkin lymphoma is examined microscopically. Which of the following accounts for the bulk of the cells seen in the specimen?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binucleate Reed-Sternberg cells, scattered and few

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lacunar cell variants of Reed-Sternberg cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Popcorn cells with multilobated convoluted nuclei

explanation.summary: In HL the malignant RS cells are scattered and sparse; benign reactive cells make up most of the tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines HL as a hematopoietic lymphoid neoplasm characterized by scattered large atypical malignant cells (RS cells) in a background of benign lymphocytes and inflammatory cells, and states that these benign reactive lymphocytes can make up the bulk of the tumor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reed-Sternberg cells are the diagnostic malignant cells but are scattered and few in number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Collagen bands are a feature of nodular sclerosis only and do not constitute the bulk of the cellular infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lacunar cells are RS variants specific to nodular sclerosis and are not the predominant cell population.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Popcorn cells are found in nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease and are also sparse when present.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with newly diagnosed Hodgkin lymphoma has not yet begun treatment. Her complete blood count shows hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL, leukocyte count of 2,200/mm3, and platelet count of 88,000/mm3. Which of the following does this finding most strongly suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of circulating blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased blood cell turnover by rapidly dividing tumor cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infiltration of the bone marrow by lymphoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration due to portal hypertension

explanation.summary: Pancytopenia on the complete blood count suggests bone marrow infiltration during staging of HL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that during staging, infiltration of the bone marrow is suggested by pancytopenia on complete blood count. This patient has anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia together, the pattern that raises concern for marrow involvement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune destruction of blood cells is not described as a cause of the cytopenias seen in HL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow suppression from agents such as dacarbazine occurs during treatment, and she has not yet started therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased cell turnover is suggested by elevated serum potassium, LDH, or ESR rather than by pancytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Portal hypertension with hypersplenism is not the mechanism the brick links to cytopenias in HL staging.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man undergoing staging for Hodgkin lymphoma has a serum potassium of 5.4 mEq/L, a markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 78 mm/h. His complete blood count is normal. These laboratory findings most likely reflect which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compression of the superior vena cava by a mediastinal mass

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extranodal spread of lymphoma to the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infiltration of the bone marrow by lymphoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Obstruction of the ureters by bulky retroperitoneal nodes

explanation.summary: Elevated potassium, LDH, and ESR during staging reflect increased blood cell turnover.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that increased blood cell turnover, typical of some HL cells, is suggested by an elevated serum potassium, lactate dehydrogenase, or erythrocyte sedimentation rate. These are part of the laboratory analysis performed during staging.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SVC compression produces facial erythema, distended veins, and headache rather than these laboratory abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HL rarely presents extranodally, and liver involvement is assessed by imaging rather than by these values.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow infiltration is suggested by pancytopenia on complete blood count, and his counts are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ureteral obstruction would be reflected in renal function and imaging, not in this pattern of turnover markers.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with Hodgkin lymphoma has cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrates lymphoma, and imaging shows multiple hepatic lesions consistent with lymphomatous involvement. Which of the following stages best describes her disease?

explanation.summary: Widespread disease involving multiple organs, such as liver and bone, is stage IV.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that staging considers the number and location of affected nodes, liver or bone involvement, and the presence of B symptoms, and that stage IV denotes widespread disease involving multiple organs with or without lymph node involvement. Hepatic and marrow involvement place this patient at stage IV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stage II is limited to two or more nodal regions on the same side of the diaphragm without organ involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beyond the B designation, stage II excludes the organ involvement demonstrated in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stage III describes nodal involvement on both sides of the diaphragm without widespread organ disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adding a B designation to stage III still does not account for the liver and bone marrow involvement.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has a cervical lymph node biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells. To determine the extent of the lymphoma and its effect on surrounding organs before treatment is selected, which of the following is the most appropriate study?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow aspiration as the sole staging study

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excisional biopsy of a second accessible lymph node

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serial measurement of serum lactate dehydrogenase

explanation.summary: FDG PET/CT defines the extent of HL and its effect on surrounding organs for staging.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that radiologic testing is crucial to stage HL and that the extent of the lymphoma and its effect on surrounding organs is determined by positron emission tomography (PET)/CT scanning. An F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan is useful for staging and can demonstrate multiple involved lymph node chains above and below the diaphragm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow sampling addresses one compartment only and is not a substitute for whole-body imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tissue diagnosis has already been made, so sampling another node adds nothing about disease extent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A chest x-ray may show a mediastinal mass but cannot define disease below the diaphragm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An elevated LDH suggests increased cell turnover but does not map anatomic extent of disease.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with early-stage Hodgkin lymphoma is counseled that she will receive both site-specific radiation therapy and chemotherapy, a combination with a higher disease-free survival rate than either alone. Which of the following best explains the rationale for combining the two modalities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemotherapy prevents fibrous band formation within the irradiated lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chemotherapy sensitizes Reed-Sternberg cells so that a lower radiation dose can be delivered

choices.label: C
choices.text: Radiation controls growth at the known tumor while chemotherapy controls occult disease outside the field

choices.label: D
choices.text: Radiation eradicates occult disease throughout the body while chemotherapy shrinks the bulky node

choices.label: E
choices.text: Radiation permits the cumulative doxorubicin dose to be reduced below the cardiotoxic threshold

explanation.summary: Radiation treats the known tumor site; chemotherapy covers occult disease beyond the radiation field.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that treatment for early stages of HL consists of radiation therapy and chemotherapy, a combination with a higher disease-free survival rate. The radiation is site or field specific, so radiation controls growth at the known tumor and chemotherapy controls any occult disease outside the radiation field.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrous bands are a histologic feature of nodular sclerosis, not a treatment complication to be prevented.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Radiosensitization is not the rationale the brick gives for combined-modality therapy in HL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the roles: radiation is field specific, while chemotherapy is the systemic component.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cardiomyopathy is a cumulative dose effect of doxorubicin, but dose sparing is not why the modalities are combined.

questions.stem: A patient with Hodgkin lymphoma is scheduled to begin ABVD. On which of the following schedules is this regimen administered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As a single dose repeated every 6 months

explanation.summary: ABVD is given every 14 days for 28 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that ABVD, a common chemotherapy regimen for HL consisting of doxorubicin (Adriamycin), bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine, is administered every 14 days for 28 days.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Single doses at 6-month intervals would not deliver effective cytotoxic therapy in HL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ABVD is not described as a continuous multiday infusion regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A weekly schedule over 21 days does not match the interval described for this regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ABVD is given intermittently rather than as daily dosing over two weeks.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman receiving ABVD for Hodgkin lymphoma develops paresthesias of the hands and feet, loss of deep tendon reflexes, weakness, and hoarseness attributed to vocal cord paralysis. The agent most likely responsible acts by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of the programmed cell death-1 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis

explanation.summary: Vinblastine inhibits microtubule function and causes dose-related peripheral and autonomic neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that vinblastine acts by inhibition of microtubule function and that dose-related peripheral neuropathy is associated with its use, causing paresthesia, loss of reflexes, weakness, and autonomic paralysis including vocal cord paralysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PD-1 blockade describes pembrolizumab, a salvage immunotherapy agent rather than a component of ABVD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fragmentation of DNA chains is the mechanism of bleomycin, whose hallmark toxicity is pulmonary fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis describes doxorubicin, which causes cumulative cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibition of DNA polymerase describes dacarbazine, which causes nausea, vomiting, and marrow suppression.

questions.stem: A patient with Hodgkin lymphoma is about to receive the component of ABVD that is a non-cell cycle-specific purine analog inhibiting DNA polymerase and leading to DNA strand breaks. Which of the following adverse effects should be anticipated as most common?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fever with hypersensitivity reactions and skin changes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nausea and vomiting in more than 90% of patients

explanation.summary: Dacarbazine inhibits DNA polymerase and causes nausea and vomiting in more than 90% of patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes dacarbazine as a non-cell cycle-specific purine analog that inhibits DNA polymerase and leads to DNA strand breaks, with common adverse effects of nausea and vomiting (>90%), bone marrow suppression, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy occurs with doxorubicin, which inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dose-related peripheral neuropathy is associated with vinblastine and its effect on microtubules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fever, hypersensitivity reactions, and skin changes are listed among the adverse effects of bleomycin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Severe pulmonary fibrosis is the characteristic toxicity of bleomycin, not of this agent.

questions.stem: Bleomycin is cytotoxic even to nondividing tumor cells. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this agent kills tumor cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody-mediated targeting of CD30 on the tumor cell surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fragmentation of DNA chains by a metal-chelating antibiotic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis in replicating cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of DNA polymerase producing DNA strand breaks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of microtubule assembly during mitosis

explanation.summary: Bleomycin is a metal-chelating chemotherapy antibiotic that fragments DNA chains.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes bleomycin as a metal-chelating chemotherapy antibiotic that has a cytotoxic effect on nondividing tumor cells by causing fragmentation of DNA chains. Its adverse effects include fever, hypersensitivity reactions, skin changes, and severe pulmonary fibrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Targeting CD30 with a monoclonal antibody describes brentuximab, a salvage agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis describes doxorubicin rather than bleomycin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibition of DNA polymerase with strand breaks describes dacarbazine, a purine analog.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microtubule inhibition is the mechanism of vinblastine and requires cells to be entering mitosis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man without symptoms has a chest radiograph obtained for a pre-employment physical, which shows a mediastinal mass. Biopsy ultimately confirms Hodgkin lymphoma. Which of the following statements about the presentation of this disease is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B symptoms are present in the majority of patients at the time of diagnosis and staging

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extranodal involvement of the liver and marrow is the usual mode of presentation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Involved lymph nodes are characteristically tender and fluctuant on palpation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most patients present with widespread stage IV disease involving distant organs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nearly half of patients have intrathoracic lymphadenopathy at the time of diagnosis

explanation.summary: Nearly half of HL patients have mediastinal lymphadenopathy on chest x-ray at diagnosis, often while asymptomatic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that HL has a variable and often vague presentation, that many patients are asymptomatic at diagnosis with disease found when the clinician feels adenopathy or sees a mediastinal mass on chest x-ray, and that nearly half of patients have evidence of mediastinal lymphadenopathy on chest x-ray at diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Approximately one-third of patients have B symptoms, so they are not present in most patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HL rarely has an extranodal presentation, in contrast to many non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lymphadenopathy of HL is characteristically nontender and hard rather than tender and fluctuant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Many patients, including this one, are found at an early stage rather than with widespread disease.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with Hodgkin lymphoma relapses after ABVD and again after salvage therapy with brentuximab. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment approach?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat the identical ABVD regimen at higher doses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Site-specific radiation to the original field alone

explanation.summary: Autologous stem cell transplantation is used for refractory or relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in cases of refractory or relapsed HL, autologous stem cell transplantation is used, and that salvage therapy regimens include targeted immunotherapy agents such as brentuximab or pembrolizumab.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Observation is not appropriate for relapsed disease, for which transplantation and salvage therapy are used.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeating a regimen the disease has already escaped is not the approach described for refractory disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radiation is site or field specific and cannot control disease that has relapsed after systemic therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is not among the treatments described for relapsed or refractory HL.

questions.stem: A patient is treated with pembrolizumab, a monoclonal antibody and immune checkpoint inhibitor targeting programmed cell death-1. Besides its use in lymphoma salvage regimens, this agent is used for unresectable or metastatic solid tumors characterized by which of the following genetic anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amplification of the HER2 receptor gene on chromosome 17

choices.label: B
choices.text: BCR-ABL fusion from the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Biallelic loss of the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mismatch repair deficiency and microsatellite instability

choices.label: E
choices.text: The t(14;18) translocation involving BCL2 and IGH

explanation.summary: Pembrolizumab is used for unresectable or metastatic solid tumors with mismatch repair deficiency and microsatellite instability.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes pembrolizumab as a monoclonal antibody and immune checkpoint inhibitor targeting programmed cell death-1 (PD-1), used to treat unresectable or metastatic solid tumors with genetic anomalies like mismatch repair deficiency and microsatellite instability. It is also listed as a salvage therapy option in HL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HER2 amplification is targeted by anti-HER2 antibodies, not by a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The BCR-ABL fusion defines chronic myeloid leukemia and is targeted by tyrosine kinase inhibitors instead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: VHL loss underlies renal cell carcinoma biology and is not the anomaly described for this agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The t(14;18) BCL2 translocation is characteristic of follicular lymphoma and is not this agent's indication.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with advanced-stage Hodgkin lymphoma asks about his likelihood of remaining free of disease 5 years after treatment. Which of the following best reflects the disease-free survival at 5 years for patients with advanced disease?

explanation.summary: Disease-free survival at 5 years ranges from 7% to 42% in advanced Hodgkin lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that the stage of the lymphoma largely determines prognosis. Prognosis is good in patients with early-stage disease, who may achieve complete remission, whereas disease-free survival at 5 years ranges from 7% to 42% in patients with advanced disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This range better reflects favorable early-stage outcomes than advanced-stage disease-free survival.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 50% to 60% figure is higher than the range given for advanced disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Advanced disease is not uniformly fatal within 5 years; a meaningful fraction remain disease free.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Survival above 95% overstates the outlook for advanced disease, which carries a substantially worse prognosis.

questions.stem: Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma carries an excellent prognosis. Which of the following best explains this favorable outlook?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the only subtype that responds to site-specific radiation therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the only subtype with no association with Epstein-Barr virus infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: It most commonly occurs in young adults and typically presents at an early stage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its fibrous bands confine the tumor and prevent contiguous lymph node spread

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its Reed-Sternberg cells lack CD30 and are therefore less aggressive

explanation.summary: Nodular sclerosis has an excellent prognosis because it affects young adults and presents early.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that nodular sclerosis is the most common type of HL in the United States (approximately 70-75% of cases) and that its prognosis is excellent because it most commonly occurs in young adults and typically presents at an early stage. Stage largely determines prognosis in HL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Radiation combined with chemotherapy is used for early-stage HL generally, not for one subtype only.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No EBV association is a feature attributed to nodular lymphocyte-predominant disease, not nodular sclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrous bands divide the node into nodules histologically but do not prevent orderly contiguous spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nodular sclerosis contains classic RS cells and lacunar variants, and classic RS cells are CD30 positive.

questions.stem: In addition to Epstein-Barr virus and human immunodeficiency virus infection, which of the following is a recognized risk factor for Hodgkin lymphoma?

explanation.summary: Cigarette smoking, obesity, and immunosuppressive disorders are additional risk factors for HL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists cigarette smoking, obesity, and immunosuppressive disorders as additional risk factors for HL beyond EBV infection, which is found in as many as 40% of cases, and HIV infection, in which most patients are also EBV positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol use is not among the risk factors identified for Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caffeine intake is not described as contributing to the development of this lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Asbestos exposure is linked to mesothelioma and lung cancer rather than to Hodgkin lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is not listed as a risk factor for developing Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man presents with fatigue, bone pain, and constipation. Laboratory studies reveal normocytic anemia, hypercalcemia, and an elevated creatinine. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike in the gamma region. A bone marrow biopsy is planned. Malignant proliferation of which of the following cell types is most likely responsible for this patient's disease?

explanation.summary: Multiple myeloma is a B-cell neoplasm characterized by malignant proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multiple myeloma is a hematopoietic B-cell neoplasm defined by malignant proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow. Plasma cells are activated B-lymphocytes whose major function is antibody (immunoglobulin) production, which explains the monoclonal spike on serum protein electrophoresis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythroid precursors are reduced, not proliferating, in myeloma because plasma cell infiltration crowds them out, causing anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Megakaryocytes are the precursors of platelets and are not the neoplastic cell in myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are mature granulocytes and are not the malignant clone in myeloma; their precursors may be suppressed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T lymphocytes are not the neoplastic cell in myeloma, which arises from the B-cell (plasma cell) lineage.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma has a peripheral blood smear that shows red blood cells stacked on one another like a roll of coins. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An intrinsic red cell membrane skeleton defect of ankyrin and spectrin proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated serum immunoglobulin prevents red cells from repelling one another

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgM cold agglutinins binding and clumping red cells at low temperature

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency causing microcytic red cells with a low ferritin level

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low serum albumin reducing plasma oncotic pressure and cell spacing

explanation.summary: Rouleaux formation in myeloma results from elevated serum immunoglobulin that reduces the normal repulsion between red blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peripheral blood smears in multiple myeloma often reveal rouleaux, stacks of red blood cells. The rouleaux arise because the elevated serum immunoglobulin prevents red blood cells from repelling each other, allowing them to aggregate into coin-like stacks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A membrane skeleton defect describes hereditary spherocytosis, not the immunoglobulin-driven rouleaux of myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cold agglutinins cause red cell clumping (agglutination) rather than the ordered stacking of rouleaux, and are not the mechanism described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency produces microcytic, hypochromic cells rather than rouleaux stacking.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Low albumin does not cause rouleaux; it is the excess immunoglobulin that reduces intercellular repulsion.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with multiple myeloma develops a rising serum creatinine. Urinalysis shows proteinaceous casts. Which of the following best describes the principal mechanism of his kidney injury?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filtered light-chain proteins damage the renal tubules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complex deposition activating glomerular complement

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polycystic replacement of the renal parenchyma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal infarction from red blood cell clumping

explanation.summary: Myeloma kidney injury is caused mostly by glomerular filtration of monoclonal light chains that damage and obstruct the tubules.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most kidney damage in myeloma is due to glomerular filtration of abnormal serum light-chain proteins (Bence-Jones protein), termed light-chain nephropathy. The filtered light chains inflame renal tubular cells when reabsorbed and obstruct tubules when they combine with glycoproteins to form casts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although myeloma patients are prone to infections including pyelonephritis, infection is not the principal cause of the kidney failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The glomerular damage in myeloma results from light-chain (amyloid) deposition, not complement activation by immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polycystic kidney disease is a separate hereditary disorder unrelated to myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Renal infarction from red cell clumping is not a recognized mechanism of myeloma kidney disease.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman is being evaluated for suspected multiple myeloma. A serum protein electrophoresis is performed. In which of the following fractions of the electrophoresis would the abnormal monoclonal (M) spike most likely appear?

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulins migrate to the gamma fraction, so the monoclonal M spike of myeloma appears there.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immunoglobulins migrate to the gamma fraction on serum protein electrophoresis. Because myeloma plasma cells are clonal, their identical monoclonal immunoglobulin molecules all migrate to the same spot, producing a tall, narrow M spike in the gamma region.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The albumin fraction contains albumin, the most abundant serum protein, not immunoglobulins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The alpha-1 fraction contains proteins such as alpha-1-antitrypsin and thyroid-binding globulin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The alpha-2 fraction contains proteins such as ceruloplasmin, alpha-2-macroglobulin, and haptoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The beta fraction contains proteins such as transferrin and beta-lipoprotein, not the monoclonal immunoglobulin.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man with multiple myeloma presents with confusion and severe bone pain. Serum calcium is markedly elevated, and skeletal x-rays show punched-out lytic lesions. Which of the following best explains the elevated serum calcium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autonomous parathyroid adenoma secreting parathyroid hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calcium released into the blood as bone is demineralized

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased renal excretion from obstructing kidney stones

choices.label: D
choices.text: Granulomatous conversion of vitamin D to its active form

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased dietary calcium absorption from excess vitamin D

explanation.summary: Hypercalcemia in myeloma results from calcium released into the blood as lytic lesions and demineralization destroy bone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myeloma causes lytic bone lesions and bone demineralization due to invading plasma cells and changes in the bone metabolic environment. As bone is broken down, calcium is released from the bone into the blood, producing hypercalcemia that, if severe, can cause confusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A parathyroid adenoma causes hyperparathyroidism, a separate cause of hypercalcemia that is not associated with lytic lesions and increased plasma cells like myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Obstructing kidney stones are not the mechanism of hypercalcemia in myeloma; the source is bone breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomatous activation of vitamin D causes hypercalcemia in conditions such as sarcoidosis, not myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D excess is not the cause; myeloma hypercalcemia arises from bone resorption by myeloma cells.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with multiple myeloma is started on bortezomib. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug kills myeloma cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding CD38 on the surface of myeloma cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cross-linking DNA strands to prevent replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibiting proteasomes so misfolded proteins accumulate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibiting thromboxane A2 to reduce platelet aggregation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lowering TNF-alpha and stimulating T cells

explanation.summary: Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor that causes toxic accumulation of misfolded proteins, inducing myeloma cell apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In myeloma the high level of immunoglobulin synthesis leads to misfolded heavy and light chains, which must be degraded by proteasomes or the cell undergoes apoptosis. Bortezomib inhibits the proteasome, preventing degradation of these misfolded proteins and thereby inducing death of the myeloma cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding CD38 is the mechanism of the monoclonal antibodies daratumumab and isatuximab, not bortezomib.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA cross-linking describes alkylating agents, not the proteasome inhibitor bortezomib.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting thromboxane A2 describes antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin and is unrelated to bortezomib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lowering TNF-alpha and stimulating T cells describes the immune modulator lenalidomide.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with multiple myeloma begins therapy with daratumumab. This monoclonal antibody exerts its antimyeloma effect by binding to which of the following targets?

explanation.summary: Daratumumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets the glycoprotein CD38, which is highly expressed on myeloma cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Daratumumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits the glycoprotein CD38. By binding CD38, it inhibits the growth of CD38-expressing tumor cells through Fc-mediated cross-linking and immune-mediated lysis. CD38 is highly expressed on myeloma cells but only in low amounts on normal cells, making it a good drug target.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The glucocorticoid receptor is engaged by corticosteroids such as dexamethasone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The IGH locus on chromosome 14 is involved in myeloma genetic translocations but is not a drug target for daratumumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The proteasome is the target of bortezomib, not the antibody daratumumab.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha is lowered by the immune modulator lenalidomide, not by daratumumab.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man has an M spike on serum protein electrophoresis and elevated serum free light chains. To firmly establish a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, a bone marrow biopsy is performed. Which of the following biopsy findings is diagnostic of multiple myeloma?

explanation.summary: A firm diagnosis of myeloma requires greater than 10% clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: A patient is considered to have multiple myeloma when the bone marrow contains at least 10% plasma cells; the normal proportion is only 2% to 3%. A bone marrow biopsy is diagnostic for myeloma if it shows greater than 10% clonal plasma cells, and the percentage can sometimes be much higher (60% to 80%) in advanced disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2% to 3% plasma cells is the normal proportion and would not indicate myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The absence of plasma cells argues against myeloma, which is defined by their proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ring sideroblasts are a feature of sideroblastic anemia and certain myelodysplastic syndromes, not myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myeloma is a plasma cell (B-cell) neoplasm; a clonal T-lymphocyte predominance points to a different disorder.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A previously healthy 62-year-old man is found to have an elevated total serum protein on routine labs. Serum electrophoresis shows a small M spike. He is asymptomatic with a normal physical exam, and a bone marrow biopsy shows 6% plasma cells with no evidence of anemia, renal failure, hypercalcemia, or bone lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Multiple myeloma with CRAB end-organ damage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary amyloidosis with cardiac and renal deposits

choices.label: D
choices.text: Smoldering myeloma with over 10% plasma cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia with an IgM spike

explanation.summary: An asymptomatic monoclonal spike with fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells and no organ damage defines MGUS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is asymptomatic and characterized by a monoclonal immunoglobulin spike with fewer than 10% plasma cells in the bone marrow and no signs of organ failure. This patient's small spike, 6% plasma cells, and absence of CRAB features fit MGUS, which carries a small but increased risk of progression to myeloma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Multiple myeloma requires greater than 10% plasma cells plus end-organ (CRAB) damage, which this patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary amyloidosis involves deposition of misfolded immunoglobulin in organs, causing organ dysfunction not seen in this asymptomatic patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Smoldering myeloma is asymptomatic but requires greater than 10% plasma cells in the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia produces an IgM spike with hyperviscosity and lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, not this asymptomatic low-level picture.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents with fatigue, blurred vision, mucosal bleeding, and headaches. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals an IgM monoclonal spike, and bone marrow shows a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Which of the following best explains his visual and neurologic symptoms?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filtered light chains obstructing the renal tubules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lytic bone lesions compressing the optic nerve

choices.label: E
choices.text: The large IgM pentamer increases blood viscosity

explanation.summary: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia causes hyperviscosity because the large IgM pentamer thickens blood and clumps red cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is characterized by an IgM spike and hyperviscosity syndrome. Because IgM is a heavy pentamer, it clumps red blood cells together and raises blood viscosity. The resulting sluggish flow and organ ischemia can cause visual loss, and there may also be abnormal bleeding and peripheral neuropathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune platelet destruction is not the mechanism; the symptoms stem from the viscous IgM pentamer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Light-chain tubular obstruction causes kidney injury, not the visual and neurologic symptoms of hyperviscosity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lytic bone lesions and the CRAB picture are features of multiple myeloma, not the hyperviscosity of Waldenstrom.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypercalcemia from bone demineralization is a myeloma complication and does not explain this IgM-driven hyperviscosity.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman with multiple myeloma has no monoclonal spike on serum protein electrophoresis, but urine protein electrophoresis reveals a monoclonal protein. This urinary monoclonal protein is composed only of light chains. Which of the following best explains why only light chains, and not intact immunoglobulins, appear in the urine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intact immunoglobulins are completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intact immunoglobulins are degraded by urinary proteases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intact immunoglobulins are too large to be filtered into the urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Light chains are actively secreted by renal tubular cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only light chains carry a negative charge that promotes filtration

explanation.summary: The urinary monoclonal protein in myeloma is always light chains because intact immunoglobulins are too large to be filtered.
explanation.whyCorrect: In some cases of myeloma there is no monoclonal spike on serum electrophoresis, but urine protein electrophoresis reveals a monoclonal protein. This urinary protein will always be light chains (Bence-Jones proteins), because the full immunoglobulins are too big to be filtered into the urine, whereas the smaller free light chains can pass into the tubule.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intact immunoglobulins do not appear in urine because their size prevents filtration, not because they are fully reabsorbed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intact immunoglobulins are excluded by size at the glomerulus rather than being degraded by urinary proteases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Light chains are filtered because of their small size, not actively secreted by tubular cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The determining factor is molecular size, not a unique negative charge on light chains.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with multiple myeloma develops an enlarged tongue, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, and worsening heart failure. Biopsy of affected tissue shows deposits of a pinkish proteinaceous material. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic granulomatous inflammation of the tongue and heart

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess monoclonal immunoglobulin misfolds into amyloid fibrils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypercalcemia calcifies soft tissues throughout the body

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron overload deposits hemosiderin in the affected organs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasma cells directly metastasize to the tongue and heart muscle

explanation.summary: In myeloma, excess immunoglobulin can misfold into amyloid fibrils that deposit in organs, causing primary amyloidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Excess immunoglobulins in myeloma can become misfolded into amyloid fibrils, a pinkish proteinaceous substance that causes primary amyloidosis when deposited in the heart, liver, kidneys, muscles, tongue, and other locations. This can produce heart failure, an enlarged tongue, and secondary carpal tunnel syndrome, matching this patient's presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Granulomatous inflammation is a different process and does not explain the amyloid deposits seen on biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypercalcemia causes confusion and other effects but does not deposit pinkish proteinaceous amyloid in these tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron overload deposits hemosiderin, which is distinct from the amyloid fibrils described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myeloma cells are largely confined to the bone marrow; the organ findings are due to amyloid deposition, not metastatic plasma cells.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A hematology practice is reviewing the demographics of its patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma. In the United States, the prevalence of this disease is less than 1% and most affected patients are middle-aged and older men. Which of the following is the approximate median age at diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Multiple myeloma is a disease of older adults, with a median age at diagnosis of approximately 70 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The median age at diagnosis of multiple myeloma is approximately 70 years, and 35% to 40% of patients are older than 75 years. Most patients are middle-aged and older men, and the prevalence in the population is less than 1%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Myeloma is essentially a disease of older adults; a median age of 25 years would be far too young.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diagnosis at 40 years would be unusual, as most patients are middle-aged or older at presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 55 years is younger than the median; only a minority of patients are diagnosed this early.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A median of 90 years is too old; only 35% to 40% of patients are even older than 75 years.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with multiple myeloma reports frequent nosebleeds and bruising after minor bumps. His bone marrow is heavily infiltrated by malignant plasma cells. Which of the following blood count abnormalities best explains his bleeding symptoms?

explanation.summary: Marrow overcrowding by plasma cells causes thrombocytopenia, which produces easy bruising and nosebleeds in myeloma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many of the presenting symptoms of myeloma are due to bone marrow infiltration and overcrowding by malignant plasma cells. Easy bruising and nosebleeds are specifically attributed to thrombocytopenia, one of the cytopenias produced when plasma cells crowd out normal hematopoiesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukocytosis is not typical of myeloma, and a high white count would not produce bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Leukopenia in myeloma leads to recurrent infection rather than bruising and nosebleeds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anemia in myeloma causes weight loss, fatigue, and weakness, not mucocutaneous bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polycythemia is not a feature of myeloma; marrow infiltration lowers rather than raises the red cell mass.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman is admitted with her third episode of pneumonia this year and develops sepsis. She has not yet begun treatment for her recently diagnosed multiple myeloma. Which of the following best explains her susceptibility to these infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amyloid infiltration of the spleen preventing bacterial opsonization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased immune function with low levels of normal immunoglobulins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rouleaux formation slowing blood flow through lymph nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urinary loss of intact immunoglobulins through damaged glomeruli

explanation.summary: Infections in myeloma reflect decreased immune function of the abnormal plasma cells and lymphocytes, with low normal immunoglobulin levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infections such as pneumonia, pyelonephritis, and sepsis are major causes of morbidity and mortality in multiple myeloma. They occur because of decreased immune function of the abnormal plasma cells and other lymphocytes, and often because of low levels of functional immunoglobulins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid deposits in the heart, liver, kidneys, muscles, and tongue cause organ dysfunction, not the immune defect underlying these infections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypercalcemia in myeloma causes confusion and polyuria; it is not the reason these patients are prone to infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rouleaux are stacked red cells on the smear and do not impair immune defense against pneumonia or sepsis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The urinary monoclonal protein in myeloma is light chains; intact immunoglobulins are too large to be filtered into the urine.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma has a monoclonal protein characterized by immunofixation. Which of the following immunoglobulin classes is most commonly produced by the malignant plasma cells in this disease?

explanation.summary: The monoclonal immunoglobulin of multiple myeloma is most often IgG, followed by IgA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the malignant plasma cells of myeloma are clonal, they all make the same immunoglobulin. That monoclonal immunoglobulin is most often IgG, with IgA being the next most common. The cells may also produce free kappa and/or lambda light chains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA is produced in myeloma, but it is less common than IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgD is not among the immunoglobulins identified as typical monoclonal products in myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE is not among the immunoglobulins identified as typical monoclonal products in myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A monoclonal IgM spike characterizes Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia rather than multiple myeloma.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is diagnosed with multiple myeloma. He asks whether anything in his past could have contributed to the disease. Which of the following is considered a possible risk factor for multiple myeloma?

explanation.summary: Risk factors for myeloma include advanced age, immunosuppression, and possibly toxins such as ionizing radiation, benzene, and herbicides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recognized risk factors for multiple myeloma are advanced age, immunosuppression, and possibly certain toxins, specifically ionizing radiation, benzene, and herbicides. Exactly how these exposures lead to myeloma is not known.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol use is not among the exposures linked to multiple myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dietary calcium does not cause myeloma; the hypercalcemia of myeloma comes from bone breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dietary iron intake is not identified as a risk factor for the development of myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Epstein-Barr virus infection is not listed among myeloma risk factors; immunosuppression in general is.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: Cytogenetic analysis of marrow plasma cells from a 68-year-old woman with multiple myeloma demonstrates a translocation. Rearrangement of which of the following loci is characteristically involved in this disease?

explanation.summary: Genetic translocations in myeloma characteristically involve the IGH locus on chromosome 14 and various proto-oncogenes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genetic translocations are common in multiple myeloma and may involve rearrangements of the IGH locus on chromosome 14 and of various proto-oncogenes such as cell cycle regulatory genes (for example, cyclins). Associated trisomies and other gene mutations occur as well, some of which change treatment choices or prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ABL locus on chromosome 9 is not the rearrangement characteristic of myeloma plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The HBB locus on chromosome 11 encodes beta-globin and is unrelated to plasma cell neoplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The PML locus on chromosome 15 is not implicated in the translocations of multiple myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 on chromosome 17 is not the locus identified as characteristically rearranged in myeloma translocations.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A bone marrow aspirate from a 74-year-old man with a monoclonal gamma spike is examined under high power. Which of the following nuclear appearances is most characteristic of the malignant cells of multiple myeloma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bilobed nucleus with coarse eosinophilic cytoplasmic granules

choices.label: B
choices.text: A horseshoe-shaped nucleus with abundant pale vacuolated cytoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: A multilobed nucleus with three to five distinct segments

choices.label: D
choices.text: A round central nucleus with a ring of iron granules around it

choices.label: E
choices.text: An eccentric nucleus with chromatin clumped in a clockface pattern

explanation.summary: Myeloma cells in the marrow typically have an eccentric nucleus, often with a clockface chromatin pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: In multiple myeloma the malignant plasma cells may appear small and benign or large and blast-like with little resemblance to normal plasma cells, but most cases show cells with an eccentric nucleus. These cells may display a clockface nucleus, in which the multiple chromatin dots suggest an old-fashioned clock face.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A bilobed nucleus with coarse eosinophilic granules describes an eosinophil, not a myeloma cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A horseshoe-shaped nucleus with abundant pale cytoplasm describes a monocyte, not a myeloma cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A multilobed segmented nucleus describes a mature neutrophil rather than a plasma cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A ring of iron granules around the nucleus describes a ring sideroblast, a feature of sideroblastic anemia.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: Complications of multiple myeloma arise from decreased normal blood cell formation in the abnormal marrow and from infiltration of organs by myeloma cells. Which of the following complications occurs in the largest proportion of patients with multiple myeloma?

explanation.summary: Anemia is the most common complication of multiple myeloma, occurring in about 73% of cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common complications of myeloma, which are important in diagnosis and follow the CRAB mnemonic, are anemia (73% of cases), bone lesions and pain (58%), kidney disease (48%), and hypercalcemia (28%). Anemia is therefore the most frequent.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone lesions and bone pain occur in about 58% of cases, less often than anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypercalcemia is the least common of the CRAB complications, occurring in about 28% of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperviscosity syndrome is a feature of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia rather than a common complication of myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Kidney disease occurs in about 48% of cases, less often than anemia.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with multiple myeloma has had a stable marrow plasma cell burden for a year, but his normocytic anemia has worsened as his serum creatinine rose to 3.4 mg/dL and his glomerular filtration rate declined. Which of the following best explains the worsening anemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased erythropoietin production by the diseased kidneys

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased red cell destruction caused by rouleaux formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron sequestration within amyloid deposits in the marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasma cells crowding out the erythroid precursors

explanation.summary: Anemia in myeloma has two mechanisms: marrow infiltration and, in those with chronic kidney disease, decreased erythropoietin production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anemia in myeloma results initially from infiltration of the bone marrow by neoplastic plasma cells, which decreases erythroid precursors. It can also be due to the anemia of chronic kidney disease, in which decreased erythropoietin production drives the anemia in patients who develop chronic kidney disease, as in this man with a rising creatinine and falling filtration rate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypercalcemia in myeloma causes confusion and polyuria; it does not suppress erythroid maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rouleaux are stacked red cells caused by elevated immunoglobulin; they are a smear finding, not a cause of red cell destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amyloid deposits in myeloma cause organ dysfunction such as heart failure and kidney disease, not marrow iron sequestration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow infiltration is the initial mechanism of anemia, but his plasma cell burden has been stable while the kidney function declined.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with multiple myeloma develops periorbital and lower extremity edema. Serum albumin is low, and urinalysis shows heavy albuminuria in the nephrotic range. Which of the following best explains this pattern of kidney injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Filtration of intact monoclonal IgG molecules across the glomerular membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypercalcemia causing calcium deposition throughout the renal medulla

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light-chain casts obstructing the renal tubules with glycoproteins

choices.label: D
