choices.text: Misfolded light chains depositing as amyloid fibrils in the glomerulus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reabsorptive injury and inflammation of the proximal tubular cells

explanation.summary: Glomerular amyloid deposition from misfolded light chains damages the filtration barrier and causes nephrotic-range albuminuria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Filtered light-chain proteins can become misfolded amyloid fibrils that deposit in the glomerulus, a process termed renal amyloidosis. The resulting glomerular damage injures the glomerular filtration barrier and causes heavy loss of albumin in the urine, producing nephrotic syndrome with hypoalbuminemia and edema.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intact immunoglobulins are too large to be filtered at the glomerulus, so they do not appear in the urine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium deposition in the medulla is not the mechanism of the heavy albumin loss described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Light-chain casts form when the proteins combine with urinary glycoproteins and obstruct tubules, causing kidney failure rather than heavy albuminuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reabsorption of filtered light chains inflames and damages tubular cells, which is a tubular rather than a glomerular injury.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with multiple myeloma undergoes a lateral skull radiograph that shows multiple sharply punched-out lesions in the calvaria. Which of the following best describes how these lesions are produced?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amyloid fibrils from light chains replacing the trabecular bone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Demineralization driven by an autonomous parathyroid adenoma in the neck

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ischemic bone necrosis caused by hyperviscous, sluggish blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osteoblastic new bone laid down around the tumor deposits in marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Osteoclast resorption of bone stimulated by the invading plasma cells

explanation.summary: Lytic lesions in myeloma are created by osteoclasts that resorb bone under the influence of invading myeloma cells, leaving a clear space.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with myeloma often develop lytic bone lesions, which are generated by osteoclasts stimulated by the invading myeloma cells. The resorbed bone leaves a clear, punched-out space on imaging and predisposes to bone pain and fractures, especially in the spinal column.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid from misfolded immunoglobulin deposits in organs such as the heart, kidney, and tongue rather than creating punched-out bone lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A parathyroid adenoma causes hyperparathyroidism, which produces hypercalcemia without the lytic lesions and plasma cell excess of myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperviscosity with organ ischemia is a feature of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, not the cause of myeloma bone lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteoblastic lesions represent new bone formation; myeloma lesions are osteolytic, which is why bone scans are a poor test.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man presents with diffuse bone pain and a serum calcium of 12.8 mg/dL. Skeletal imaging shows no lytic lesions, serum protein electrophoresis shows no monoclonal spike, bone marrow biopsy shows 3% plasma cells, and the serum parathyroid hormone level is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Hypercalcemia with bone pain also occurs in severe hyperparathyroidism, which lacks the lytic lesions and increased plasma cells of myeloma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Other causes of hypercalcemia with bone pain include severe hyperparathyroidism and severe renal failure, but these are not associated with lytic bone lesions and increased plasma cells as myeloma is. This man has no lytic lesions, a normal plasma cell percentage, no M spike, and a markedly elevated parathyroid hormone level, pointing to hyperparathyroidism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance requires a monoclonal spike, and this patient has none.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myeloma would be expected to show lytic bone lesions and greater than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells, neither of which is present.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Smoldering myeloma requires a monoclonal IgG or IgA spike with greater than 10% marrow plasma cells in an asymptomatic patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia produces an IgM spike with hyperviscosity and lymphoplasmacytic marrow involvement, not isolated hypercalcemia with a high parathyroid hormone level.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a solitary nasopharyngeal mass; biopsy shows a monoclonal plasma cell tumor. Serum protein electrophoresis shows no monoclonal spike, bone marrow biopsy shows 2% plasma cells, and she has no anemia, hypercalcemia, renal failure, or bone lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

explanation.summary: A solitary plasmacytoma in a patient without myeloma is treated with radiation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasmacytomas are plasma cell tumors that arise outside the bone marrow, most often in the head and neck, bladder, gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system, thyroid gland, breast, testes, and skin. Solitary plasmacytomas can arise in patients who do not have myeloma; these patients have no monoclonal spike, renal failure, or bone lesions, and they are treated with radiation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stem cell transplantation is reserved for multiple myeloma, which this patient does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bortezomib is used as part of combination chemotherapy for myeloma rather than as therapy for a solitary plasmacytoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The DVRd combination is a chemotherapy regimen for multiple myeloma, not for an isolated solitary plasmacytoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Solitary plasmacytomas are treated rather than simply observed; radiation is the treatment used.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: Serum protein electrophoresis performed on serum from a healthy volunteer shows a broad, gentle hill-shaped curve in the gamma region rather than a tall narrow peak. Which of the following best explains this appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Albumin overlaps the gamma region and flattens the immunoglobulin peak

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immunoglobulins in healthy serum migrate with the beta fraction instead

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal immunoglobulins are degraded by the electrical current during the run

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal immunoglobulins are polyclonal and migrate to slightly different positions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal serum contains very little immunoglobulin, which blunts the peak

explanation.summary: Normal serum immunoglobulins are polyclonal and migrate to slightly different positions, producing a gentle hill rather than a sharp M spike.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immunoglobulins migrate to the gamma fraction on serum protein electrophoresis. In normal serum they are all slightly different from one another, so they migrate to slightly different places within the gamma fraction and create a gentle hill-shaped curve. In myeloma the plasma cells are clonal, so the identical monoclonal molecules all migrate to the same spot and produce a huge narrow M spike.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin is the largest peak on a normal tracing but migrates at the opposite end of the gel from gamma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulins migrate in the gamma fraction; the beta fraction contains proteins such as transferrin and beta-lipoprotein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proteins are separated rather than degraded by electrophoresis; the applied charge only moves them through the medium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The gamma region in normal serum reflects a substantial amount of immunoglobulin; the shape reflects heterogeneity, not low quantity.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has a monoclonal spike in the gamma region on serum protein electrophoresis. Which of the following tests is used to confirm that the monoclonal protein is IgG lambda?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete blood count with peripheral smear

explanation.summary: Immunofixation separates and identifies the immunoglobulin types in blood and confirms the identity of an M spike.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serum protein electrophoresis detects the monoclonal spike, but the identity of the M spike is confirmed by immunofixation analysis, which separates and identifies the different types of immunoglobulins in the blood. It is immunofixation that establishes a pattern such as IgG lambda.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A complete blood count and smear show anemia and rouleaux but cannot identify the immunoglobulin class.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluorescence in situ hybridization is a genetic analysis of the plasma cells used to guide treatment and prognosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The serum free light chain assay measures kappa and lambda light chains and shows an excess of one, but it does not identify the heavy chain class.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urine protein electrophoresis detects a monoclonal urinary protein, which is always light chains, and does not characterize the serum heavy chain.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: Both monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and smoldering myeloma are asymptomatic plasma cell disorders with a monoclonal immunoglobulin spike. Which of the following findings distinguishes smoldering myeloma from monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A monoclonal IgM spike on serum electrophoresis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow plasma cells greater than 10%

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypercalcemia with an elevated serum creatinine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lytic bone lesions on skeletal imaging

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rouleaux formation on the peripheral blood smear

explanation.summary: Smoldering myeloma has greater than 10% marrow plasma cells, whereas monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance has fewer than 10%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both disorders are asymptomatic. Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance shows a monoclonal IgM, IgG, or IgA spike with fewer than 10% plasma cells in the bone marrow, while smoldering myeloma shows an IgG or IgA spike with greater than 10% plasma cells. Smoldering myeloma also carries a higher risk than monoclonal gammopathy of progression to multiple myeloma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An IgM spike may be seen in monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and characterizes Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia; smoldering myeloma shows IgG or IgA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypercalcemia and renal insufficiency are CRAB features of multiple myeloma; both of these disorders are asymptomatic without organ damage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lytic bone lesions indicate end-organ damage and would place the patient in the multiple myeloma category, not smoldering myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rouleaux reflect elevated serum immunoglobulin and do not separate these two asymptomatic disorders from each other.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman is evaluated for an incidental IgG kappa monoclonal spike. She feels well. Bone marrow biopsy shows 65% clonal plasma cells. Hemoglobin, serum calcium, and creatinine are all normal, and skeletal imaging shows no lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Greater than 60% clonal marrow plasma cells satisfies the diagnosis of multiple myeloma even without CRAB organ damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: A formal diagnosis of myeloma requires clonal bone marrow plasma cells of at least 10% plus one of the following: related organ failure or damage (CRAB), or the presence of greater than 60% plasma cells in the marrow, elevated serum free light chains, or MRI showing more than one lesion in bone or bone marrow. Her 65% plasma cells meets the second criterion, so she has myeloma despite the absence of CRAB features.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance requires fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells, far below her 65%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Smoldering myeloma is asymptomatic with greater than 10% plasma cells, but greater than 60% plasma cells meets a myeloma-defining criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A solitary plasmacytoma is a plasma cell tumor outside the marrow in a patient without marrow involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is characterized by an IgM spike and a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in the marrow, not an IgG spike with clonal plasma cells.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma is referred for imaging to look for bone involvement, and a nuclear medicine bone scan is suggested. Which of the following is the best reason that a bone scan is a poor choice in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot image the axial skeleton

choices.label: B
choices.text: It delivers far more radiation than positron emission tomography

choices.label: C
choices.text: It demonstrates osteoblastic lesions rather than osteolytic ones

choices.label: D
choices.text: It detects amyloid deposits rather than bone turnover

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires iodinated contrast that worsens myeloma kidney injury

explanation.summary: Myeloma lesions are osteolytic, so a bone scan, which shows osteoblastic lesions, is not the right imaging test.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bone scan demonstrates osteoblastic lesions rather than the osteolytic lesions present in multiple myeloma. Positron emission tomography, MRI, or CT scanning is done routinely instead to look for myeloma bone lesions; skeletal x-rays are less sensitive but may show lytic lesions caused by resorption from infiltrating plasma cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone scans do image the axial skeleton; the problem is the type of lesion they detect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The choice against a bone scan is based on lesion biology, not on a radiation dose comparison with positron emission tomography.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bone scans reflect bone turnover rather than amyloid, and amyloid detection is not the goal of skeletal imaging here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iodinated contrast is not the issue with a bone scan; the preferred alternatives include CT and MRI.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with fatigue, rib pain, and weight loss. Laboratory studies show normocytic anemia and hypercalcemia, and a chest radiograph shows punched-out lesions in several ribs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow biopsy with immunophenotyping and genetic analysis of plasma cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nuclear medicine bone scan of the whole skeleton with technetium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peripheral blood smear examination for rouleaux formation and plasma cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with serum free light chain analysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum parathyroid hormone and vitamin D levels with ionized calcium

explanation.summary: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with light chain analysis are the appropriate initial tests when myeloma is suspected.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a patient whose hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, anemia, and weight loss suggest myeloma, serum protein electrophoresis, urine protein electrophoresis, and serum light chain analysis are the appropriate initial tests. A bone marrow biopsy is typically performed after these studies demonstrate an M spike or light chains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow biopsy with immunophenotyping and genetic analysis is definitive, but it is done after electrophoresis demonstrates a monoclonal protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A bone scan demonstrates osteoblastic lesions, whereas myeloma lesions are osteolytic; positron emission tomography or CT is preferred for imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A peripheral smear showing rouleaux can support the diagnosis of myeloma, but it is not diagnostic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypercalcemia can be due to an increased parathyroid hormone level, but her painful lytic lesions point to myeloma as the more likely cause.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with multiple myeloma is judged eligible for transplantation. Which of the following best describes the autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation she will undergo?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donor lymphocytes are infused to generate a graft-versus-myeloma response in her marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her own stem cells are harvested, chemotherapy wipes out the marrow, and the cells are re-seeded

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marrow from an HLA-matched sibling donor is infused after her own marrow is ablated by chemotherapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasma cells are removed from her blood by repeated apheresis sessions and then discarded

choices.label: E
choices.text: Umbilical cord blood stem cells are infused without any preceding chemotherapy or radiation

explanation.summary: Autologous transplantation in myeloma uses the patient's own harvested stem cells to re-seed the marrow after intensive chemotherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond chemotherapy, the best treatment for myeloma is autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The patient's own normal stem cells are harvested from the blood, the patient is then given intensive chemotherapy to wipe out the bone marrow, and the marrow is re-seeded with the harvested and stored cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infusing donor lymphocytes is not part of the autologous transplantation described for myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infusing an HLA-matched sibling's marrow describes an allogeneic transplant, not the autologous procedure used in myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Apheresis to remove plasma cells is not how transplantation works; stem cells are collected and later returned.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cord blood stem cells are not the source, and intensive chemotherapy precedes the re-infusion in this procedure.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man scheduled for autologous stem cell transplantation for multiple myeloma asks whether the procedure will cure his disease. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It eliminates the need for any further chemotherapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is curative in most patients, unlike chemotherapy alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is curative only when performed in the first year after diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is generally avoided because it does not improve survival

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is not curative, but may increase survival and delay recurrence

explanation.summary: Unlike transplantation for some other neoplasms, transplantation for myeloma is not curative but improves survival and delays relapse.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike transplantation for other neoplasms such as primary myelofibrosis, transplantation for multiple myeloma is not curative. However, it may increase overall survival and does delay the time until the disease recurs after initial treatment. Patients will likely need to stay on low-dose chemotherapy after the transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Patients will likely need to stay on low-dose chemotherapy after the transplant, so it does not eliminate further treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transplantation is not curative in myeloma, in contrast to its role in some other hematologic neoplasms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Timing does not convert the procedure into a cure; myeloma transplantation is not curative at any point.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transplantation is recommended for eligible patients precisely because it may increase overall survival.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: An 84-year-old frail man with multiple comorbidities is diagnosed with multiple myeloma. He is evaluated for transplantation and judged ineligible because he is frail and highly likely to develop infections and other complications. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single cycle of marrow-ablative high-dose chemotherapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation from a sibling instead

choices.label: C
choices.text: Observation until the CRAB features clearly worsen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Radiation therapy directed at each individual lytic lesion

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same chemotherapy regimens, given for more cycles

explanation.summary: Transplant-ineligible patients receive the same chemotherapy regimens, but for a greater number of cycles.
explanation.whyCorrect: All myeloma patients should be evaluated for transplant eligibility; those who are frail or highly likely to suffer infections and other complications are kept on chemotherapy only. The same chemotherapy regimens are used in these patients, but more cycles are given, for example 8 cycles rather than 3.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intensive high-dose chemotherapy is used to ablate the marrow before stem cell re-infusion, which he is not receiving.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Allogeneic transplantation is not the alternative offered to a patient deemed too frail for transplantation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple myeloma with organ damage is treated rather than observed; observation applies to asymptomatic plasma cell disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radiation is the treatment for a solitary plasmacytoma, not the primary management of multiple myeloma.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with multiple myeloma who may wish to become pregnant is counseled about her DVRd regimen. Which of the following components of this regimen carries a black box warning as a teratogen?

explanation.summary: Lenalidomide carries black box warnings as a teratogen if used during pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lenalidomide is the immune-modulating component of DVRd that lowers TNF-alpha and stimulates T cells. Because of its wide range of effects it has multiple adverse effect concerns, including severe neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity, and risk of thrombosis, and it carries black box warnings as a teratogen if used during pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bortezomib is the proteasome inhibitor in the regimen and is not the component identified as a teratogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Daratumumab is the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody in DVRd; its common adverse effects are pancytopenia, fatigue, and diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dexamethasone is the corticosteroid component, which suppresses B- and T-cell function rather than acting as a teratogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isatuximab is the anti-CD38 antibody used in IsaVRd rather than DVRd, and it shares daratumumab's adverse effect profile.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for multiple myeloma has serial serum protein electrophoresis studies performed to follow his response to therapy. Which of the following best explains why this test is useful for monitoring?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serum albumin rises in proportion to the number of plasma cells killed

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amount of monoclonal immunoglobulin closely correlates with the size of the tumor mass

choices.label: C
choices.text: The immunoglobulin level reflects the degree of recovery of kidney function

choices.label: D
choices.text: The M spike disappears as soon as chemotherapy begins, regardless of response

choices.label: E
choices.text: The width of the gamma fraction predicts the likelihood of transplant eligibility

explanation.summary: The quantity of monoclonal immunoglobulin in serum or urine tracks tumor burden, so SPEP and UPEP are used to follow treatment response.
explanation.whyCorrect: During treatment, serum protein electrophoresis or urine protein electrophoresis can be used to follow the patient's response to therapy, because the amount of monoclonal immunoglobulin present in serum or urine closely correlates to the size of the tumor mass. These tests are used to guide therapy, since patients often require prolonged low-dose chemotherapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin is a separate fraction on electrophoresis and does not serve as the marker of plasma cell killing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The monoclonal immunoglobulin level tracks tumor mass; creatinine and proteinuria are the measures of kidney damage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The M spike falls in proportion to tumor response rather than disappearing immediately once treatment starts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplant eligibility is determined by frailty and the risk of infections and other complications, not by the shape of the gamma fraction.

questions.topicName: Multiple Myeloma and Other Plasma Cell Disorders

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with fatigue and a markedly elevated white blood cell count. Cytogenetic testing reveals a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 that produces a fusion gene encoding a constitutively active protein kinase. He is started on the first tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved by the FDA, which competitively inhibits ATP binding to this fusion kinase. Which of the following drugs was he most likely given?

explanation.summary: Imatinib is the first FDA-approved TKI and targets the BCR-ABL fusion kinase of the Philadelphia chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the Philadelphia chromosome results from a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, creating the BCR-ABL fusion gene, a constitutively active protein kinase that drives chronic myeloid leukemia. Imatinib, the first TKI approved by the FDA, binds the kinase site of BCR-ABL and competitively inhibits ATP binding, blocking downstream phosphorylation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor (modulator of protein degradation), not a BCR-ABL inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating chemotherapeutic agent and does not target the BCR-ABL kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody against CD20, not a TKI targeting BCR-ABL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody directed against a tumor cell-surface receptor, not the intracellular BCR-ABL kinase.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A pharmacology instructor explains that tyrosine kinase inhibitors and monoclonal antibodies block receptor tyrosine kinase signaling by two different mechanisms. Which of the following best describes how a tyrosine kinase inhibitor works?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It alkylates DNA to prevent replication

choices.label: B
choices.text: It cross-links surface receptors to trigger complement-mediated lysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits the 26S proteasome to prevent protein degradation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a small molecule that competitively inhibits ATP binding

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an antibody that binds the extracellular ligand-binding domain of the receptor

explanation.summary: TKIs are small molecules that competitively inhibit ATP binding at the intracellular kinase domain, preventing receptor phosphorylation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that TKIs are not antibodies but small molecules that chemically block receptor function at its intracellular domain. They competitively inhibit ATP binding, preventing phosphorylation of the receptor and interrupting the signaling pathway. The mnemonic notes that tyrosine kinase inhibitors attach on the inside domain of the receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alkylating DNA describes classic cytotoxic chemotherapy, not targeted TKI action.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement-mediated lysis from cross-linking surface receptors is an antibody-mediated effect, not the mechanism of a small-molecule TKI.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting the 26S proteasome is the mechanism of bortezomib, not a TKI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Binding the extracellular ligand-binding domain describes monoclonal antibodies, which act on the outside of the receptor.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A student compares small-molecule inhibitors with monoclonal antibodies used in cancer therapy. Compared with small molecules, which of the following is a characteristic feature of monoclonal antibodies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They act on multiple targets with a broad spectrum of effects

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are taken orally and undergo cytochrome P450 metabolism

choices.label: C
choices.text: They have half-lives of 12 to 24 hours requiring frequent dosing

choices.label: D
choices.text: They readily enter the cell to inhibit intracellular kinase pathways

choices.label: E
choices.text: They target proteins on the cell surface

explanation.summary: Monoclonal antibodies target cell-surface proteins, are highly specific for a single antigen, and are given parenterally with long half-lives.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's comparison table states that monoclonal antibodies target proteins on the cell surface, are generally specific for a single antigen, are more selective with specific effects, are given parenterally, and have half-lives of days to weeks. Small molecules, by contrast, target mostly intracellular proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Multiple targets and a broad spectrum of effects characterize small molecules, whereas antibodies have specific effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oral administration with CYP metabolism is a property of small molecules, not monoclonal antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Half-lives of 12 to 24 hours describe small molecules; antibodies have half-lives of days to weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Entering the cell to inhibit intracellular pathways describes small molecules; antibodies act on cell-surface targets.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A medical student is taught that the syllables in a monoclonal antibody's name reveal its target and its source. Based on the components of its name, the antibody trastuzumab targets which of the following, and from what source is it derived?

explanation.summary: In trastuzumab, -tu- denotes a tumor target and -zu- denotes a humanized source.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's nomenclature table shows that the syllable -t- or -tu- indicates a tumor target and the syllable -zu- indicates a humanized source. Trastuzumab contains both -tu- and -zu-, so by its name it targets a tumor and is a humanized antibody.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A virus target is denoted by -v- or -vi- and a chimeric source by -xi-, neither of which matches trastuzumab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An interleukin target is -k- or -ki- and a rat source is -a-, which do not appear in trastuzumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A bone target is -o- or -os-, which is not present in trastuzumab even though it is humanized.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A cardiovascular target is -c- or -ci- and a human source is -u-, not the syllables in trastuzumab.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is treated with a monoclonal antibody directed against a glycosylated tetra-transmembrane phosphoprotein widely expressed on developing B-cells and B-cell malignancies. The drug reduces B-cell proliferation and induces complement activation, macrophage phagocytosis, and natural killer cell attack. Which of the following is the target of this antibody?

explanation.summary: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody against the B-cell surface protein CD20.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes rituximab as a monoclonal antibody against cell-surface protein CD20, a glycosylated tetra-transmembrane phosphoprotein expressed on developing B-cells and many B-cell malignancies. Binding CD20 reduces B-cell proliferation, promotes apoptosis, and induces complement activation, phagocytosis by macrophages, and cytotoxic attack by natural killer cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCR-ABL is an intracellular fusion kinase targeted by TKIs such as imatinib, not by an anti-B-cell antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase overactive in many cancers but is not the B-cell protein described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NF-kB is an intracellular transcription factor affected by bortezomib, not a cell-surface antibody target.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 26S proteasome is the target of bortezomib, a small molecule, not a monoclonal antibody.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman received rituximab as part of treatment for B-cell lymphoma. Two years later, routine blood tests show newly elevated liver enzymes, and her HBsAg, previously negative, is now positive. Which of the following adverse effects of rituximab best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Rituximab can reactivate hepatitis B, sometimes up to 24 months after therapy, requiring pre-treatment screening and monitoring.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that rituximab may reactivate hepatitis B virus and other viral infections, potentially leading to fulminant hepatitis. Patients should be screened for prior hepatitis B before starting therapy and monitored for reactivation for up to 24 months after completing treatment, which fits this delayed conversion to a positive hepatitis B surface antigen with rising liver enzymes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody and does not alkylate hepatocyte DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluid retention is an adverse effect of imatinib, not the cause of hepatitis B reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: QT prolongation and pleural effusion are adverse effects of dasatinib, not rituximab.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenia from proteasome inhibition is an effect of bortezomib and does not explain a positive hepatitis B antigen.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with multiple myeloma is treated with bortezomib. The drug binds the 26S proteasome and prevents the degradation of IkB. Which of the following best explains how this action produces an anticancer effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of the extracellular ligand-binding domain of a surface receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive inhibition of ATP binding at the BCR-ABL kinase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross-linking of CD20 to recruit natural killer cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased NF-kB entry into the nucleus enhances transcription of survival genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retained IkB sequesters NF-kB in the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: By inhibiting the proteasome, bortezomib prevents IkB degradation, so NF-kB stays sequestered in the cytoplasm and less enters the nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that NF-kB is normally sequestered in the cytoplasm by IkB. The proteasome degrades IkB, freeing NF-kB to enter the nucleus and transcribe factors that keep the cell alive. Bortezomib inhibits the proteasome and prevents IkB degradation, so less NF-kB reaches the nucleus, decreasing survival signaling and favoring apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking the extracellular ligand-binding domain describes monoclonal antibodies, not a proteasome inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Competitive inhibition of ATP binding at BCR-ABL describes imatinib, not bortezomib.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cross-linking CD20 to recruit natural killer cells describes rituximab, not bortezomib.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bortezomib decreases, rather than increases, NF-kB entry into the nucleus.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with multiple myeloma has been receiving bortezomib. He now reports numbness and tingling in his feet, and laboratory studies show a low platelet count. These are the two most common adverse effects of this agent, occurring in about 28% and 12% of patients. Which of the following pairs of adverse effects is he most likely experiencing?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infusion reactions and hepatitis B reactivation

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia and peripheral neuropathy are the most common adverse effects of bortezomib.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that thrombocytopenia and neuropathy are the most common adverse effects of bortezomib, occurring in about 28% and 12% of patients respectively. Dose reduction or discontinuation decreases the neuropathic symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fluid retention and muscle cramps are adverse effects of imatinib, not bortezomib.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Infusion reactions and hepatitis B reactivation are adverse effects of rituximab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pleural effusion and QT prolongation are adverse effects of dasatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polycythemia and hyperviscosity are not adverse effects of bortezomib described in the brick.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A student is learning drug-name suffixes to predict a targeted agent's class. A drug whose name ends in -zomib belongs to which of the following classes?

explanation.summary: The -zomib suffix identifies drugs that inhibit proteasomal degradation, such as bortezomib.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the -zomib suffix is used for drugs that inhibit proteasome degradation. Bortezomib is the example given, a modulator of protein degradation that inhibits the 26S proteasome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide are cytotoxic chemotherapies without the -zomib suffix.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antimetabolites are a class of cytotoxic drugs and are not designated by the -zomib suffix.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monoclonal antibodies carry the suffix -mab, not -zomib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors carry the suffix -tinib, not -zomib.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia initially responded to imatinib but has relapsed because of a mutation in the BCR-ABL kinase. He is switched to a second tyrosine kinase inhibitor that binds both the active and inactive conformations of the Abl kinase domain and can overcome imatinib resistance. Which of the following adverse effects is most characteristic of this second agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody infusion reactions with fever and rigors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aquagenic pruritus after warm showers or bathing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatitis B reactivation with rising transaminases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombocytopenia in about 28% of treated patients

explanation.summary: Dasatinib binds both active and inactive Abl conformations to overcome imatinib resistance and can cause QT prolongation and pleural effusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes dasatinib as a TKI that inhibits BCR-ABL and, unlike imatinib, binds both the active and inactive conformations of the Abl kinase domain, allowing it to overcome imatinib resistance from BCR-ABL kinase mutations. Its characteristic adverse effects are QT-interval prolongation and pleural effusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infusion reactions are typical of monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab, not of a small-molecule TKI.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aquagenic pruritus is a feature of polycythemia vera, not an adverse effect of dasatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatitis B reactivation is characteristic of rituximab, not dasatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenia in about 28% of patients describes bortezomib.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A researcher studies a receptor tyrosine kinase that is overactive in most cancers. After the ligand binds and the receptor dimerizes, its tyrosines are autophosphorylated, creating docking sites that activate the PI3K-AKT and Ras-ERK pathways. Which of the following pairs of effects best describes the downstream consequence of this signaling in cancer cells?

explanation.summary: RTK signaling through PI3K-AKT decreases apoptosis and through Ras-ERK increases proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that once the phosphorylated receptor initiates its two main pathways, the PI3K-AKT pathway leads to decreased apoptosis and the Ras-ERK pathway leads to increased proliferation. These pathways are overactive in most cancers, producing the increased proliferation and decreased apoptosis characteristic of cancer cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Decreased apoptosis is correct, but RTK signaling increases, not decreases, proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased apoptosis and decreased proliferation is the opposite of what overactive RTK signaling produces.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement activation and phagocytosis are effects of monoclonal antibody binding, not RTK downstream signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased proteasomal degradation of IkB relates to NF-kB signaling and bortezomib, not the RTK pathways described.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia is started on imatinib. At follow-up she reports new swelling of both legs and some shortness of breath. Which of the following is the most common adverse effect of imatinib responsible for these findings?

explanation.summary: Fluid retention is a common adverse effect of imatinib and can cause leg swelling and shortness of breath.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that fluid retention is a common side effect of imatinib that can cause leg swelling and shortness of breath. Elevated liver function enzymes, GI distress, muscle cramps, and rash (which can progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome) may also occur.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatitis B reactivation is an adverse effect of rituximab, not imatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infusion reactions occur with monoclonal antibodies such as rituximab, not with the oral small molecule imatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral neuropathy is a characteristic adverse effect of bortezomib, not the most common effect of imatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pleural effusion is associated with dasatinib rather than imatinib.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: Bone marrow karyotyping in a 38-year-old woman with chronic myelocytic leukemia shows a shortened chromosome 22. The abnormality creates a fusion gene in which the tyrosine kinase ABL (Abelson murine leukemia viral oncogene homolog) is joined to a partner gene, and the product is a constitutively active protein kinase. To which of the following is ABL fused?

explanation.summary: The Philadelphia chromosome is a fusion of the tyrosine kinase ABL with the breakpoint cluster region (BCR).
explanation.whyCorrect: The short Philadelphia chromosome (Ph1) is a fusion between the tyrosine kinase ABL, the Abelson murine leukemia viral oncogene homolog, and the breakpoint cluster region (BCR). The resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene is a constitutively active protein kinase that produces continuous, uncontrollable cell division and drives the malignant phenotype of chronic myelocytic leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD20 is a B-cell surface protein targeted by rituximab and is not part of a fusion kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase overactive in many cancers, but it is not a partner in the Philadelphia chromosome fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NF-kB is an intracellular transcription factor regulated by IkB and the proteasome, not a fusion partner of ABL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF is another receptor tyrosine kinase example and is unrelated to the 9;22 fusion gene.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A student is learning to recognize targeted cancer agents from their generic names, since an entire drug class may share one ending. Which of the following name endings identifies a tyrosine kinase inhibitor?

explanation.summary: All tyrosine kinase inhibitors end in -tinib.
explanation.whyCorrect: An easy method to recall tyrosine kinase inhibitors is that they all end in -tinib, as in imatinib, dasatinib, ponatinib, erlotinib, and crizotinib. These are small molecules that chemically block receptor function at the intracellular domain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The suffix -mab is typically used for monoclonal antibodies, whose prefixes are variable.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The syllable -xi- within an antibody name indicates a chimeric source, not a kinase inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The suffix -zomib designates drugs that inhibit proteasome degradation, such as bortezomib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The syllable -zu- within an antibody name indicates a humanized source, not a kinase inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: Monoclonal antibodies are not limited to oncology practice. In which of the following additional settings are monoclonal antibodies used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chelation of excess iron in overload states

choices.label: B
choices.text: Induction of general anesthesia before surgery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replacement of deficient plasma clotting factors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Treatment of rheumatoid diseases and antiviral protocols

explanation.summary: Monoclonal antibodies are used outside cancer therapy, including for rheumatoid diseases and some antiviral protocols.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monoclonal antibodies are developed in the laboratory to attach to a specific cell protein, and this specificity is exploited well beyond oncology. Examples of non-oncologic use include treatment of rheumatoid diseases and some antiviral protocols. These agents can still be recognized by name because the suffix is typically -mab even though the prefix varies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron overload is managed by chelation, which is unrelated to antibody-based targeting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anesthetic induction has nothing to do with antibodies directed at specific cell proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clotting factor deficiency is corrected with factor replacement, not with antibodies against a cell protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reversing warfarin anticoagulation is not among the uses of monoclonal antibodies described here.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A new monoclonal antibody is directed against an interleukin and is derived from a rat. Which of the following pairs of syllables would be expected within its generic name?

explanation.summary: In antibody nomenclature, -k- or -ki- marks an interleukin target and -a- marks a rat source.
explanation.whyCorrect: The syllables of a monoclonal antibody name reveal both its target and its source, which in turn helps predict adverse reactions and kinetics. An interleukin target is designated -k- or -ki-, and a rat source is designated -a-, so an anti-interleukin antibody of rat origin would carry both syllables.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The syllable -c- or -ci- designates a cardiovascular target and -xi- a chimeric source.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The syllable -l- or -li- designates an immunomodulating target and -u- a human source, neither of which matches an anti-interleukin rat antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The syllable -o- or -os- designates a bone target and -xi- a chimeric source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The syllable -t- or -tu- designates a tumor target and -zu- a humanized source.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A patient treated with an intravenous monoclonal antibody given every few weeks is switched to an oral small-molecule inhibitor that must be taken every day. Which of the following properties of small molecules accounts for the more frequent administration?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Targeting of proteins on the cell surface

explanation.summary: Small molecules have half-lives of 12 to 24 hours and therefore require more frequent dosing than monoclonal antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Small molecules are given orally, undergo cytochrome P450 metabolism, and have half-lives of 12 to 24 hours, which requires more frequent administration. Monoclonal antibodies are given parenterally and have half-lives of days to weeks, so they are administered less frequently.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A half-life of days to weeks describes monoclonal antibodies and would allow less frequent dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parenteral administration is the route used for monoclonal antibodies; the small molecule here is oral.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Specificity for a single antigen characterizes monoclonal antibodies, and it does not determine dosing interval.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cell-surface targets belong to monoclonal antibodies, whereas small molecules act mostly on intracellular targets.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A patient receiving a tyrosine kinase inhibitor develops adverse effects attributed to inhibition of kinases other than the one the drug was designed to block. Which of the following properties of tyrosine kinase inhibitors best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They activate complement at the cell surface after binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are generally specific for a single antigen

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are given parenterally and remain outside the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: They inhibit the 26S proteasome along with the kinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: They may also interact with unintended tyrosine kinase receptors

explanation.summary: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are not highly specific and may hit receptors other than the intended target, increasing adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are not nearly as specific in their targeting as monoclonal antibodies. They may interact with tyrosine kinase receptors other than the ones they were originally intended to target, and this off-target activity can increase adverse effects. Small molecules in general have multiple targets and a broad spectrum of effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement activation follows antibody binding at the cell surface and is not a property of a small-molecule kinase inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Specificity for a single antigen describes monoclonal antibodies and would reduce, not cause, off-target effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are small molecules given orally that enter the cell to reach the intracellular kinase domain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteasome inhibition is the mechanism of bortezomib and is not an off-target action of tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A researcher wants to study a cell-surface protein that initiates intracellular signaling by forming a dimer and becoming phosphorylated when its ligand binds. Which of the following is an example of such a protein?

explanation.summary: EGFR, VEGF, and the hepatocyte growth factor receptor are examples of tyrosine kinase receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tyrosine kinase receptors are cell-surface receptors that initiate intracellular signaling pathways; examples include the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), VEGF, and the hepatocyte growth factor receptor. They are transmembrane proteins with an extracellular portion and an intracellular domain whose two parts join to form a dimer when ligand binds, inducing kinase activity and receptor phosphorylation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The 26S proteasome is an intracellular protein complex that degrades proteins, not a surface receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD20 is a tetra-transmembrane phosphoprotein on B-cells; its normal ligand is not even known, and it is not a tyrosine kinase receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IkB is a cytoplasmic molecule that sequesters NF-kB and is not a membrane receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NF-kB is a transcription factor acting in the nucleus, not a ligand-binding surface receptor.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: In a cultured tumor cell, a ligand binds a tyrosine kinase receptor, the two receptor halves join to form a dimer, kinase activity is stimulated, and the receptor's tyrosines become phosphorylated. Which of the following occurs next in this sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ATP binding to the kinase domain is competitively blocked by a drug

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement is activated at the tumor cell surface membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intracellular proteins bind to the phospho-tyrosine docking sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proteasome degrades IkB in the cytoplasm of the cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: The receptor separates into two inactive monomer halves

explanation.summary: Phosphorylated tyrosines serve as docking sites where intracellular proteins bind to propagate the signal.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the signal dimer binds and kinase activity is stimulated, the receptor's tyrosines are phosphorylated. Intracellular proteins then bind to these phospho-tyrosine docking sites, and the activated receptor initiates the PI3K-AKT and Ras-ERK pathways.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Competitive blockade of ATP binding is what a tyrosine kinase inhibitor drug does; it is not a physiologic next step.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement activation is an effect of monoclonal antibody binding, not a step in receptor tyrosine kinase activation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteasomal degradation of IkB belongs to the NF-kB pathway targeted by bortezomib, not to the receptor phosphorylation cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dimerization and phosphorylation activate the receptor; the receptor does not revert to inactive monomers at this step.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A monoclonal antibody interrupts signaling through a receptor tyrosine kinase even though it never attaches to the receptor protein itself. Which of the following explains how signaling is blocked?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It attaches to the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds the circulating ligand before it reaches the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: It competitively inhibits ATP binding at the kinase domain

choices.label: D
choices.text: It crosses the membrane and inhibits Ras-ERK signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: It prevents proteasomal degradation of IkB

explanation.summary: A monoclonal antibody can block signaling by binding either the cell-surface receptor or its ligand.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monoclonal antibodies can target a cell surface receptor or the ligand of that receptor, and either way cell signaling is blocked. Because these antibodies are highly specific for a particular receptor or ligand, crossover reactions with nontargeted receptors or ligands are uncommon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies act at the outside of the receptor; the intracellular kinase domain is where tyrosine kinase inhibitors attach.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Competitive inhibition of ATP binding is the mechanism of a small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies do not enter the cell, so they cannot act directly on the intracellular Ras-ERK pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Preventing IkB degradation is the mechanism of bortezomib at the proteasome, not of an antibody.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: Targeted agents may act at a cell-surface receptor, at an intermediate step further along a signaling pathway, or at the proteasome. Which of the following drugs acts on an intermediate step of a cell signaling pathway?

explanation.summary: Vemurafenib targets an intermediate step on a cell signaling pathway rather than the receptor itself or the proteasome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the cancer cell targets and the drugs designed to block them, tyrosine kinase cell signaling receptors are targeted by crizotinib, erlotinib, imatinib, panitumumab, and trastuzumab; intermediate steps on cell signaling pathways are targeted by vemurafenib; and proteasomes are targeted by bortezomib.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bortezomib targets the proteasome, a protein degradation complex rather than a signaling intermediate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erlotinib is listed among the agents that target tyrosine kinase cell signaling receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Panitumumab also acts at the level of a tyrosine kinase cell signaling receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trastuzumab is an antibody against a tyrosine kinase cell signaling receptor, not an intermediate pathway step.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: An oncologist plans to add a targeted inhibitor to a patient's existing cytotoxic chemotherapy in order to enhance its effectiveness. Which of the following is a class of cytotoxic cancer drugs that can be combined with targeted therapy in this way?

explanation.summary: Targeted therapies can be combined with cytotoxic cancer drugs such as alkylating agents and antimetabolites to enhance effectiveness.
explanation.whyCorrect: An increasing number of drugs are designed to inhibit the oncogenic pathways responsible for uncontrolled cancer cell growth and survival, and these targeted therapies can be combined with cytotoxic cancer drugs such as alkylating agents and antimetabolites to enhance their effectiveness. Cyclophosphamide, given as part of the lymphoma regimen in this brick's case, is such an alkylating agent.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antiviral agents treat viral infection, such as reactivated hepatitis B, and have no cytotoxic antitumor role here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monoclonal antibodies are targeted agents directed at a specific cell-surface protein rather than cytotoxic chemotherapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteasome inhibitors such as bortezomib are themselves targeted agents, not the cytotoxic class being combined with them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are targeted small molecules, so pairing one with another does not describe this combination.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: Drug development in oncology is directed at the primary pathways by which cancers grow. Besides oncogenic kinase signaling and evasion of the host immune response, which of the following is one of these primary pathways?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phagocytosis of tumor cells by macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of NF-kB by IkB in the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: The primary pathways of cancer growth are oncogenic kinase signaling, tumor microenvironment reactions (angiogenesis), and evasion of host immune surveillance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The primary pathways of cancer growth are oncogenic signaling pathways (kinase pathways), reactions of the tumor microenvironment (angiogenesis), and evading the host immune response or surveillance. This is why cancer cells can also be attacked by promoting an immune system attack or by depriving the tumor of oxygen and blood supply.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity is a host immune mechanism recruited by therapy, not a pathway of tumor growth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Competitive inhibition of ATP binding is how a drug blocks a kinase, not a pathway the tumor uses to grow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophage phagocytosis destroys tumor cells and therefore opposes rather than drives cancer growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sequestration of NF-kB by IkB is a normal regulatory step within a cell, not one of the primary growth pathways of cancer.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man taking imatinib for chronic myelocytic leukemia develops a widespread rash. Which of the following is the most important concern about this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It indicates hepatitis B reactivation and requires antiviral therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It may progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome and require intervention

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reflects fluid retention and requires diuresis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It represents an infusion reaction and requires a slower infusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: It signals thrombocytopenia and requires platelet transfusion

explanation.summary: Rash from imatinib may require intervention because it can develop into Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Along with fluid retention, elevation of liver function test enzymes, GI distress, and muscle cramps, imatinib can cause a rash. Rash developing from imatinib might require intervention because it could progress to Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatitis B reactivation is an adverse effect of rituximab and presents with rising liver enzymes rather than as a rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fluid retention from imatinib causes leg swelling and shortness of breath, not a widespread rash.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infusion reactions with urticaria occur with monoclonal antibodies given parenterally; imatinib is an oral small molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenia is the most common adverse effect of bortezomib and is not the explanation for an imatinib rash.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: After a monoclonal antibody attaches to a protein on a cancer cell, it contributes to killing the cell beyond simply blocking signal transduction. Which of the following is one of these other effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It attracts additional chemotherapeutic agents to the tumor cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: It competitively displaces ATP from the intracellular kinase domain

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases hepatic CYP metabolism of the cytotoxic drugs given

choices.label: D
choices.text: It induces dimerization of the receptor it binds and activates it

choices.label: E
choices.text: It prevents proteasomal degradation of IkB at the 26S proteasome

explanation.summary: Once bound, monoclonal antibodies can attract other substances such as additional chemotherapeutic agents to the cancer cell and stimulate host immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: After attachment, monoclonal antibodies can attract other substances to the cancer cell to assist in its destruction, such as additional chemotherapeutic agents. They can also stimulate inherent host cell immunity, for example antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Displacing ATP at the kinase domain is the mechanism of a small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor acting inside the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytochrome P450 metabolism applies to orally administered small molecules and is not an antibody effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ligand binding induces receptor dimerization and activation; an antibody blocks signaling rather than promoting it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Preventing IkB degradation describes bortezomib at the 26S proteasome, not an antibody bound at the cell surface.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A researcher characterizes the CD20 protein that rituximab binds. Which of the following best describes the normal biology of this protein?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It degrades inactive or old intracellular proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a transcription factor held in the cytoplasm by IkB

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a tyrosine kinase that autophosphorylates after ligand binding

choices.label: D
choices.text: It promotes proliferation of B-cells, but its normal ligand is unknown

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its ligand is a growth factor that triggers receptor dimerization

explanation.summary: CD20 normally promotes B-cell proliferation, but its physiologic ligand has not been identified.
explanation.whyCorrect: CD20 is a glycosylated tetra-transmembrane phosphoprotein with intracellular N- and C-terminal regions and a small and a large extracellular loop, widely expressed on developing B-cells and many B-cell malignancies. The protein normally functions to promote proliferation of B-cells, but its normal ligand is not known.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Degrading inactive or old proteins is the role of the proteasome, the target of bortezomib.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A transcription factor sequestered by IkB describes NF-kB, an intracellular molecule rather than a surface phosphoprotein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD20 is not a kinase and does not autophosphorylate; that describes a receptor tyrosine kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Growth factor ligands that trigger dimerization belong to tyrosine kinase receptors such as EGFR, not CD20.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: Rituximab bound to CD20 on a malignant B-cell activates the complement cascade. Which of the following directly produces lysis of the B-cell through this pathway?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytotoxic attack by natural killer cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Induction of apoptosis within the B-cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phagocytosis of the B-cell by macrophages

explanation.summary: In complement-dependent cytotoxicity, the complement cascade forms the membrane attack complex that lyses the antibody-coated B-cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Binding of CD20 by rituximab induces activation of complement, and in complement-dependent cytotoxicity the cascade generates the membrane attack complex on the B-cell, leading to cell death. This is one of three routes to killing shown for rituximab, alongside antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Natural killer cell attack is part of antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, a separate mechanism from the complement cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Apoptosis is promoted by CD20 binding itself and represents a third, distinct route to cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocyte-mediated killing is another form of antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity rather than a complement product.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophage phagocytosis of the antibody-coated B-cell is also antibody-dependent cell-mediated killing, not complement-mediated lysis.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops fever, chills, throat itching, urticaria, and mild hypotension shortly after her first rituximab infusion is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halve the dose and recheck liver function enzymes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Permanently discontinue the drug and begin an antiviral

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slow the rate of administration and give an antihistamine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfuse platelets and repeat a complete blood count

explanation.summary: Rituximab infusion reactions are managed with reduced infusion rates and antihistamines.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rituximab is associated with potentially life-threatening infusion reactions consisting of fever, chills, throat itching, urticaria, and mild hypotension. These reactions can be managed with reduced infusion rates and antihistamines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diuresis treats the fluid retention seen with imatinib, not urticaria and hypotension during an antibody infusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rechecking liver enzymes addresses hepatic toxicity and does not treat the acute reaction occurring during the infusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antivirals address reactivated hepatitis B, a delayed complication, and permanent discontinuation is not required for a manageable infusion reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion addresses thrombocytopenia, which is an adverse effect of bortezomib rather than an infusion reaction.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A patient who has completed rituximab therapy is monitored for reactivation of latent viral infections. Besides hepatitis B virus, which of the following viruses may also reactivate?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Influenza A virus and respiratory syncytial virus

explanation.summary: Rituximab may reactivate hepatitis B and other viruses, including cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and West Nile virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rituximab may reactivate hepatitis B virus and other viral infections, with cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and West Nile virus given as examples. Hepatitis B reactivation can potentially lead to fulminant hepatitis, so patients are screened beforehand and monitored afterward.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatitis A and rotavirus are acute enteric infections rather than latent viruses that reactivate after rituximab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Human papillomavirus and parvovirus B19 are not among the infections named as reactivating with this therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Influenza A and respiratory syncytial virus cause acute respiratory infection and are not listed as reactivating viruses here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rubella and mumps are not among the viral infections described as reactivating with rituximab.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a B-cell lymphoma is scheduled to begin rituximab. Which of the following is the most appropriate step before starting therapy?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Obtain an ECG to measure the QT interval

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screen for prior hepatitis B infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Test for a mutation in the BCR-ABL kinase

explanation.summary: Patients should be screened for prior hepatitis B infection before rituximab and monitored for reactivation for up to 24 months afterward.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because rituximab may reactivate hepatitis B virus and lead to fulminant hepatitis, patients should be screened for prior hepatitis B infection before starting therapy. After treatment is completed, they should be monitored for signs of reactivation for up to 24 months, which is why routine blood work including liver function tests is performed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A baseline platelet count anticipates the thrombocytopenia seen with bortezomib rather than a rituximab toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: QT-interval prolongation is an adverse effect of dasatinib, not a concern that governs rituximab therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nerve conduction studies would track the peripheral neuropathy associated with bortezomib, not with rituximab.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BCR-ABL kinase mutations cause imatinib resistance in chronic myelocytic leukemia and are unrelated to a CD20-directed antibody.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: Bortezomib, a modulator of protein degradation, is used in the treatment of multiple myeloma. For which of the following additional malignancies is it used?

explanation.summary: Bortezomib is used to treat multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bortezomib is used in the treatment of multiple myeloma and mantle cell lymphoma. It inhibits the proteasome, an intracellular protein complex essential for the breakdown of cellular proteins, and it also prevents adhesion of multiple myeloma cells to bone marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic myelocytic leukemia is driven by BCR-ABL and is treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib and dasatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the B-cell malignancy treated with regimens containing rituximab in this brick's case.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatocellular carcinoma is not among the malignancies for which bortezomib is indicated here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hodgkin lymphoma is not listed as an indication for bortezomib.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: Beyond inhibiting the proteasome, bortezomib has additional antitumor actions in multiple myeloma. Which of the following is one of them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It activates complement on the malignant cell surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks the extracellular loop of CD20

choices.label: C
choices.text: It competitively inhibits ATP binding at BCR-ABL

choices.label: D
choices.text: It increases NF-kB entry into the nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: It prevents adhesion of the malignant plasma cells to bone marrow

explanation.summary: Bortezomib prevents adhesion of multiple myeloma cells to bone marrow and sensitizes tumor cells to other cytotoxic drugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to inhibiting the 26S proteasome, bortezomib promotes the sensitivity of tumor cells to other cytotoxic drugs such as the anthracyclines, and it prevents adhesion of multiple myeloma cells to bone marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement activation at the cell surface follows monoclonal antibody binding, as with rituximab on CD20.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding the extracellular loop of CD20 describes rituximab, an antibody, not a proteasome inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Competitive inhibition of ATP binding at BCR-ABL is the mechanism of imatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bortezomib decreases NF-kB entry into the nucleus by preventing degradation of IkB.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: In a myeloma cell treated with bortezomib, less NF-kB reaches the nucleus. Which of the following combinations of effects results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased angiogenesis, decreased proliferation, increased apoptosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased angiogenesis, increased proliferation, increased apoptosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased angiogenesis, decreased proliferation, decreased apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased angiogenesis, increased proliferation, decreased apoptosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unchanged angiogenesis, decreased proliferation, decreased apoptosis

explanation.summary: Decreasing NF-kB lowers angiogenesis and proliferation while increasing apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: NF-kB is a transcription factor critical to the initiation of the cell response to cell damage and to promotion of cell survival; without it, the cell is unable to grow or to survive apoptosis. When bortezomib inhibits the proteasome, IkB is not degraded and less NF-kB enters the nucleus, resulting in decreased angiogenesis, decreased proliferation, and increased apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Proliferation falls rather than rises when NF-kB-driven survival and growth signaling is lost.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Angiogenesis decreases and apoptosis increases with less nuclear NF-kB, so both of these are reversed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This is the profile of a cell with abundant nuclear NF-kB, the opposite of what proteasome inhibition produces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Angiogenesis does decrease, and apoptosis increases rather than decreases, when NF-kB signaling is reduced.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: The proteasome inhibited by bortezomib performs an essential housekeeping role in normal cells. Which of the following best describes that role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Degrading old or inactive proteins and cutting molecules to make active ones

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phosphorylating tyrosine residues on activated surface receptors of the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Presenting processed tumor antigens to circulating natural killer cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transcribing the genes that promote cell survival inside the nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transporting NF-kB from the cytoplasm into the nucleus of the cell

explanation.summary: The proteasome breaks down proteins, both to clear old or inactive molecules and to cut molecules into new active ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: The proteasome is a crucial intracellular protein complex essential for the breakdown of proteins in the cell, either to get rid of inactive or old molecules or to cut a molecule and create a new active molecule. One such cut is the degradation of IkB, which frees NF-kB to enter the nucleus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Phosphorylating receptor tyrosines is done by the kinase activity of tyrosine kinase receptors, not by the proteasome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antigen presentation to natural killer cells is an immune function unrelated to this protein complex's housekeeping role.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transcription of survival genes is carried out by NF-kB once it reaches the nucleus, not by the degradation complex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The proteasome frees NF-kB indirectly by degrading IkB; it is not a transporter across the nuclear membrane.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man receiving bortezomib for multiple myeloma reports worsening numbness, burning in both feet, and limb pain. Which of the following is most likely to decrease these symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adding an antihistamine before each dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing the dose or discontinuing the drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: Slowing the rate of the infusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Starting an antiviral for viral reactivation

explanation.summary: Dose reduction or discontinuation of bortezomib decreases its neuropathic symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peripheral neuropathy is one of the two most common adverse effects of bortezomib, along with thrombocytopenia, and it may be accompanied by headache and limb pain. Dose reductions or discontinuation of bortezomib decreases the neuropathic symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamines are used for the infusion reactions caused by monoclonal antibodies, not for drug-induced neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reducing the infusion rate also addresses antibody infusion reactions rather than neuropathic symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antiviral therapy treats reactivated viral infection, a concern with rituximab and not the cause of this neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet transfusion would address thrombocytopenia, which is a different adverse effect and does not relieve neuropathy.

questions.topicName: Targeted Inhibitors Used in Cancer Therapy

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man is found to have a white blood cell count of 92,000/mm3 on a routine complete blood count. He feels well but has mild left upper quadrant fullness, and a spleen tip is palpable. The differential shows neutrophils with a left shift and rare myelocytes. Which of the following additional peripheral blood or serum findings is most likely in this patient?

explanation.summary: Chronic-phase CML characteristically produces a basophilia, a clue that is otherwise rare on the CBC.
