explanation.whyCorrect: In CML all myeloid lines proliferate, so eosinophils and basophils rise along with neutrophils. Because it is unusual to see a basophil on a routine CBC, the basophilia is a notable pointer toward CML.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blasts greater than 20% define the blast crisis phase; in chronic phase the blast count is low, usually 2%-3% and not more than 10%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase is decreased in CML; an elevated LAP points toward a benign leukocytosis such as a leukemoid reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CML produces a leukocytosis rather than a leukopenia, with a mean WBC around 100,000/mm3.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets are typically normal or increased in chronic-phase CML; thrombocytopenia appears only as the disease advances.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukemia after molecular testing shows the t(9;22) translocation. This translocation joins the ABL gene from chromosome 9 to the BCR gene on chromosome 22. Production of which of the following aberrant proteins most directly drives her disease?

choices.label: B
choices.text: JAK2 protein with a V617F mutation

explanation.summary: The t(9;22) creates the BCR::ABL fusion gene, which encodes an overactive (constitutively active) tyrosine kinase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fusing the ABL oncogene next to BCR produces the BCR::ABL fusion gene on the Philadelphia chromosome. Its product is an always-on tyrosine kinase that drives increased cell proliferation and defective DNA repair.

whyWrongByChoice.B: JAK2 mutations are found in several other myeloproliferative neoplasms, not in CML.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p53 is a tumor suppressor mutated across a wide variety of cancers, not the fusion protein of CML.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RAS is mutated in many cancers but is not the product of the t(9;22) translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retinoblastoma protein is a tumor suppressor altered in diverse cancers, not the BCR::ABL kinase.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia has been switched from imatinib to a different tyrosine kinase inhibitor after developing resistance. Several months later he develops dyspnea, and imaging shows a pleural effusion. Which tyrosine kinase inhibitor is most specifically associated with this adverse effect?

explanation.summary: Dasatinib is characteristically associated with pleural effusion (and prolonged QTc).
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the TKIs used after imatinib, dasatinib is specifically known for causing pleural effusions and can also prolong the QTc interval.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydroxyurea is a less-specific chemotherapy used in later stages, not the TKI linked to pleural effusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imatinib is most associated with GI side effects such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, not pleural effusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interferon alpha is a later-stage option and is not the agent classically tied to pleural effusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ponatinib is specifically associated with thrombosis and liver toxicity rather than pleural effusion.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is evaluated after routine studies reveal a white blood cell count of 120,000/uL. She reports mild fatigue but denies fever, weight loss, or night sweats. Examination shows a palpable spleen tip and no lymphadenopathy. A peripheral smear shows numerous mature and immature granulocytes, and molecular testing reveals the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene. Which of the following best explains the natural course of this disease if left untreated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Development of pancytopenia due to severe marrow fibrosis within months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediate need for bone marrow transplantation from a matched donor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rapid progression to marrow failure and blast crisis within weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spontaneous remission in most patients without any treatment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stable disease for several years followed by possible transformation

explanation.summary: Untreated chronic-phase CML is relatively stable for years before transforming toward a blast phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has chronic-phase CML, often found incidentally with only mild symptoms. Untreated, the chronic phase typically lasts about 3 to 4 years before potentially transforming into a blast phase that resembles acute leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Patients can develop some marrow fibrosis, but severe fibrosis causing pancytopenia is not the typical natural course.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immediate transplantation is not required initially; TKIs are generally started first because they have fewer side effects and often control the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rapid progression to marrow failure within weeks is characteristic of the blast phase, not chronic-phase CML.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CML does not spontaneously remit; it does not resolve without treatment.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with newly diagnosed chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia is started on imatinib. Which of the following best describes how this drug works?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It alkylates DNA to prevent replication of dividing cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It competitively binds the kinase site of BCR::ABL

choices.label: C
choices.text: It corrects the t(9;22) translocation at the DNA level

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits the proteasome, causing accumulation of misfolded proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a monoclonal antibody that blocks ligand binding to a surface receptor

explanation.summary: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that competitively binds the BCR::ABL kinase site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Imatinib binds the kinase site of the BCR::ABL protein and competitively inhibits it, so the phosphorylation of downstream signaling driven by the receptor tyrosine kinase is blocked.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Imatinib is a targeted kinase inhibitor, not an alkylating chemotherapy agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TKIs inhibit the fusion protein's activity; they do not repair or reverse the underlying translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteasome inhibition is the mechanism of other drug classes, not of imatinib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Monoclonal antibodies block ligand binding at the cell surface; imatinib acts intracellularly on the kinase domain.

questions.stem: A hematology resident notes that a patient's karyotype shows the Philadelphia chromosome. Why is the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, by itself, not diagnostic of chronic myeloid leukemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It disappears once treatment with a TKI begins

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is also seen in acute lymphoblastic leukemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an inherited finding rather than an acquired one

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is present in a small fraction of healthy adults

choices.label: E
choices.text: It only appears during the blast crisis phase of CML

explanation.summary: The Philadelphia chromosome is characteristic of CML but is also less commonly seen in ALL and AML.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although the Philadelphia chromosome is characteristic of CML, it is also seen less commonly in acute lymphoblastic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia, so its presence alone is not diagnostic of CML.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The molecular abnormality is monitored during therapy and does not simply vanish at the start of treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CML has no recognized familial inheritance; the translocation is an acquired, spontaneous event.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It is not a normal finding in healthy adults; it arises from an acquired translocation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It defines the disease throughout its course, including the chronic phase, not only blast crisis.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man has a neutrophilic leukocytosis with a left shift discovered during a severe pneumonia. His physician is trying to distinguish a leukemoid reaction from chronic myeloid leukemia. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor CML over a leukemoid reaction?

choices.label: E
choices.text: WBC count that normalizes after the infection is treated

explanation.summary: A low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase favors CML, whereas secondary leukocytosis raises the LAP.
explanation.whyCorrect: In CML the neoplastic neutrophils lack leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, so the LAP level is low. In secondary causes such as infection or a leukemoid reaction, the LAP is normal or increased.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absence of splenomegaly does not favor CML, which is often associated with an enlarged spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An elevated LAP points to a secondary or benign leukocytosis, not to CML.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prominent basophilia favors CML; a leukemoid reaction lacks prominent basophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A leukemoid reaction returns to normal once the infection or disease is treated; this favors a reactive process, not CML.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 3-year history of chronic-phase CML now has a rapidly rising white blood cell count, new fever, and bone pain. His physician suspects transformation to blast crisis. Which of the following findings best defines progression to the blast crisis phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decreased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase staining score

choices.label: B
choices.text: Basophils greater than 20% in the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blasts greater than 20% in the blood or bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: New palpable splenomegaly below the costal margin

choices.label: E
choices.text: White blood cell count greater than 100,000/mm3 on repeat

explanation.summary: Blast crisis is defined by a blast count greater than 20%, behaving like acute leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: In blast crisis the WBC count rises rapidly and the blast count is now more than 20%, essentially the same as an acute leukemia, in contrast to the chronic phase where blasts are usually 2%-3% and not more than 10%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low LAP is a feature of CML in general and does not mark the transition to blast crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Basophilia is a feature of chronic-phase CML and is not the defining criterion for blast crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenomegaly can occur in chronic phase and is not the defining feature of blast transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A markedly elevated WBC is seen throughout CML and does not by itself define blast crisis.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia develops an acutely painful, swollen great toe. Serum studies show an elevated uric acid level. Which of the following best explains this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of articular cartilage in the joint

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct crystal-forming toxicity of tyrosine kinase inhibitors used

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expansion of the bone marrow into the adjacent joint space

choices.label: D
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis within the synovium of the joint

choices.label: E
choices.text: High uric acid from rapid turnover and lysis of white blood cells

explanation.summary: Gouty arthritis in CML results from hyperuricemia driven by rapid WBC turnover and lysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The explosive WBC proliferation in CML causes high production of uric acid from the fast turnover and lysis of the many white blood cells in the circulation, which can precipitate gouty arthritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gout in CML is a metabolic consequence of high cell turnover, not an autoimmune process.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The gouty arthritis is due to hyperuricemia from cell turnover, not a direct crystal-forming toxicity of TKIs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow expansion causes complications such as retrosternal pain, not gout.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Extramedullary hematopoiesis in CML causes splenic enlargement, not intra-articular gout.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing risk factors for chronic myeloid leukemia. Which of the following is the only known risk factor for CML?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inherited BCR mutation passed within families

explanation.summary: Ionizing radiation is the only known risk factor for CML, which otherwise arises from spontaneous mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The only recognized risk factor for CML is ionizing radiation. There is no recognized familial inheritance, so most cases arise from spontaneous gene mutations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CML has no recognized familial inheritance; the driver mutation is acquired, not inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic autoimmune disease is not identified as a cause of CML.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cigarette smoking is not the recognized risk factor described for CML.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epstein-Barr virus is not identified as a risk factor for CML.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with CML develops rising BCR::ABL levels on imatinib, and testing reveals a mutation in the BCR::ABL kinase. Her oncologist switches her to dasatinib. Which of the following best explains why this second agent may work despite imatinib resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts only on the JAK2 pathway to bypass BCR::ABL

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds both the active and inactive conformations of the ABL kinase domain

choices.label: C
choices.text: It eliminates the Philadelphia chromosome from the genome

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a monoclonal antibody targeting a surface receptor rather than a kinase

choices.label: E
choices.text: It works by suppressing uric acid production from cell turnover

explanation.summary: Dasatinib and ponatinib bind both active and inactive ABL conformations, overcoming imatinib-resistance mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike imatinib, dasatinib and ponatinib bind both the active and inactive conformations of the ABL kinase domain and can overcome imatinib resistance resulting from mutations in the BCR::ABL kinase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dasatinib targets the BCR::ABL kinase, not the JAK2 pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TKIs inhibit the fusion protein's activity; they do not remove the Philadelphia chromosome from the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dasatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, not a monoclonal antibody against a surface receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lowering uric acid manages a complication of CML and is unrelated to overcoming kinase-domain resistance.

questions.stem: A bone marrow biopsy is performed on a 55-year-old patient with newly diagnosed chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia. Which of the following findings is most characteristic of the marrow in this phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hypercellular marrow with small, hypolobated megakaryocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: A hypocellular, aplastic marrow with fatty replacement

choices.label: C
choices.text: A marrow dominated by red blood cell precursors

choices.label: D
choices.text: A marrow with greater than 20% blasts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extensive fibrosis replacing nearly all hematopoietic tissue

explanation.summary: Chronic-phase CML marrow is markedly hypercellular with characteristic small, hypolobated megakaryocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bone marrow in chronic-phase CML is moderately to markedly hypercellular, with neutrophils and their precursors predominating and numerous megakaryocytes that are characteristically small with hypolobated nuclei.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The marrow is hypercellular with little fat, the opposite of a hypocellular aplastic marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils and their precursors predominate; red blood cell precursors are present but fewer than the neutrophilic cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Greater than 20% blasts defines the blast crisis phase, not chronic phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow can show some fibrosis, but extensive fibrosis replacing nearly all hematopoietic tissue is not the characteristic chronic-phase picture.

questions.stem: A 53-year-old man has a leukocytosis composed mostly of neutrophils together with increased eosinophils and basophils. His bone marrow is packed with myelocytes and their precursors, which are also spilling into the blood. His disease belongs to which of the following categories of hematopoietic neoplasm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia with excess blasts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasma cell dyscrasia of the marrow

explanation.summary: CML is one of the myeloproliferative neoplasms, a group of chronic diseases in which the marrow overproduces mature myeloid cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are chronic, slowly progressive diseases in which the bone marrow produces large numbers of neoplastic, mature myeloid cells that spill out into the blood. In CML it is the myeloid cell line (neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils) that undergoes excess proliferation, so marrow and blood fill with myelocytes and their precursors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myeloid leukemia is marked by blasts greater than 20%, not by an excess of maturing myelocytes and granulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aplastic anemia produces a hypocellular marrow with failure of cell production, the opposite of this hypercellular, overproducing marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A mature B-cell lymphoma is a lymphoid neoplasm; the cells proliferating here are myeloid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cell dyscrasias involve neoplastic plasma cells, not proliferation of the granulocytic lines.

questions.stem: A hematologist is reviewing the epidemiology of chronic myeloid leukemia with a group of students. CML accounts for approximately what proportion of leukemias in adults?

explanation.summary: CML makes up 15% to 20% of adult leukemias and usually affects adults 50 to 60 years of age.
explanation.whyCorrect: CML accounts for 15% to 20% of adult leukemias. It usually affects adults age 50 to 60 years but can also occur in adolescents and, less often, in children. Like the other myeloproliferative neoplasms, roughly 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 people occur annually.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This understates the burden of CML, which is one of the more common adult leukemias at 15% to 20%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This overstates the share; the figure for CML is 15% to 20% of adult leukemias.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No single leukemia subtype accounts for this majority share in adults, and CML's share is 15% to 20%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CML is not the overwhelming majority of adult leukemias; its incidence is about 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 annually.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a white blood cell count of 88,000/mm3. Her peripheral smear shows mature segmented neutrophils, erythrocytes, occasional lymphocytes, adequate platelets, and a number of myelocytes. Which of the following elements of this smear represents the left shift that characterizes her disease?

explanation.summary: A left shift means immature neutrophil precursors, such as myelocytes, are circulating alongside mature neutrophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: The leukocytosis of chronic-phase CML is mostly neutrophils but includes a left shift, meaning that in addition to mature, segmented neutrophils there are immature neutrophil precursors such as myelocytes that typically are not present in the blood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythrocytes are a normal constituent of the smear and are unrelated to the maturation of the granulocytic line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocytes are normally present in the peripheral blood and are not neutrophil precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelets are a normal finding on the smear and do not reflect granulocyte maturity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mature segmented neutrophils are the normal circulating form and do not by themselves indicate a left shift.

questions.stem: The peripheral blood in chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia shows a slowly increasing leukocytosis with a mean count of approximately 100,000 cells/mm3. How high can the white blood cell count rise in this disease?

explanation.summary: Although the mean WBC count in chronic-phase CML is about 100,000 cells/mm3, counts can climb as high as 1,000,000/mm3.
explanation.whyCorrect: The chronic phase produces a slowly increasing leukocytosis. The mean count is approximately 100,000 cells/mm3, well above the normal range, but the count can increase much more, up to 1,000,000/mm3.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A count in this range is common in CML but is nowhere near the upper limit the disease can produce.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is only modestly above the mean of about 100,000 cells/mm3 and understates how high the count may rise.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is above the mean count but still well below the ceiling of 1,000,000/mm3 that CML can reach.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This falls short of the maximum described for CML, where counts can reach 1,000,000/mm3.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with a 4-year history of chronic myeloid leukemia develops fever and bone pain. His marrow shows 40% blasts, and flow cytometry identifies these blasts as lymphoblasts rather than myeloblasts. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A second, unrelated acute lymphoblastic leukemia has arisen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphoblasts are the usual blast type seen in CML blast crisis

choices.label: C
choices.text: The BCR::ABL fusion gene has been lost from the neoplastic clone

choices.label: D
choices.text: The original mutation arose in a stem cell not yet committed to a lineage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy converts myeloblasts into lymphoblasts

explanation.summary: In blast crisis the blasts are lymphoblasts about 30% of the time because the founding mutation occurs in an uncommitted stem cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: In myeloproliferative disorders the initial genetic mutation occurs in a stem cell that is so early and undifferentiated that it has not yet decided whether it will be lymphoid or myeloid. Therefore, in blast crisis a lymphoblastic leukemia can occur, and roughly 30% of the time the blasts are lymphoblasts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is a transformation of the existing CML clone, not the coincidental emergence of a separate leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Most of the time blast crisis is myeloid; lymphoblasts account for approximately 30% of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blast crisis represents progression of the BCR::ABL-driven clone; loss of the fusion gene is not what produces lymphoblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TKIs block the BCR::ABL kinase and do not redirect the lineage of blasts.

questions.stem: A student reading an article published in 2019 encounters a description of an intermediate "accelerated phase" of chronic myeloid leukemia, said to lie between the chronic phase and the blast phase. Which of the following is true of this intermediate phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It denotes the phase in which the Philadelphia chromosome first appears

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has replaced the blast phase in the current classification

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is defined by a blast count greater than 20% in the marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is not included in the fifth edition of the WHO classification

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the phase in which most patients are first diagnosed

explanation.summary: The accelerated phase appears in literature prior to 2022 but is not part of the fifth edition WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Literature published before 2022 describes an intermediate accelerated phase between the chronic phase and the blast phase. However, the accelerated phase is not included in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Philadelphia chromosome is present from the outset in CML, including the chronic phase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The blast phase remains part of the classification; it is the accelerated phase that was dropped.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A blast count greater than 20% defines the blast phase, not an intermediate accelerated phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Most patients are diagnosed in the chronic phase, which is the most common phase of CML.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has had chronic myeloid leukemia for several years. His hemoglobin, previously normal, is now 9.8 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 89 fL, and his platelet count, previously elevated, has fallen into the normal range. Which of the following best accounts for these changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolysis triggered by the neoplastic clone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crowding out of normal hematopoiesis by the neoplastic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency from occult gastrointestinal blood loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marrow aplasia induced by tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency from increased cellular consumption

explanation.summary: As CML progresses, neoplastic cells squeeze out normal hematopoiesis, so platelets slowly fall and about half of patients develop a normocytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic-phase CML the neoplastic cells squeeze out the few normal hematopoietic cells in the hypercellular marrow. Platelets are normal or increased at first, but as the disease progresses thrombocyte levels slowly decrease and half of patients develop a normocytic anemia, matching this patient's normal MCV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemolysis is not the mechanism of the anemia that develops as CML progresses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency produces a microcytic anemia, whereas this patient's MCV is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors improve the counts in responding patients; marrow aplasia is not their described effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anemia and is not the described consequence of marrow crowding.

questions.stem: Two patients present with marked leukocytosis. The first has chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia; the second has acute myeloid leukemia. Compared with the second patient, which of the following best characterizes the blood counts of the first patient over the following days?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The counts will change slowly rather than wildly

choices.label: B
choices.text: The counts will return to normal without treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hemoglobin will rise sharply above normal

choices.label: D
choices.text: The platelet count will plummet abruptly

choices.label: E
choices.text: The white blood cell count will double within a few days

explanation.summary: The counts in chronic-phase CML drift slowly, in contrast to acute leukemia where they can swing wildly over days.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic-phase CML, neoplastic cells gradually squeeze out normal hematopoietic cells, so the red blood cell, normal leukocyte, and platelet counts drop slowly. By comparison, in acute leukemia the counts can vary wildly: the WBC count may double in a few days and the platelet count plummets.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CML does not spontaneously remit, so the counts will not normalize without treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The hemoglobin does not rise in CML; as the disease progresses half of patients become anemic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An abruptly plummeting platelet count is characteristic of acute leukemia; in CML platelets are normal or increased and fall slowly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Doubling of the WBC count within a few days describes acute leukemia, not the slowly increasing leukocytosis of chronic-phase CML.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with chronic myeloid leukemia reports several weeks of steady pain behind her sternum. She has had no chest trauma, and a cardiac workup is unremarkable. Which of the following best explains her pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pleural effusion caused by her medication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gouty arthritis of the sternoclavicular joint

choices.label: E
choices.text: Infiltration of the pericardium by blasts

explanation.summary: Retrosternal pain in CML comes from expansion of the hypercellular bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: The explosive white blood cell proliferation of CML causes most of its complications. One of these is retrosternal pain arising from expansion of the bone marrow as the proliferating neoplastic cells fill it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pleural effusion is an adverse effect specifically linked to dasatinib and would produce dyspnea rather than isolated sternal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extramedullary hematopoiesis in CML enlarges the spleen and causes left upper quadrant symptoms, not sternal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hyperuricemia of CML causes gouty arthritis, but that presents as an acutely painful, swollen joint rather than steady retrosternal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pericardial infiltration is not among the described complications of CML.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia has a spleen palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin and reports early satiety and a dragging sensation in the left upper quadrant. Which of the following processes best accounts for the splenic enlargement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of uric acid crystals in the splenic pulp

explanation.summary: The spleen enlarges in CML because hematopoiesis takes place outside the marrow, within the splenic tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Splenic enlargement is listed among the complications produced by the explosive WBC proliferation of CML, and it results from extramedullary hematopoiesis. The resulting splenomegaly produces the fullness or dragging feeling in the left upper quadrant, abdominal pain, and early satiety that patients describe.

whyWrongByChoice.A: High uric acid from WBC turnover precipitates gouty arthritis, not splenic enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Portal hypertension from hepatic infiltration is not the described mechanism of splenomegaly in CML.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic infarction is not given as the cause of the enlarged spleen in this disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenia appears only as CML advances and does not explain a chronically enlarged spleen.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has a neutrophilic leukocytosis with basophilia, and chronic myeloid leukemia is suspected. His oncologist orders a rapid test that will report only whether the t(9;22) is present or absent and will not examine any other chromosomes. Which of the following tests was ordered?

explanation.summary: FISH is the fast test for t(9;22), but it reports only that translocation and looks at no other chromosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: FISH for t(9;22) is used because it is fast, but it only tells you about this translocation, whether it is positive or negative; it does not look at any other chromosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A bone marrow biopsy assesses blast percentage and fibrosis rather than returning a rapid yes-or-no translocation result.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A karyotype visualizes all the chromosomes and takes up to 1 to 2 weeks, which is the opposite of the described test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PCR for BCR::ABL takes longer than FISH and is used to establish a baseline quantitative level for monitoring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The LAP level is a nonspecific screen that helps exclude secondary leukocytosis; it does not detect the translocation.

questions.stem: A clinician evaluating a newly diagnosed patient with chronic myeloid leukemia wants to know whether the patient also carries additional chromosomal abnormalities that would confer a worse prognosis, and is willing to wait 1 to 2 weeks for the result. Which of the following tests best meets this need?

explanation.summary: Only the karyotype visualizes all the chromosomes, so it can reveal additional abnormalities that worsen prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A karyotype will also show the t(9;22), but by visualizing all the chromosomes it can identify additional abnormalities that may create a worse prognosis. It takes longer than FISH, up to 1 to 2 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH is fast but reports only whether t(9;22) is present; it does not look at any other chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A smear discerns WBC subtypes and cell maturity but cannot detect chromosomal abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PCR establishes a baseline quantitative level of BCR::ABL for monitoring rather than surveying other chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The LAP level helps separate CML from secondary leukocytosis and carries no cytogenetic information.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with newly diagnosed chronic myeloid leukemia is about to begin imatinib. Her oncologist orders a test to establish a baseline quantitative level that will be followed during the course of her treatment. Which of the following tests serves this purpose?

explanation.summary: PCR for BCR::ABL establishes the baseline quantitative level that is monitored during treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: PCR for BCR::ABL usually takes a bit longer than FISH, but it establishes a baseline quantitative level of BCR::ABL that is then monitored during the course of the patient's treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH gives a fast positive-or-negative answer for t(9;22) rather than a quantitative level to follow over time.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The karyotype surveys all chromosomes for additional abnormalities; it does not provide a quantitative transcript level.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The LAP level is characteristically low in CML but is not the value tracked to gauge treatment response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uric acid reflects white blood cell turnover and the risk of gout, not the burden of the neoplastic clone.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman receives a diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukemia from peripheral blood testing alone. Her oncologist nevertheless schedules a bone marrow biopsy. Which of the following is the best rationale for this additional procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biopsy establishes the phase of disease and assesses blasts and fibrosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A biopsy is needed to measure the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase level

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biopsy is required before tyrosine kinase inhibitors can be started

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only marrow examination can detect the basophilia of CML

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral blood cannot demonstrate the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene

explanation.summary: Marrow biopsy is added to stage the disease and to monitor blast percentage and fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A diagnosis of CML can be made on peripheral blood. However, providers typically perform bone marrow biopsies as well to establish the phase of disease at diagnosis (chronic versus blast phase) and to monitor disease, following the percentage of blasts and the presence or absence of marrow fibrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The LAP score is a blood test on circulating neutrophils and does not require a marrow sample.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Treatment selection is guided by disease phase and risk score, not by a mandatory pre-treatment biopsy requirement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Basophilia is a peripheral blood finding seen readily on the CBC and smear.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The fusion gene can be demonstrated from peripheral blood, which is why the diagnosis was already made.

questions.stem: A senior resident asks why the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score, although characteristically low in chronic myeloid leukemia, is seldom ordered in current clinical practice. Which of the following is the best answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Testing for the BCR::ABL1 translocation is used to make the diagnosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: The assay requires a bone marrow aspirate rather than blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: The LAP score cannot distinguish CML from a leukemoid reaction

choices.label: D
choices.text: The LAP score is falsely normal in most patients with CML

choices.label: E
choices.text: The LAP score rises once a tyrosine kinase inhibitor is started

explanation.summary: Molecular testing for BCR::ABL1 has displaced the LAP score in routine practice.
explanation.whyCorrect: A decreased LAP score is not commonly used in routine clinical practice, given the use of the BCR::ABL1 translocation for diagnosis. The LAP level is still conceptually useful for excluding secondary causes of neutrophilia and other myeloproliferative neoplasms, in which the LAP is normal or increased.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The LAP score is measured on circulating neutrophils and does not require a marrow aspirate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The LAP score does distinguish the two: it is low in CML and normal or increased in a leukemoid reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The neutrophils of CML lack leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, so the score is genuinely low rather than falsely normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The score is not described as rising with therapy; it has been displaced by molecular testing.

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews the smear of a patient with a white blood cell count of 110,000/mm3 and reports that the numerous neutrophils appear entirely normal in appearance. A resident concludes that a myeloid neoplasm is therefore excluded. Which of the following is the best response to the resident?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A normal-appearing smear predicts a high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutrophils in CML are characteristically hypersegmented

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutrophils in CML look normal but are genetically abnormal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal-appearing neutrophils do exclude a myeloid neoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Philadelphia chromosome is visible within neutrophils on the smear

explanation.summary: The neutrophils of CML are morphologically normal yet genetically abnormal, so a normal-looking smear does not exclude the disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Morphologically, the neutrophils in CML appear normal. However, they are genetically abnormal and lack the normal neutrophil enzyme leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, and they carry the genetic abnormality that defines the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The LAP level is low in CML because the neoplastic neutrophils lack the enzyme, despite appearing normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypersegmentation is not the described morphology of neutrophils in CML, which look normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Normal morphology is exactly what is expected in CML and therefore excludes nothing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A chromosomal translocation cannot be seen on a routine smear; it requires cytogenetic or molecular testing.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man began imatinib 6 weeks ago for chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia. He reports a mild rash, some ankle edema, fatigue, and aching muscles. His examination is otherwise unremarkable and his blood counts are improving. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add interferon alpha to counteract the drug's toxicity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue therapy and adjust the dose if the symptoms persist

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discontinue kinase inhibitor therapy permanently and begin hydroxyurea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Refer urgently for bone marrow transplantation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch immediately to dasatinib because of kinase inhibitor intolerance

explanation.summary: The mild toxicities common to all TKIs in the first months usually resolve on their own or respond to dose adjustment.
explanation.whyCorrect: All TKIs are associated with common, generally mild toxicities such as rash, nausea, edema, fatigue, and myalgias or arthralgias during the first months of treatment. Most resolve spontaneously or can be controlled by dose adjustments, so therapy that is working should be continued.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Interferon alpha is an alternative later-stage therapy, not an antidote to TKI side effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Less-specific chemotherapy such as hydroxyurea is reserved for later stages when TKIs have been tried or are ineffective.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transplantation is considered for younger patients with advanced disease, not for a responding patient with mild side effects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A switch to another TKI is warranted for resistance or genuine intolerance, not for expected mild early toxicities.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man whose chronic myeloid leukemia progressed on imatinib was switched to a second tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Four months later he develops a deep venous thrombosis, and his liver enzymes are three times the upper limit of normal. Which of the following agents is he most likely taking?

explanation.summary: Thrombosis and liver toxicity are the adverse effects specific to ponatinib.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dasatinib and ponatinib are the TKIs tried after imatinib because they bind both the active and inactive conformations of the ABL kinase domain. Among the specific adverse effects of these agents, thrombosis and liver toxicity belong to ponatinib.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dasatinib is specifically linked to pleural effusion and prolonged QTc rather than thrombosis and hepatotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydroxyurea is a less-specific chemotherapy used in later stages, not the second-line TKI described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The patient was switched off imatinib for progression, and imatinib is associated with GI effects such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interferon alpha is an alternative later-stage therapy rather than a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia has progressed despite trials of two different tyrosine kinase inhibitors. His comorbidities make him a poor candidate for transplantation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A monoclonal antibody directed against the BCR::ABL protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Observation with serial complete blood counts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeating the original tyrosine kinase inhibitor at a higher dose

explanation.summary: When TKIs have been tried or are ineffective, less-specific chemotherapy such as hydroxyurea or interferon alpha is considered.
explanation.whyCorrect: In later stages of the disease, if TKIs have already been tried or are ineffective, less-specific chemotherapeutic drugs may be considered. These include interferon alpha, hydroxyurea, or other chemotherapies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The BCR::ABL fusion protein is an intracellular kinase blocked by TKIs; monoclonal antibodies act at cell-surface receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lowering uric acid manages the gouty complication of high cell turnover and does not treat the leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Observation is inappropriate for progressive disease, which would advance toward blast phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resistance arising from mutations in the BCR::ABL kinase is addressed by changing agents, not by re-escalating a failed one.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with chronic myeloid leukemia has progressed despite tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy. Which of the following treatments is most likely to benefit a patient of his age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow or stem cell transplantation

explanation.summary: Younger patients whose disease is not controlled by TKIs may benefit from bone marrow or stem cell transplantation.
explanation.whyCorrect: When TKIs have already been tried or are ineffective, less-specific chemotherapies may be considered, and younger patients in particular may benefit from bone marrow or stem cell transplants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydroxyurea is a less-specific chemotherapy option but is not the therapy singled out as benefiting younger patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon alpha is likewise an alternative chemotherapy rather than the age-specific option described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Waiting for blast crisis is dangerous, because that phase is extremely difficult to treat and survival is weeks to a few months.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The LAP score is a diagnostic aid, not a treatment for progressive disease.

questions.stem: An oncologist is choosing among the several tyrosine kinase inhibitors available for a patient with newly diagnosed chronic myeloid leukemia. Side effect profile, comorbid illnesses, drug interactions, cost, and patient preference all enter the decision. Which of the following pairs of factors principally guides the selection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disease phase and CML risk score

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase level and uric acid level

choices.label: E
choices.text: White blood cell count and basophil percentage

explanation.summary: TKI selection is guided primarily by the phase of disease and the CML risk score.
explanation.whyCorrect: In practice, selection of a TKI is guided by disease phase and CML risk score. Other considerations include side effect profile, comorbid illnesses, medications that may interact with TKIs, availability, cost, and patient preference or convenience. Most often imatinib is the first choice.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These laboratory values help with diagnosis and with managing hyperuricemia, not with drug selection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow findings establish the pathologic picture of chronic phase but do not direct the choice of agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Age matters when considering transplantation, and spleen size reflects disease burden, but neither is the principal pair guiding TKI choice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The WBC count and basophilia support the diagnosis rather than determine which inhibitor to use.

questions.stem: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors and monoclonal antibodies are both used as targeted cancer therapies, but they act at different points on the same signaling receptor. At which site does a tyrosine kinase inhibitor act?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The circulating ligand, before it reaches the receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: The extracellular ligand-binding domain of the receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: The intracellular ATP-binding domain of the receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nuclear DNA of the dividing cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: The phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane

explanation.summary: TKIs block the intracellular kinase domain, whereas monoclonal antibodies act outside the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: A tyrosine kinase inhibitor binds the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain of the receptor, so the phosphorylation of downstream signaling is inhibited and the signal transduction cascade is blocked. Imatinib does exactly this at the kinase site of the BCR::ABL protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding the free ligand before it reaches the receptor is the other mechanism used by monoclonal antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The extracellular ligand-binding domain is where monoclonal antibodies bind the receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TKIs are targeted kinase inhibitors and do not act on nuclear DNA the way cytotoxic chemotherapy does.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lipid bilayer is not the target; the drug reaches the kinase domain on the intracellular side of the receptor.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukemia asks what would happen if she chose no treatment at all. Untreated, the life expectancy of a patient with CML is approximately which of the following?

explanation.summary: Untreated CML carries a life expectancy of roughly 5 years; TKIs have made it a chronic, manageable condition.
explanation.whyCorrect: If left untreated, the life expectancy for patients with CML is approximately 5 years. Targeted drug therapy transformed CML from what used to be a 5-year survival into a chronic treatable condition, at least for those patients who respond to TKIs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This substantially understates the untreated course, which is relatively stable for years before transformation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is shorter than even the untreated chronic phase, which itself lasts about 3 to 4 years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Roughly 3 to 4 years is the duration of the untreated chronic phase, not the overall life expectancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Survival measured in weeks to a few months applies to the blast phase, not to newly diagnosed untreated CML.

questions.stem: A hematology fellow notes that the BCR::ABL1 translocation, the hallmark of chronic myeloid leukemia, is also found in some cases of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which of the following best describes how the translocation in ALL differs from that in CML?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It fuses the ABL gene to a partner gene other than BCR

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is inherited within families rather than acquired during life

choices.label: C
choices.text: It joins the ABL gene to chromosome 21 rather than to chromosome 22

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs at a different breakpoint in BCR, giving a different sized protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: It yields a fusion gene that is transcribed but never translated to protein

explanation.summary: The BCR::ABL1 translocation of ALL uses a different breakpoint in BCR, so the fusion protein is a different size.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Philadelphia chromosome is characteristic of CML but is also seen less commonly in acute lymphoblastic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia. Of note, the BCR::ABL1 translocation in ALL is created at a different breakpoint in the BCR gene, causing a different sized fusion protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The partner gene is BCR in both diseases, which is why both are called BCR::ABL1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no recognized familial inheritance for these translocations; they arise from acquired, spontaneous mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The partner chromosome is still 22; the ABL oncogene moves from the long arm of chromosome 9 to the BCR region on 22.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A fusion protein is indeed produced in ALL; it simply differs in size from the CML product.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension reports intense itching after hot showers and burning pain in his hands and feet. He does not smoke. On examination his vital signs are normal, oxygen saturation is 98%, and a spleen tip is palpable. Laboratory studies show elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, splenomegaly, and elevated Hgb/Hct with normal oxygen saturation point to polycythemia vera.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes exactly this presentation: itching after warm showers (aquagenic pruritus), burning pain in the hands and feet (erythromelalgia), splenomegaly, and an elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit. A normal oxygen saturation in a non-smoker argues against a hypoxia-driven secondary cause, making primary polycythemia (PV) most likely.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CML is driven by a leukocyte proliferation and BCR-ABL, not the erythroid-dominant picture with pruritus and erythromelalgia described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron deficiency anemia produces a low, not elevated, hemoglobin and does not cause aquagenic pruritus or erythromelalgia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Relative polycythemia from dehydration does not cause splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus, or erythromelalgia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secondary polycythemia from hypoxemia is typically accompanied by a low oxygen saturation; this patient's saturation is normal at 98%.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is found to have an elevated red blood cell mass and is diagnosed with polycythemia vera. Molecular testing reveals a mutation that produces a tyrosine kinase which remains constitutively active, driving red cell precursors to proliferate even without erythropoietin. A mutation in which of the following genes is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Virtually all cases of polycythemia vera are associated with an activating JAK2 mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that virtually all cases of PV are associated with activating mutations in JAK2, a tyrosine kinase in the JAK-STAT pathway. The mutation keeps JAK2 constitutively active, so RBC precursors are continuously stimulated regardless of erythropoietin, causing uncontrolled RBC proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCR-ABL is the driver of chronic myeloid leukemia, not polycythemia vera.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HER2 is amplified in some breast cancers and is unrelated to PV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RET mutations are associated with medullary thyroid cancer and MEN syndromes, not PV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 is a tumor suppressor implicated broadly in cancer but is not the characteristic driver mutation of PV.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has an elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit. To distinguish polycythemia vera from secondary polycythemia, his physician measures the serum level of the hormone that normally stimulates the marrow to make red blood cells. In polycythemia vera, which of the following results would be expected for this hormone?

explanation.summary: Serum erythropoietin is low in polycythemia vera, an important diagnostic clue.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that because the JAK2 pathway is constitutively active and red cell numbers are already high, serum erythropoietin (EPO) levels in PV are low. This contrasts with secondary polycythemia, where EPO is high, so a low EPO is a key clue to primary disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high EPO is characteristic of secondary polycythemia, not PV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Haptoglobin relates to hemolysis and is not the diagnostic test described for polycythemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick uses erythropoietin, not thrombopoietin, to distinguish primary from secondary polycythemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ferritin reflects iron stores and is not the hormone used to differentiate these disorders.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is found to have an elevated hematocrit. His oxygen saturation is 88%. His serum erythropoietin is elevated, and testing for the JAK2 mutation is negative. Which of the following best explains his polycythemia?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aberrant erythropoietin production by a renal tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone marrow fibrosis with extramedullary hematopoiesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secondary polycythemia due to tissue hypoxia

explanation.summary: A high EPO, low oxygen saturation, and absent JAK2 mutation indicate hypoxia-driven secondary polycythemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that secondary polycythemia results from an identifiable cause, most often tissue hypoxia (from chronic hypoxemia such as lung disease, high-altitude living, or smoking) that raises serum EPO. A high EPO, low oxygen saturation, and a negative JAK2 test fit hypoxia-driven secondary polycythemia rather than PV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A constitutively active JAK2 kinase defines PV; his JAK2 test is negative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A renal tumor causes aberrant EPO production but would not explain the low oxygen saturation and clear hypoxic lung disease he has.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow fibrosis with extramedullary hematopoiesis is a late spent-phase feature of PV, not a cause of secondary polycythemia in a hypoxic smoker.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polycythemia vera has a low EPO, a normal oxygen saturation, and a JAK2 mutation, none of which are present here.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is newly diagnosed with polycythemia vera. He has no history of thrombosis and is not considered high risk. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment to reduce his red cell mass?

explanation.summary: First-line treatment of PV is regular therapeutic phlebotomy (plus low-dose aspirin).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists regular/therapeutic phlebotomy and low-dose aspirin as the primary treatments for PV. Phlebotomy removes a controlled volume of blood to maintain the hematocrit in the normal range (below 45%), decreasing blood viscosity and clot risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The goal is to decrease the hematocrit; giving more blood via transfusion would be harmful.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow transplantation is used for some other hematopoietic neoplasms but is not the initial treatment for PV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Corticosteroids are not part of the described treatment for PV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cyclophosphamide is a chemotherapy agent that is not used to treat PV.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with polycythemia vera is started on low-dose aspirin. In addition to reducing her thrombotic risk, aspirin also relieves her microvascular symptoms such as aquagenic pruritus and erythromelalgia. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which aspirin achieves these antiplatelet effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of antithrombin to inhibit thrombin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct inhibition of the JAK2 tyrosine kinase

explanation.summary: Aspirin is a non-selective COX inhibitor that blocks thromboxane-A2, reducing platelet aggregation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that aspirin is a non-selective COX inhibitor that blocks the tissue-specific prostaglandin thromboxane-A2, and it is this action that reduces platelet aggregation. This antiplatelet effect both alleviates the microvascular complications of PV and helps reduce thrombotic risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activating antithrombin describes heparin, not aspirin's antiplatelet action.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aspirin does not act at the erythropoietin receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting JAK2 describes ruxolitinib, not aspirin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase is the mechanism of hydroxyurea.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with high-risk polycythemia vera continues to have an elevated hematocrit and platelet count despite phlebotomy and aspirin. He is started on an oral cytoreductive agent that lowers RBC and platelet counts by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase and halting the cell cycle at the G1/S phase. Which of the following medications is most consistent with this description?

explanation.summary: Hydroxyurea lowers RBC and platelet counts by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase, arresting the cell cycle at G1/S.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that hydroxyurea lowers RBC and platelet counts by interfering with DNA repair through inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase, halting the cell cycle at the G1/S phase. It is an oral agent with a favorable toxicity profile and is generally the first cytoreductive drug chosen.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interferon alfa works by inducing cell cycle arrest and apoptosis and is given by subcutaneous injection, not by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prednisone is a corticosteroid that is not used as a cytoreductive agent in PV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ruxolitinib is a JAK inhibitor, not a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin is an anticoagulant and does not reduce red cell or platelet production.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman with high-risk polycythemia vera requires a cytoreductive agent because phlebotomy and aspirin alone have not controlled her disease. Which of the following agents is preferred in this pregnant patient?

explanation.summary: Pegylated interferon alfa is preferred over hydroxyurea for cytoreduction in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that interferon alfa is a subcutaneous injection given every two weeks that is preferred in pregnant patients. It also notes that hydroxyurea can cause teratogenicity and should be used cautiously in pregnancy, making interferon the better choice here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cyclophosphamide is not used to treat PV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydroxyurea can be teratogenic and should be used cautiously in pregnancy, so it is not preferred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy and is not a treatment for PV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ruxolitinib is reserved for patients failing hydroxyurea or interferon and is not the described preferred agent in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with untreated polycythemia vera presents with an acute ischemic stroke. His physician explains that the most common complications of PV arise largely from the overproduction of red blood cells. Which of the following pairs of complications is most characteristic of polycythemia vera?

explanation.summary: The most common complications of PV are thrombosis and hemorrhage.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the most common complications of PV are thrombosis and hemorrhage. The increased cell number raises blood viscosity and precipitates thrombosis (stroke, MI, DVT, PE), while impaired platelet function contributes to bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PV causes a high red cell mass, not anemia; jaundice is not a described feature.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypocalcemia and tetany are not associated with PV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphadenopathy and night sweats are not the characteristic complications of PV described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PV usually raises the white cell count rather than causing neutropenia and infection.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with long-standing untreated polycythemia vera develops progressive fatigue and massive enlargement of the spleen and liver. A bone marrow biopsy now shows extensive fibrosis that has replaced most of the normal marrow elements. Which of the following best explains his splenic and hepatic enlargement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute erythropoietin overproduction by the enlarged liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extramedullary hematopoiesis during the spent phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron overload from repeated red cell transfusions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metastatic spread of an occult solid tumor to both organs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Portal vein thrombosis alone with venous congestion

explanation.summary: In the spent phase of PV, marrow fibrosis shifts blood production to the spleen and liver (extramedullary hematopoiesis), enlarging them.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that untreated PV can exhaust the marrow, producing a spent phase characterized by bone marrow fibrosis. The body compensates by making red cells in alternate sites such as the spleen and liver, a process called extramedullary hematopoiesis, which leads to enlargement of both organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin is low in PV, and hepatic EPO overproduction does not explain marrow fibrosis with organ enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron overload is not the mechanism the brick describes for splenic and hepatic enlargement in PV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes the organ enlargement to extramedullary hematopoiesis in the spent phase, not to metastatic solid tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Portal vein thrombosis alone does not account for the marrow fibrosis and compensatory blood production described.

questions.stem: A hematopathologist reviews the bone marrow biopsy of a patient being worked up for polycythemia vera. Which of the following marrow findings is part of the diagnostic criteria and most characteristic of PV?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypocellular marrow with extensive fatty replacement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marrow packed with sheets of lymphoblasts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Numerous ring sideroblasts on iron staining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sheets of Reed-Sternberg cells in the marrow

explanation.summary: PV marrow is hypercellular with erythroid predominance and trilineage (panmyeloid) growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists bone marrow biopsy showing hypercellular marrow with trilineage growth among the diagnostic criteria for PV. The marrow is hypercellular with an increase in all myeloid cells but a predominance of erythroid cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A hypocellular, fatty marrow is the opposite of the hypercellular marrow seen in PV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A marrow packed with lymphoblasts indicates acute lymphoblastic leukemia, not PV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ring sideroblasts characterize sideroblastic anemia and certain myelodysplastic syndromes, not PV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma, not PV.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with polycythemia vera asks about his prognosis. His physician notes that outcomes depend heavily on treatment. Which of the following statements about the prognosis of PV is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Median survival is under one year regardless of treatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients transform to acute myeloid leukemia within a year

choices.label: C
choices.text: The disease is reliably cured by a single course of chemotherapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Treatment has no effect on survival in PV

choices.label: E
choices.text: Untreated patients may survive only a few months

explanation.summary: Untreated PV may allow only a few months of survival, but frequent phlebotomy extends median survival to about 10 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that untreated individuals may live only a few months, whereas with frequent phlebotomy median survival is around 10 years, underscoring the major impact of treatment on prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Median survival with phlebotomy is around 10 years, not under one year.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transformation to acute myeloid leukemia occurs in only about 2% of patients and is not the usual course within a year.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick does not describe PV as curable by a single course of chemotherapy; management centers on phlebotomy, aspirin, and cytoreduction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Treatment clearly affects survival, extending it from months to years.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with polycythemia vera is told that his disease belongs to a group of disorders called myeloproliferative neoplasms. Which of the following best characterizes the disorders in this group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clonal proliferation of lymphoid blasts that replace the normal marrow elements

choices.label: B
choices.text: Destruction of circulating red cells by autoantibodies directed at their membranes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expansion of plasma cells that secrete a monoclonal immunoglobulin into serum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marrow failure with pancytopenia and fatty replacement of hematopoietic tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Marrow production of large numbers of mature myeloid cells that spill into the blood

explanation.summary: Myeloproliferative neoplasms are diseases in which the marrow makes large numbers of neoplastic, mature myeloid cells that spill into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines myeloproliferative neoplasms as a cluster of neoplastic diseases in which the bone marrow produces large numbers of neoplastic, mature myeloid cells that end up spilling out into the blood. In several of these, one cell line (red cells, white cells, or platelets) dominates over the others. Patients usually have a more chronic, slow development of disease compared with the acute leukemias.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Proliferation of lymphoid blasts describes acute lymphoblastic leukemia; these disorders are myeloid and produce mature cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody-mediated red cell destruction describes autoimmune hemolysis, which reduces rather than increases circulating cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A monoclonal plasma cell expansion describes plasma cell disease, not a myeloproliferative neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marrow failure with pancytopenia is the opposite of the overproduction that defines the myeloproliferative neoplasms.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with a myeloproliferative neoplasm has a markedly elevated hematocrit with only mild elevations of her white blood cell and platelet counts. Proliferation of which of the following cell lines predominates in polycythemia vera?

explanation.summary: In polycythemia vera the erythroid cell line proliferates more than the other myeloid cell lines.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in PV the erythroid cell line proliferates more than do the other myeloid cell lines, so the peripheral blood contains a massive number of mature red blood cells. This erythroid predominance is also seen in the marrow, which is hypercellular with an increase in all myeloid cells but a predominance of erythroid cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulocyte precursors are increased as well, yet they are not the predominant line in PV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphoid cells are not part of the myeloid expansion that characterizes PV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Megakaryocytes are increased in PV, but platelet elevation is secondary to the dominant erythroid proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Monocyte proliferation is not the defining feature of PV.

questions.stem: A student is reviewing the epidemiology of chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms. Polycythemia vera appears in people of all ages and populations, with a mean age at diagnosis of 60 years. Its annual incidence is approximately which of the following?

explanation.summary: Like the other myeloproliferative neoplasms, PV has an annual incidence of about 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 people.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PV appears in those of all ages and in all populations, with a mean age at diagnosis of 60 years, and that similar to the other myeloproliferative neoplasms the annual incidence is approximately 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 people.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This figure is 100-fold lower than the incidence the brick gives.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 1 to 2 per 1000 would make PV a common disease, which it is not.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An incidence of 10 to 20 per 100,000 would be about ten times higher than reported.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An incidence of 50 to 60 per 100,000 far overstates how common PV is.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man has a complete blood count before elective hernia repair; his hemoglobin is 18.9 g/dL. He feels well and has no complaints. Which of the following best describes the typical way polycythemia vera comes to medical attention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A patient presenting with acute myeloid leukemia at the time of diagnosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A patient presenting with fever and generalized lymphadenopathy

choices.label: C
choices.text: A patient presenting with jaundice and dark-colored urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: An asymptomatic patient with an elevated hematocrit found on routine labs

choices.label: E
choices.text: An asymptomatic patient with pancytopenia found on routine labs

explanation.summary: The typical presentation of PV is an asymptomatic patient whose elevated hemoglobin or hematocrit is discovered on routine laboratory testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis, so the condition is frequently discovered when an elevated hemoglobin or hematocrit turns up on routine laboratory testing. The summary repeats this as the typical presentation of PV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transformation to acute myeloid leukemia is a rare late event in about 2% of patients, not the usual way PV presents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fever with generalized lymphadenopathy is not the described presentation of PV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Jaundice and dark urine suggest hemolysis, not the erythrocytosis of PV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PV produces elevated counts, not pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with polycythemia vera reports feeling full after only a few bites of food and a constant heaviness in her left upper abdomen. Which of the following most likely accounts for these symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep vein thrombosis of the left iliac vein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peptic ulceration causing epigastric burning pain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urate deposition in joints and cartilage

explanation.summary: Splenomegaly in PV causes abdominal heaviness or tightness and early satiety.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists splenomegaly among the symptomatic findings of PV and states that it might cause abdominal heaviness or tightness or early satiety. The spleen sits in the left upper quadrant, matching this patient's localized heaviness and her inability to finish a meal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An iliac vein thrombosis causes leg swelling and pain rather than early satiety.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatic enlargement occurs in the spent phase and would produce right upper quadrant fullness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptic ulcer disease in PV produces epigastric pain from reduced gut blood flow, not left upper quadrant heaviness with early satiety.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gouty tophi from high uric acid deposit in joints, cartilage, and skin and do not cause abdominal symptoms.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with advanced polycythemia vera describes intermittent blurring of his vision. His hematocrit is 62% and his blood is markedly thickened by an excess of red cells. Which of the following best explains his visual symptoms?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infiltration of the optic nerve by neoplastic blasts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Optic neuritis caused by pegylated interferon alfa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced retinal blood flow caused by hyperviscosity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vitreous hemorrhage caused by severe thrombocytopenia

explanation.summary: Hyperviscosity from too many circulating red cells reduces retinal blood flow and causes visual disturbances in advanced PV.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in advanced cases too many RBCs cause hyperviscosity, somewhat like replacing the water in a hose with thick syrup. Among the consequences listed are visual disturbances from reduced retinal blood flow, along with venous thrombi, abdominal pain, headaches, plethora, and strokes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The urate excess in PV deposits as tophi in joints, cartilage, and skin rather than in the cornea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PV is a proliferation of mature myeloid cells; blast infiltration of the optic nerve is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon alfa causes effects such as depression, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes, and this patient's hyperviscosity explains the symptom.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet counts in PV are elevated, not severely decreased.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with untreated polycythemia vera develops epigastric pain and is found on endoscopy to have peptic ulcer disease. Her hematocrit is 61%. Which of the following best explains the link between her ulcer disease and her polycythemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the gastric parietal cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct infiltration of the gastric wall by neoplastic myeloid cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased gastric acid secretion driven by erythropoietin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron overload deposited within the gastric mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced blood flow to the gut caused by hyperviscosity

explanation.summary: Hyperviscosity in advanced PV reduces gut blood flow, producing abdominal pain and peptic ulcer disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that hyperviscosity from too many circulating red cells produces abdominal pain and peptic ulcer disease from reduced gut blood flow. The same thickened blood also produces venous thrombi, visual disturbances, headaches, plethora, and strokes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Parietal cell autoimmunity is not a described feature of PV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PV is characterized by mature cells spilling into the blood rather than tissue infiltration of the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythropoietin acts on marrow red cell precursors, and its level in PV is low.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Repeated phlebotomy removes iron; iron deposition in the stomach is not part of PV.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man reports burning pain in both hands accompanied by erythema. On examination his fingers show patchy pallor and cyanosis and his radial pulses are easily palpable. This finding is common in polycythemia vera and in which of the following other disorders?

explanation.summary: Erythromelalgia is burning pain in the hands or feet with erythema, pallor, or cyanosis and palpable pulses, and is common in both PV and essential thrombocythemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes erythromelalgia as burning pain in the feet or hands accompanied by erythema, pallor, or cyanosis, in the presence of palpable pulses, and states that it is common in both essential thrombocythemia and polycythemia vera. Essential thrombocythemia is another myeloproliferative neoplasm that can overlap with PV in presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a lymphoid blast disease and is not linked to erythromelalgia here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia is driven by BCR-ABL and is not the disorder the brick pairs with PV for this finding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hodgkin lymphoma is a lymphoid malignancy unrelated to this microvascular finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell disorder and is not among the myeloproliferative neoplasms discussed.

questions.stem: A researcher studying activating JAK2 mutations notes that they are not confined to polycythemia vera. JAK2 mutations are also present in which of the following pairs of chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and follicular lymphoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chronic myeloid leukemia and essential thrombocythemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic myeloid leukemia and hairy cell leukemia

explanation.summary: JAK2 mutations also occur in essential thrombocythemia and chronic myelofibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that JAK2 mutations are also present in two other chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms, essential thrombocythemia and chronic myelofibrosis, and that it is not clear why a JAK2 mutation sometimes results in polycythemia vera and sometimes in another myeloproliferative neoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome are not the two chronic neoplasms the brick pairs with PV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both of these are lymphoid neoplasms, not chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Essential thrombocythemia is correct, but chronic myeloid leukemia is driven by BCR-ABL rather than JAK2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic myeloid leukemia is a BCR-ABL disease, and hairy cell leukemia is not among the JAK2-associated neoplasms described.

questions.stem: The JAK2 gene encodes a tyrosine kinase. In a normal red blood cell precursor, erythropoietin binds its receptor and JAK2 is activated. Which of the following best describes what the activated kinase then does?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cleaves the erythropoietin receptor to terminate the signal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Converts arachidonic acid into tissue-specific prostaglandins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase to arrest the cell cycle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphorylates signaling proteins that activate growth-promoting genes

choices.label: E
