choices.text: Inhibits DNA polymerase to prevent replication of the malignant clone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits the tyrosine kinase activity of the BCR-ABL fusion protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selectively inhibits JAK1 and JAK2 to regulate the JAK-STAT pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulates erythropoietin production in the kidney to increase RBC counts

explanation.summary: Ruxolitinib selectively inhibits JAK1 and JAK2 to counter the dysregulated JAK-STAT signaling caused by the JAK2 mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because about 50% of PMF cases carry a JAK2 mutation, the JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib can be used. It selectively inhibits JAK1 and JAK2 to mediate the dysregulated activity of the mutated JAK2, targeting the overactive JAK-STAT signaling pathway and helping with proliferation and symptoms such as anemia and splenomegaly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA cross-linking describes alkylating chemotherapy agents, not ruxolitinib.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibiting DNA polymerase is more aligned with certain antiviral or chemotherapeutic agents, not ruxolitinib.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase is the mechanism of imatinib used in chronic myeloid leukemia, not PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ruxolitinib does not stimulate erythropoietin; it can actually cause anemia and pancytopenia.

questions.stem: A high-risk patient with primary myelofibrosis is treated with hydroxyurea to reduce the white blood cell count. Which of the following best describes how this antimetabolite works?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds CD20 on the surface of B cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits the proteasome to accumulate misfolded proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selectively inhibits JAK1 and JAK2 kinases

explanation.summary: Hydroxyurea is an antimetabolite that inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and halts the cell cycle at the G1/S phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hydroxyurea is an antimetabolite chemotherapy drug that can help reduce WBC counts in PMF. It interferes with DNA repair by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase, halting the cell cycle at the G1/S phase. It is teratogenic, so it should be used cautiously in women of childbearing age, and live vaccines are contraindicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding CD20 describes rituximab, an antibody used for B-cell disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking microtubule assembly describes vinca alkaloids and taxanes, not hydroxyurea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteasome inhibition describes bortezomib used in multiple myeloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inhibiting JAK1 and JAK2 is the mechanism of ruxolitinib, not hydroxyurea.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing primary myelofibrosis develops a rapid clinical decline. A repeat bone marrow evaluation raises concern for transformation of the disease. Which of the following outcomes is most consistent with this concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion to a benign reactive marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spontaneous resolution of the marrow fibrosis

explanation.summary: PMF can transform into acute myeloid leukemia in about 3% to 4% of cases, which is usually a fatal outcome.
explanation.whyCorrect: PMF can transform into acute myeloid leukemia in approximately 3% to 4% of cases, which is usually a fatal outcome. This kind of transformation can occur in any myeloproliferative neoplasm, and it explains a rapid clinical decline.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PMF is a clonal neoplasm and does not convert to a benign reactive marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The fibrosis of PMF progresses rather than spontaneously resolving.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a lymphoid neoplasm and is not the transformation seen in PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hodgkin lymphoma is unrelated to the progression of myeloproliferative neoplasms.

questions.stem: A hematologist counsels a 66-year-old man that, of the myeloproliferative neoplasms, the one he has carries the worst prognosis, and that his bone marrow will gradually fill with collagen fibers. Which of the following disorders does he have?

explanation.summary: Primary myelofibrosis is the myeloproliferative neoplasm with the worst prognosis, and its marrow progressively fills with fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: PMF is a hematopoietic neoplasm in which the bone marrow gradually becomes filled with fibrosis. It is one of a group of disorders called myeloproliferative neoplasms, and it is the one with the worst prognosis. Like the other MPNs it is a slow, chronic, progressive disease rather than a rapidly progressive acute malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a lymphoid neoplasm and is not a myeloproliferative neoplasm at all.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia is an MPN in which the neutrophil series predominates, and it does not carry the worst prognosis of the group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Essential thrombocythemia is an MPN with increased megakaryocytes but a better prognosis than PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polycythemia vera is the MPN in which red blood cells steal the show, and its prognosis is better than that of PMF.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with newly diagnosed primary myelofibrosis asks whether she inherited the disease or whether an exposure caused it. Which of the following is the only known risk factor for this disorder?

explanation.summary: Ionizing radiation is the only known risk factor for PMF; most cases arise from spontaneous gene mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The only known risk factor for primary myelofibrosis is ionizing radiation. There is no recognized familial inheritance of the disease, and most cases arise from spontaneous gene mutations such as those in JAK2, CALR, and MPL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no recognized familial inheritance pattern for PMF; the driver mutations are acquired rather than inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epstein-Barr virus infection is not a recognized risk factor for this myeloproliferative neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alcohol use has not been identified as a risk factor for developing PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron overload is not among the risk factors identified for PMF.

questions.stem: A trainee is compiling epidemiologic data on the myeloproliferative neoplasms. Which of the following best approximates the annual incidence of primary myelofibrosis?

explanation.summary: PMF has an annual incidence of roughly 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 people, similar to the other myeloproliferative neoplasms.
explanation.whyCorrect: The annual incidence of primary myelofibrosis is approximately 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 people, similar to the other myeloproliferative neoplasms. It typically occurs in patients in their 60s or older, with a median age at presentation of 67 years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1 to 2 cases per 1,000 people vastly overstates how often PMF occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 1 to 2 cases per 1,000,000 people underestimates the incidence by roughly a factor of ten.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 10 to 20 cases per 100,000 people is an order of magnitude higher than the reported incidence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 50 to 60 cases per 100,000 people would make PMF a common disorder, which it is not.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with primary myelofibrosis reports that he feels uncomfortably full after eating only a few bites of a meal, along with left upper quadrant fullness. Which of the following best explains his early satiety?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An enlarged spleen impinging on the stomach

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delayed gastric emptying from autonomic neuropathy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Esophageal narrowing from a peptic stricture

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gastric outlet obstruction by a pyloric mass

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tense ascites compressing the gastric lumen

explanation.summary: Early satiety in PMF results from the massively enlarged spleen pressing on the stomach.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms in PMF may result from splenomegaly, including left upper quadrant fullness or discomfort and early satiety from the spleen impinging on the stomach. The spleen enlarges because it takes over blood cell production through extramedullary hematopoiesis when the fibrotic marrow cannot keep up.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autonomic neuropathy with gastroparesis is not part of the presentation of PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A peptic stricture would cause dysphagia rather than early satiety with left upper quadrant fullness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pyloric mass is not a feature of PMF, and the left upper quadrant fullness points to the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ascites is not a described feature of PMF, whereas massive splenomegaly is its hallmark finding.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with primary myelofibrosis is found to have an enlarged liver and mildly abnormal liver function test results. Ultrasonography shows no biliary dilation and patent hepatic vessels. Which of the following best explains her hepatic findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Biliary obstruction from a retained gallstone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Congestive hepatopathy from right heart failure

explanation.summary: Extramedullary hematopoiesis in PMF occurs in the liver as well as the spleen and can produce abnormal liver function test results.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the fibrotic marrow cannot produce blood cells, hematopoiesis moves to other sites. Extramedullary hematopoiesis is most clinically obvious in the spleen but also occurs in the liver, where it can cause hepatomegaly and abnormal liver function test results.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ultrasound shows no biliary dilation, making obstruction from a stone unlikely.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Viral hepatitis is unrelated to the pathophysiology of PMF and is not suggested by this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no evidence of right heart failure, and congestive hepatopathy is not a complication of PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amyloid deposition in the liver is a feature of plasma-cell disorders, not of PMF.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man being evaluated for massive splenomegaly has a peripheral smear showing left-shifted granulocytic precursors including rare blasts, together with nucleated red blood cells. This smear pattern is best described by which of the following terms?

explanation.summary: Left-shifted granulocytic precursors with rare blasts plus nucleated RBCs define a leukoerythroblastic reaction, the typical PMF smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: The typical appearance on the peripheral smear in PMF is referred to as a leukoerythroblastic reaction, in which left-shifted granulocytic precursors (including rare blasts) and nucleated RBCs are seen. Teardrop-shaped RBCs accompany this picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A leukemoid reaction refers to a marked benign granulocytosis and does not describe the accompanying nucleated RBCs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Megaloblastic change refers to hypersegmented neutrophils and macrocytosis from B12 or folate deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactive lymphocytosis describes increased atypical lymphocytes, which are not part of this myeloid picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rouleaux formation is stacking of RBCs caused by elevated plasma proteins, not this precursor pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with primary myelofibrosis has numerous teardrop-shaped red blood cells on the peripheral smear. Which of the following best explains how these cells acquire their shape?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A congenitally defective membrane skeleton makes them spherical

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abnormal hemoglobin polymerizes when oxygen tension falls

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bound antibody leads macrophages to remove pieces of membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrin strands in small vessels shear them as they pass

choices.label: E
choices.text: They elongate while squeezing between fibrous strands in the marrow

explanation.summary: Teardrop cells form as RBCs are deformed while squeezing out of a fibrotic marrow into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the bone marrow is fibrotic, it is hard for RBCs to migrate out into the blood. As they squeeze through the tiny spaces created by all those fibrous strands, they elongate into a teardrop shape. Nucleated RBCs appear alongside them because the marrow releases some red cells a little too early while trying to keep up with demand.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A congenital membrane defect produces spherocytes, as in hereditary spherocytosis, not dacryocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin polymerization at low oxygen tension produces sickled cells in sickle cell disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibody-mediated partial phagocytosis also produces spherocytes rather than teardrop cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shearing by intravascular fibrin strands produces schistocytes in microangiopathic processes.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman is evaluated early in the course of primary myelofibrosis, before marrow failure has developed. Which of the following complete blood count patterns is most likely at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated white blood cell count with a left shift and anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Isolated marked thrombocytosis with normal hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leukopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils and macrocytosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Markedly elevated hematocrit with a normal white blood cell count

explanation.summary: The CBC in PMF typically shows an elevated WBC count with a left shift and anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: In PMF there typically is an elevated white blood cell count with a left shift and anemia, as is seen in the other myeloproliferative neoplasms and particularly in chronic myeloid leukemia. Later, as marrow fibrosis worsens, the counts fall and the patient becomes pancytopenic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Isolated marked thrombocytosis is the pattern of essential thrombocythemia rather than PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isolated thrombocytopenia suggests immune thrombocytopenia, not this myeloproliferative process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypersegmented neutrophils with macrocytosis indicate megaloblastic anemia from B12 or folate deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A markedly elevated hematocrit is characteristic of polycythemia vera, where the red cells predominate.

questions.stem: A patient with primary myelofibrosis diagnosed many years ago now has pancytopenia, and a repeat core biopsy is performed. Which of the following findings is most likely at this late stage of disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fatty marrow with complete absence of reticulin fibers

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypercellular marrow with clustered atypical megakaryocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Massive fibrosis with few remaining hematopoietic cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normocellular marrow with thinned bony trabeculae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sheets of high-grade dysplastic marrow precursors

explanation.summary: Late in PMF the core biopsy shows massive fibrosis with few residual cells, in contrast to the hypercellular fibrotic marrow of early disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: A core biopsy in PMF shows either hypercellularity with fibrosis early in the disease or massive fibrosis with few cells in later stages. Eventually the marrow becomes nearly completely replaced by fibrosis, leaving no room for normal hematopoietic cells and producing the falling counts seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reticulin and collagen are abundant rather than absent in PMF, especially late in the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A hypercellular marrow with clustered megakaryocytes describes the early phase, not advanced disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A normocellular marrow would not explain the pancytopenia, and the marrow here is densely fibrotic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PMF does not cause dysplasia of bone marrow cells at any point in the disease process.

questions.stem: A core bone marrow biopsy from a patient with suspected primary myelofibrosis is submitted with a request to demonstrate the fibers filling the marrow space. Which of the following stains is most appropriate for this purpose?

explanation.summary: Reticulin staining demonstrates the fibers that fill the marrow in primary myelofibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bone marrow in PMF eventually becomes nearly completely replaced by fibrosis, and this is demonstrated by reticulin-stained fibers filling the marrow space on the core biopsy. Increased reticulin and collagen deposition is the defining pathologic feature of the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Congo red is used to demonstrate amyloid deposits, which are not the issue here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Periodic acid-Schiff stains glycogen and related carbohydrates rather than marrow fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prussian blue stains iron stores and would not highlight the fibrous strands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wright-Giemsa is the routine stain for cell morphology and does not specifically show fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man has massive splenomegaly, teardrop cells, and a densely fibrotic marrow on core biopsy. Review of his records shows he was managed for polycythemia vera for the preceding 12 years. Which of the following best distinguishes his fibrotic marrow disease from primary myelofibrosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His prior history of another myeloproliferative neoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: The amount of reticulin and collagen in his marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: The presence of an activating JAK2 mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The presence of teardrop cells on his peripheral smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: The size of his spleen on physical examination

explanation.summary: End-stage polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia look like PMF, so a prior history of one of those neoplasms is what distinguishes them.
explanation.whyCorrect: The end stage of polycythemia vera and essential thrombocythemia can have a fibrotic marrow appearance identical to that of PMF, so it may be hard to distinguish these three neoplasms at this stage. Usually, having a prior history of one of these neoplasms is how they are differentiated.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The degree of reticulin and collagen is similar once these neoplasms reach the fibrotic end stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: JAK2 mutations occur in PMF as well as in polycythemia vera, so the finding is not discriminating.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Teardrop cells reflect any fibrotic marrow and do not separate PMF from end-stage PV or ET.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenomegaly is a feature of all the myeloproliferative neoplasms and cannot resolve the distinction.

questions.stem: A patient newly diagnosed with primary myelofibrosis asks about survival. Which of the following best approximates the overall life expectancy for patients with this disorder?

explanation.summary: Median survival in PMF averages about 6 years but varies widely with disease severity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The overall life expectancy for patients with PMF is 6 years, but it varies depending on the severity of disease. Asymptomatic patients may live 15 years or more, whereas patients with massive marrow fibrosis, cytopenias, and symptoms survive for a much shorter time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two years underestimates the average survival, which is closer to 6 years.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 6-month survival would be typical of an acute malignancy, whereas PMF is slow and chronic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Twelve years overstates the average, although asymptomatic patients may do better than average.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Twenty-five years far exceeds the reported average life expectancy in this disorder.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with high-risk primary myelofibrosis is being evaluated for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Which of the following donor characteristics is most important in selecting a suitable donor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A donor chronologic age of younger than 30 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acceptable matching of human leukocyte antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: An identical ABO blood group and Rh type

choices.label: E
choices.text: The same biological sex as the transplant recipient

explanation.summary: Allogeneic transplantation requires a donor whose human leukocyte antigens are acceptable matches to the patient's.
explanation.whyCorrect: An allogeneic transplant uses stem cells collected from the blood or bone marrow of a donor whose human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) are acceptable matches to the patient's. This is the procedure that currently offers the only curative potential for PMF.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A specific donor age threshold is not what defines an acceptable donor for this procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ABO identity is not the determining factor in selecting a stem cell donor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytomegalovirus serology is not the characteristic that determines donor suitability here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Matching biological sex is not the criterion used to select a stem cell donor.

questions.stem: A patient who underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for primary myelofibrosis is counseled about a dangerous complication in which the transplanted cells attack the recipient's tissues. Which of the following is this complication?

explanation.summary: Graft-versus-host disease is the complication in which transplanted donor cells attack the recipient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation has dangerous potential side effects, including immunosuppression with increased infections and early graft-versus-host disease, in which the transplanted cells attack the recipient. The immunosuppressive drugs given after transplantation also carry many potential adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hemolytic transfusion reaction is recipient antibody destroying transfused red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is widespread activation of coagulation, not donor cell attack.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Graft failure means the donor cells fail to engraft, not that they attack the recipient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor lysis syndrome results from rapid tumor cell breakdown after cytotoxic therapy.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is 4 weeks out from allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for primary myelofibrosis. He now has a diffuse skin rash, abdominal cramping with diarrhea, nausea and vomiting, and elevated liver function test results. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his findings?

explanation.summary: Rash, cramping diarrhea, nausea and vomiting, and elevated liver function tests early after allogeneic transplant indicate acute graft-versus-host disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute graft-versus-host disease can cause skin rashes, cramping, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and elevation in liver function tests. It is an early complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation, in which the transplanted cells attack the recipient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sepsis would present with fever and hemodynamic instability rather than this triad of organ involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transfusional iron overload develops over years and does not cause an acute rash with diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrent marrow fibrosis would cause falling blood counts rather than this rash and diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral gastroenteritis would not account for the skin rash and abnormal liver function tests.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman is found to have low-risk primary myelofibrosis. She has no symptoms, her hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL, and her platelet count is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Observation with monitoring of blood counts

explanation.summary: Low-risk asymptomatic patients with PMF are observed, with treatment guided by symptoms and counts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of PMF depends on disease severity. Patients without symptoms (low-risk asymptomatic) can be observed, or treatment may be guided by their symptoms. This often includes monitoring and replacement, if needed, of platelet and RBC counts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transplantation is recommended soon after diagnosis for high- or intermediate-risk patients, not low-risk asymptomatic ones.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydroxyurea is reserved for high-risk disease requiring cytoreduction rather than asymptomatic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ruxolitinib is used for high-risk patients who are not eligible for transplantation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenectomy is not among the described treatments for primary myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with high-risk primary myelofibrosis has been taking ruxolitinib for 6 months. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is an expected adverse effect of this drug?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Marked erythrocytosis with a high hematocrit

explanation.summary: Ruxolitinib can cause hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia, along with pancytopenia and bruising.
explanation.whyCorrect: As with other targeted therapies, immunosuppression and graft-versus-host disease are concerns with ruxolitinib. Other concerns include pancytopenia, bruising, and hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia, so lipid levels are followed during therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pancreatic enzyme elevation is not a described toxicity of ruxolitinib.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypercalcemia is not a recognized adverse effect of this JAK1 and JAK2 inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperkalemia with renal failure is not among the adverse effects attributed to ruxolitinib.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ruxolitinib does not raise the hematocrit; it can cause anemia and pancytopenia instead.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with high-risk primary myelofibrosis is not a transplant candidate, and hydroxyurea is being considered. She tells her physician that she and her partner hope to conceive. Which of the following is the most important concern with this drug in her case?

explanation.summary: Hydroxyurea is teratogenic and must be used cautiously in women of childbearing age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hydroxyurea can cause teratogenicity in the fetus, so it should be used cautiously in women of childbearing age. Its other adverse effects include cytopenia, mucocutaneous ulcers, diarrhea, and peripheral neuropathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fetal iron overload is not a recognized effect of hydroxyurea therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gestational hypertension is not among the adverse effects attributed to this drug.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Permanent sterility is not the described reproductive concern with hydroxyurea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyurea does not cause maternal hypercalcemia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man taking hydroxyurea for primary myelofibrosis asks about immunizations before an overseas trip. Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated while he remains on this drug?

explanation.summary: Live vaccine administration is contraindicated while a patient is taking hydroxyurea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Live vaccine administration is a contraindication while a patient is on hydroxyurea, which suppresses blood cell production and can cause cytopenias. The yellow fever vaccine is a live attenuated preparation and therefore must be avoided.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The inactivated influenza vaccine contains no live organism and is not contraindicated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is not a live preparation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine is a subunit product rather than a live vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoid vaccines such as tetanus and diphtheria contain no live organism.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman has taken hydroxyurea for 8 months for primary myelofibrosis. She now has painful ulcers of the oral mucosa and lower legs and reports several weeks of loose stools. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency from occult blood loss

explanation.summary: Mucocutaneous ulcers and diarrhea are recognized adverse effects of hydroxyurea.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adverse effects of hydroxyurea include cytopenia, mucocutaneous ulcers, diarrhea, and peripheral neuropathy. Painful oral and leg ulcers with loose stools in a patient taking the drug fit this toxicity profile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Graft-versus-host disease follows allogeneic transplantation, which this patient has not undergone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disseminated herpes infection would be expected to cause fever and vesicular lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia rather than mucocutaneous ulceration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leukemic transformation causes a rapid clinical decline with blasts, not isolated ulcers and diarrhea.

questions.stem: A hematologist is choosing between hydroxyurea and ruxolitinib for a high-risk patient with primary myelofibrosis who cannot undergo transplantation. Which of the following statements best characterizes hydroxyurea relative to ruxolitinib?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A less favorable adverse effect profile and less effectiveness

choices.label: B
choices.text: A less favorable adverse effect profile but greater effectiveness

choices.label: C
choices.text: A more favorable adverse effect profile and greater effectiveness

choices.label: D
choices.text: A more favorable adverse effect profile but possibly less effectiveness

choices.label: E
choices.text: An identical adverse effect profile and equal effectiveness

explanation.summary: Hydroxyurea has shown a more favorable adverse effect profile than ruxolitinib but may not be as effective.
explanation.whyCorrect: In studies, hydroxyurea has shown a more favorable adverse effect profile than ruxolitinib; however, it may not be as effective. Both are the two medications primarily used for PMF in high-risk patients who are not eligible for transplantation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydroxyurea is better tolerated, so describing its adverse effect profile as less favorable is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydroxyurea has the more favorable, not the less favorable, adverse effect profile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hydroxyurea is not described as the more effective of the two agents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The two drugs differ in both tolerability and effectiveness rather than being equivalent.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with JAK2-mutated primary myelofibrosis has troublesome anemia. His hematologist mentions a recently FDA-approved JAK inhibitor that may provide better anemia-related benefits than ruxolitinib. Which of the following is this drug?

explanation.summary: Momelotinib is a newer JAK inhibitor approved for PMF that may offer better anemia-related benefits than ruxolitinib.
explanation.whyCorrect: Momelotinib is a new JAK inhibitor that was recently approved by the FDA for primary myelofibrosis. Initial studies show that it is an effective treatment and that it may provide better anemia-related benefits over ruxolitinib.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor used in plasma-cell disorders, not a JAK inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydroxyurea is an antimetabolite chemotherapy drug rather than a JAK inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imatinib inhibits the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase and is used in chronic myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody directed at B cells and has no role here.

questions.stem: In which of the following myeloproliferative neoplasms is a JAK2 mutation present in nearly 100% of cases?

explanation.summary: Almost 100% of polycythemia vera cases carry a JAK2 mutation, a higher proportion than in the other myeloproliferative neoplasms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Knowing the proportion of cases with a JAK2 mutation matters because it is an important molecular correlate with implications for prognosis and treatment. Almost 100% of polycythemia vera cases exhibit the mutation, compared with 50% to 60% in PMF and about 50% in essential thrombocythemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myeloid leukemia is not a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by JAK2 mutation status.
whyWrongByChoice.B: None of the chronic myeloid leukemia cases carry the JAK2 mutation; CML is defined by BCR::ABL1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 50% of essential thrombocythemia cases exhibit a JAK2 mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary myelofibrosis carries a JAK2 mutation in approximately 50% to 60% of cases.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with biopsy-confirmed primary myelofibrosis undergoes molecular testing of cells isolated from his bone marrow, and no JAK2 mutation is found. Which of the following mutations is most likely present?

explanation.summary: In JAK2-negative PMF, CALR mutations are the most common finding, occurring in 20% to 30% of cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Approximately 50% to 60% of PMF cases carry activating JAK2 mutations. In JAK2-negative cases, there can be mutations in CALR (20% to 30% of cases) and MPL (5% to 10% of cases), so CALR is the most likely mutation to be found in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCR::ABL1 defines chronic myeloid leukemia and is not a driver mutation in PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FLT3 mutations are relevant to acute myeloid leukemia rather than to PMF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MPL mutations occur in only 5% to 10% of cases, making them less likely than CALR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TP53 mutation is not one of the driver mutations described in primary myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: A hematology instructor explains that myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS) are a group of hematopoietic neoplasms that arise from a single cell line, which normally gives rise to red blood cells, some white blood cells, and platelets. Which of the following cell lines is involved in MDS?

explanation.summary: MDS are neoplasms of the myeloid cell line, which produces red blood cells, some white blood cells, and platelets.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myelodysplastic neoplasms involve the myeloid cell line, the line that gives rise to red blood cells, some of the white blood cells, and platelets. The disorder is characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis, cytopenias, and dysplasia in at least one hematopoietic lineage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells and are not the lineage affected in MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lymphoid cell line gives rise to lymphocytes and is involved in lymphoid neoplasms, a separate branch of hematologic malignancies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells are not the lineage that defines MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes; their neoplasm is multiple myeloma, not MDS.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man has routine bloodwork before elective prostate surgery. He feels well aside from age-appropriate fatigue. His complete blood count shows a mild decrease in white blood cell count, hemoglobin, and platelet count. The peripheral smear notes macro-ovalocytes and hyposegmented, hypogranular neutrophils, with no blasts seen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Pancytopenia with macro-ovalocytes and dysplastic (hyposegmented, hypogranular) neutrophils but no blasts in an older adult is characteristic of MDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: MDS often presents in older adults and may be found incidentally when a complete blood count shows one or more cytopenias. The smear reflects the dysplastic changes of MDS: macrocytic red cells and neutrophils with hyposegmentation and hypogranularity. The absence of a large blast population argues against acute leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myeloid leukemia would show 20% or more blasts, which are explicitly absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic myeloid leukemia presents with a markedly elevated white blood cell count, not the pancytopenia seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes and hemolysis, not pancytopenia with dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron-deficiency anemia causes microcytic, not macrocytic, red cells and does not produce dysplastic neutrophils and tri-lineage cytopenia.

questions.stem: A bone marrow biopsy from a patient being evaluated for a hematologic disorder shows dysplastic changes in more than 10% of cells in two lineages. The pathologist notes that the finding used to distinguish this condition from acute myeloid leukemia is the blast percentage. Which of the following blast counts is consistent with myelodysplastic neoplasms rather than acute myeloid leukemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blast percentage is irrelevant to the distinction

explanation.summary: MDS requires a bone marrow blast count below 20%; 20% or more defines acute myeloid leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: To diagnose MDS, the bone marrow blast count must be lower than 20%. If it is 20% or more, the diagnosis becomes acute myeloid leukemia. The marrow must also show at least 10% dysplastic cells in one or more lineages, which this patient meets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The blast percentage is precisely the feature that separates MDS from acute myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A count of 25% blasts is 20% or greater and therefore indicates acute myeloid leukemia, not MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A count of 50% blasts far exceeds the 20% cutoff and defines acute myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A count above 75% blasts is well within the range of acute myeloid leukemia.

questions.stem: A patient with newly diagnosed myelodysplastic neoplasm undergoes cytogenetic testing. Which of the following is the single most common chromosomal abnormality found in MDS?

explanation.summary: Deletions on chromosome 5, del(5q), are the single most common chromosomal abnormality in MDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: MDS is caused by one or more genetic mutations, including chromosomal abnormalities such as monosomy or trisomy. Among these, del(5q), a deletion on chromosome 5, represents the single most common chromosomal abnormality in MDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deletion of chromosome 13 is not the characteristic or most common MDS abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), defines chronic myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The t(15;17) translocation defines acute promyelocytic leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomy 12 is associated with chronic lymphocytic leukemia, not MDS.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with symptomatic low-risk myelodysplastic neoplasm has isolated del(5q) on cytogenetic testing and anemia with a nearly normal platelet count. Which of the following medications has been found to be particularly effective in this specific subtype?

explanation.summary: Lenalidomide is particularly effective in MDS associated with isolated del(5q).
explanation.whyCorrect: Lenalidomide is an immune-modulating drug that lowers TNF-alpha, stimulates some T-cell subsets, and inhibits cell growth. It has been found to be particularly effective in patients with MDS associated with isolated del(5q), the subtype that classically affects older women with anemia but fairly normal platelet counts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydroxyurea is a cytoreductive antimetabolite and is not the agent singled out for del(5q) MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Imatinib targets the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase of chronic myeloid leukemia, not MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prednisone is not a typical treatment for MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody used for B-cell disorders, not for del(5q) MDS.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear is reviewed for a patient with myelodysplastic neoplasm. Compared with the dramatic dysplasia seen in the bone marrow, the circulating red blood cells show a more subtle but characteristic change. Which of the following best describes the typical red blood cell finding in the peripheral blood?

explanation.summary: In the peripheral blood of MDS, red blood cells are usually macrocytic with a high mean cell volume.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike the marrow, which is packed with dysplastic cells, the peripheral blood shows cytopenias and more subtle dysplasia. The red blood cells that do reach the circulation in MDS are usually macrocytic, meaning large with a high mean cell volume.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Microcytic, hypochromic red cells are characteristic of iron-deficiency anemia, not MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickled red cells occur in sickle cell disease, an unrelated hemoglobinopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spherocytes are seen in hereditary spherocytosis and immune hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Teardrop cells (dacryocytes) are characteristic of primary myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: A bone marrow specimen from a patient with suspected myelodysplastic neoplasm is stained with Prussian blue. The pathologist identifies red blood cell precursors with a ring of iron-containing granules encircling the nucleus. Which of the following terms best describes these cells?

explanation.summary: Red blood cell precursors with perinuclear granules of iron seen on Prussian blue stain are ring sideroblasts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the dysplastic red blood cell precursor changes in the MDS bone marrow, ring sideroblasts, which are cells with perinuclear granules of iron, may be seen and are highlighted with a Prussian blue (iron) stain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Auer rods are needle-like inclusions of fused granules seen in blasts of acute myeloid leukemia, not ringed iron granules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heinz bodies are precipitated denatured hemoglobin seen in oxidative hemolysis, such as G6PD deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants seen after splenectomy or in hyposplenism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Smudge cells are fragile lymphocytes seen in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

questions.stem: A physician evaluating an older patient with pancytopenia and dysplastic-appearing cells emphasizes that myelodysplastic neoplasm is a diagnosis of exclusion, because several more common conditions can produce overlapping morphologic dysplasia. Which of the following must be excluded before diagnosing MDS?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Osteoarthritis of the knees and hips

explanation.summary: Because deficiencies of vitamin B12 and folate can cause morphologic dysplasia that overlaps with MDS, they must be excluded before making the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: MDS is a diagnosis of exclusion. Other, more common conditions that can demonstrate overlapping dysplasia should be ruled out first, and nutritional deficiencies such as vitamin B12 and folate are the prototypical example. Alcohol abuse, heavy metal exposure, certain drugs, and HIV must also be excluded.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastroesophageal reflux disease is unrelated to hematopoietic dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Essential hypertension does not cause dysplastic blood cell morphology and is not part of the MDS exclusion list.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoarthritis is a joint disorder with no effect on blood cell morphology.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 2 diabetes mellitus does not mimic the dysplasia of MDS.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with low-risk myelodysplastic neoplasm is troubled mainly by fatigue caused by his anemia. His physician selects a medication that is an endogenous hormone normally secreted by the kidneys to stimulate red blood cell production. Which of the following medications is being described?

explanation.summary: Erythropoietin, an endogenous kidney hormone that stimulates marrow red cell production, is often used for the anemia-related fatigue of low-risk MDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because fatigue due to anemia is a major symptom in MDS, erythropoietin is often used. It is an endogenous hormone secreted by the kidneys that stimulates the bone marrow to produce red blood cells, and it is available for IV infusion to help with the fatigue and anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Azacitidine is a pyrimidine nucleoside analog that inhibits DNA methylation, not a red-cell-stimulating hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytarabine is a pyrimidine nucleoside analog chemotherapy agent, not a hormone that raises red cell counts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Daunorubicin is an anthracycline chemotherapy agent used in high-potency regimens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Venetoclax is a BCL-2 inhibitor added to azacitidine for high-risk disease, not used for anemia-related fatigue.

questions.stem: A patient with low-risk myelodysplastic neoplasm is started on azacitidine. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this pyrimidine nucleoside analog?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It inhibits ribonucleotide reductase at the G1/S phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is incorporated into DNA and inhibits DNA methylation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lowers TNF-alpha and modulates T-cell subsets

choices.label: D
choices.text: It selectively inhibits the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates the kidneys to release erythropoietin

explanation.summary: Azacitidine is a pyrimidine nucleoside analog that is incorporated into DNA and inhibits DNA methylation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Azacitidine (like decitabine) is a pyrimidine nucleoside analog, similar to cytarabine, that is incorporated into DNA and inhibits DNA methylation. Its adverse effects, like those of other pyrimidine analogs, include nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, skin reactions, and myelosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase at the G1/S phase describes hydroxyurea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lowering TNF-alpha and modulating T-cell subsets describes lenalidomide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selective inhibition of BCL-2 is the mechanism of venetoclax, not azacitidine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating red cell production through erythropoietin describes erythropoietin therapy, not azacitidine.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man was diagnosed 3 years ago with a myelodysplastic neoplasm after presenting with anemia and a low neutrophil count. He now returns with worsening fatigue and bruising, and his hematocrit, red blood cell count, and platelet count are markedly decreased. A repeat bone marrow biopsy shows 40% blasts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A rise in marrow blasts to 20% or more marks transformation of MDS into acute myeloid leukemia, which occurs in roughly 30% of patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Roughly 30% of patients with MDS develop full-blown acute myeloid leukemia. AML is suggested here by the worsening symptoms and the bone marrow biopsy showing more than 20% blasts (40%), which is not consistent with MDS. The higher the blast count, the closer the disease is to the 20% cutoff that defines AML.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anemia of chronic disease does not produce 40% marrow blasts or this degree of pancytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic myeloid leukemia presents initially with a markedly increased peripheral white blood cell count, not the low counts here, and is not a complication of MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron-deficiency anemia causes microcytic anemia and does not raise marrow blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A blast count of 40% is far above the under-20% threshold, so the disease is no longer stable MDS.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has high-risk myelodysplastic neoplasm with a very high risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia. She is otherwise healthy. Her physician recommends the one therapy that may offer a potential cure. Which of the following is being recommended?

explanation.summary: For high-risk MDS patients with a very high risk of progressing to AML, allogeneic (donor) stem cell transplantation is the option that may offer a potential cure.
explanation.whyCorrect: High-risk patients can be treated with the same drugs used for low-risk disease, but for some patients who have a very high risk of progression to AML, allogeneic (donor) stem cell transplantation may offer a potential cure by replacing the diseased marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow radiotherapy is used for certain lymphomas, not for MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lenalidomide can control symptoms, especially in del(5q) disease, but is not curative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythropoietin helps with anemia-related fatigue but does not cure MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Observation is appropriate for asymptomatic low-risk patients, not for a patient at very high risk of AML who is a transplant candidate.

questions.stem: Myelodysplastic neoplasms occur in 1 to 5 cases per 100,000 people overall, but the rate rises to more than 20 cases per 100,000 in one segment of the population. Which of the following best describes the age distribution of myelodysplastic neoplasms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Incidence is evenly distributed across all ages, with a mean age of 45 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients are older than 60 years, with a mean age of onset of 70 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Onset is most common between 20 and 40 years and risk falls after age 60

choices.label: D
choices.text: Onset peaks in the fourth decade of life, with a mean age of 35 years

choices.label: E
choices.text: Onset peaks in the second decade of life, with a mean age of 15 years

explanation.summary: MDS occurs most frequently in patients older than 60 years, with a mean age of onset of 70 years, and risk rises with age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myelodysplastic neoplasms occur most frequently in patients older than 60 years, with a mean age of onset of 70 years. The risk increases with age: the overall risk is 1 to 5 cases per 100,000 people, but more than 20 cases per 100,000 in those older than age 70.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Incidence is not evenly distributed; it climbs steeply with advancing age.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Risk rises rather than falls after age 60, exceeding 20 cases per 100,000 after age 70.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A peak in the fourth decade does not match the strongly age-dependent incidence of MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MDS is not a disease of adolescence; onset in the second decade would be exceptional.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is being evaluated for unexplained cytopenias with dysplastic changes on his blood smear. He worked for 30 years at a petrochemical refinery, and his physician asks specifically about one chemical exposure known to predispose to myelodysplastic neoplasms. Which of the following exposures is the physician asking about?

explanation.summary: Benzene is one of the environmental exposures associated with the development of MDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although most cases of MDS have no known predisposing factor, recognized environmental associations include tobacco, radiation, benzene, petrochemicals, and pesticides. Benzene is the classic chemical exposure asked about in a patient with a petrochemical work history.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Asbestos is linked to mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma, not to myeloid dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crystalline silica causes silicosis, a pneumoconiosis, and is not among the MDS-associated exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Formaldehyde is not one of the environmental factors associated with MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mercury vapor causes neurologic and renal toxicity and is not an MDS risk factor.

questions.stem: A physician taking a family history from a patient with newly diagnosed myelodysplastic neoplasm notes that inherited genetic abnormalities are a rare but real cause of this disease. Which of the following inherited conditions is recognized as a cause of MDS?

explanation.summary: Rare familial cases of MDS arise from inherited genetic abnormalities such as Fanconi anemia and trisomy 21.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most cases of MDS have no known predisposing factor, but familial disease is one recognized etiology: inherited genetic abnormalities, including trisomy 21 and Fanconi anemia, can cause MDS.

whyWrongByChoice.B: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidative hemolysis and is not listed among inherited causes of MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hereditary hemochromatosis causes iron overload in parenchymal organs and does not predispose to MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hereditary spherocytosis is a membrane defect causing hemolytic anemia, not a predisposition to myeloid neoplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Willebrand disease is an inherited bleeding disorder of platelet adhesion, unrelated to marrow dysplasia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman treated 7 years ago with cytotoxic chemotherapy and radiation for breast cancer now has pancytopenia. Her bone marrow shows dysplasia in two lineages with 6% blasts, and she is diagnosed with therapy-related myelodysplastic neoplasm. Compared with MDS arising without a known predisposing factor, which of the following is expected in her case?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bone marrow blast count that must exceed 20% for the diagnosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A lower likelihood of ever requiring transfusion support

choices.label: C
choices.text: A poorer prognosis with lower survival

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absence of any identifiable chromosomal abnormality on karyotype

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spontaneous resolution once the marrow recovers from prior therapy

explanation.summary: MDS that follows previous cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiation is termed therapy-related MDS and carries a poorer prognosis and lower survival.
explanation.whyCorrect: Previous cytotoxic chemotherapy and/or radiation is one of the recognized etiologies of MDS, and disease arising this way is termed therapy-related MDS. Therapy-related MDS is associated with a poorer prognosis and lower survival than MDS without this history.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A blast count of 20% or more would make the diagnosis acute myeloid leukemia rather than MDS, regardless of etiology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Worse disease means more, not less, need for supportive care such as transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromosomal abnormalities are common in MDS, and additional abnormalities beyond del(5q) predict poor outcome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Therapy-related MDS is a clonal neoplasm; it does not simply resolve as the marrow recovers.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with a myelodysplastic neoplasm has a low white blood cell count, and the white cells he does produce function abnormally. His physician counsels him that he is more susceptible to infection and describes the type of infection seen most commonly in this setting. Which of the following infections is most common in patients with MDS?

explanation.summary: Dysfunctional white blood cells in MDS make patients susceptible to infection, with skin infections being the most common.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reduced numbers and impaired function of white blood cells in MDS increase susceptibility to infection, and skin infections are specifically identified as the most common type in these patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute otitis media is chiefly a pediatric infection and is not associated with MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacterial meningitis is not a typical manifestation of the leukopenia of MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Septic arthritis is uncommon and is not the infection emphasized in MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary tract infections are common in older adults generally but are not the characteristic infection of MDS.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected myelodysplastic neoplasm undergoes genetic testing of a bone marrow aspirate. In approximately what proportion of patients with MDS does such testing identify one or more chromosomal abnormalities or gene mutations?

explanation.summary: One or more chromosomal abnormalities or gene mutations are identified in 75% to 90% of patients with MDS during genetic testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: MDS is caused by one or more gene mutations leading to cellular dysplasia in bone marrow myeloid precursors. These include chromosomal abnormalities such as monosomy or trisomy as well as single or isolated gene mutations, and one or more is identified in 75% to 90% of MDS patients during genetic testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A yield under 10% would make genetic testing nearly useless, yet it is the key to management in MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A yield of 20% to 35% substantially understates the detection rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A yield of 45% to 60% still falls well below the reported 75% to 90%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Detection is high but not near-universal; a minority of patients have no identifiable abnormality.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman has anemia with a normal white blood cell count and a platelet count at the upper limit of normal. Cytogenetic testing shows isolated del(5q). Which of the following best describes the natural history of this specific subtype of myelodysplastic neoplasm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It arises almost exclusively after prior alkylating chemotherapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It characteristically presents with severe thrombocytopenia and bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: It occurs predominantly in men younger than 40 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: It transforms into acute myeloid leukemia faster than other subtypes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its rate of progression to leukemia is low compared with other subtypes

explanation.summary: MDS with isolated del(5q) is seen mostly in older women, presents with anemia and fairly normal white cell and platelet counts, and has a low rate of progression to leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The specific type of MDS characterized by del(5q) is seen mostly in older females and presents with anemia but fairly normal white blood cell and platelet counts, with the platelet count sometimes even elevated. Progression to leukemia in this form is low compared with other types of MDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prior chemotherapy defines therapy-related MDS, a separate etiology that carries a poorer prognosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet counts are fairly normal or even elevated; severe thrombocytopenia is not characteristic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This subtype is seen mostly in older females, not in young men.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Accelerated leukemic transformation is the opposite of the low progression rate of del(5q) disease.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a myelodysplastic neoplasm has karyotype analysis showing several cytogenetic abnormalities other than del(5q). Which of the following does this finding predict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A blast count that will remain below 5% indefinitely

choices.label: B
choices.text: A poor prognosis with likely progression to acute myeloid leukemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: An excellent prognosis with essentially no risk of transformation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reclassification of the disease as a lymphoid neoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spontaneous remission of the cytopenias within several months

explanation.summary: Cytogenetic abnormalities other than del(5q) are associated with a poor prognosis and a likely progression to acute myeloid leukemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The specific mutations present in MDS affect prognosis and clinical management. Additional cytogenetic abnormalities beyond del(5q) are associated with poor prognosis and a likely progression to acute myeloid leukemia, in contrast to isolated del(5q), in which progression is low.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adverse cytogenetics predict a rising blast count and movement toward the 20% threshold for AML.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An excellent prognosis with no transformation risk describes isolated del(5q), not additional cytogenetic abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MDS is a myeloid neoplasm regardless of karyotype and is not reclassified as lymphoid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MDS is a clonal neoplasm; spontaneous remission of the cytopenias is not expected.

questions.stem: A hematopathologist is reviewing a bone marrow biopsy to determine whether the morphologic criteria for a myelodysplastic neoplasm are met. Dysplastic cells must account for at least what percentage of cells in one or more lineages?

explanation.summary: The MDS diagnosis requires at least 10% dysplastic cells in one or more lineages in the bone marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: To make the MDS diagnosis there must be at least 10% dysplastic cells in one or more lineages in the bone marrow. This morphologic criterion is paired with a blast count below 20%, which separates MDS from acute myeloid leukemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 1% threshold would be met by trivial or reactive changes and is far below the required proportion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 30% threshold is higher than the criterion and would exclude many patients who truly have MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 50% threshold greatly overstates the required degree of dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 75% threshold is not a recognized morphologic criterion for MDS.

questions.stem: A bone marrow aspirate from a patient with a myelodysplastic neoplasm shows red blood cell precursors in which the nucleus is developing slowly compared with the rate of development of the cytoplasm. Which of the following terms describes this dysplastic change?

explanation.summary: Slow development of the nucleus relative to the cytoplasm in red blood cell precursors is called nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony.
explanation.whyCorrect: Red blood cell precursors in MDS may show all manner of unusual changes, including nuclear budding, multiple nuclei, tiny nuclear fragments within a large cell, vacuolization of the cytoplasm of early precursors, and nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony, which is specifically defined as slow development of the nucleus compared with the rate of development of the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vacuolization is the appearance of clear spaces in the cytoplasm of early red cell precursors, a separate change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypogranulation refers to a lack of granules in neutrophils, not to precursor maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyposegmentation refers to too few nuclear lobes in neutrophils, not to red cell precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear budding describes protrusions of nuclear material, not a mismatch in maturation rates.

questions.stem: A bone marrow biopsy from a patient with a myelodysplastic neoplasm is examined for megakaryocyte morphology. Which of the following findings is characteristic of dysplastic megakaryocytes in MDS?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete absence of megakaryocytes from the marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enlarged megakaryocytes with more than eight nuclear lobes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Megakaryocytes with perinuclear granules of iron

explanation.summary: Dysplastic megakaryocytes in MDS are often much smaller than normal and have abnormal nuclear lobation, classically a single monolobated nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Megakaryocytes in MDS are often much smaller than normal, with more or fewer nuclei than the normal single multilobulated nucleus. The classic image is of small dysplastic megakaryocytes with monolobated nuclei.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Megakaryocytes are present but dysplastic; complete absence is not the described finding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Megakaryocytes in MDS are typically smaller than normal, not enlarged with excess lobes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Needle-shaped cytoplasmic rods are Auer rods, seen in blasts with myeloid differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Perinuclear iron granules define ring sideroblasts, which are red blood cell precursors.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a patient with a myelodysplastic neoplasm is reported as showing neutrophil hyposegmentation. Which of the following nuclear appearances corresponds to this term?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A nucleus displaced to the periphery by clear vacuoles

choices.label: B
choices.text: A nucleus fragmented into several small separate pieces

choices.label: C
choices.text: A nucleus surrounded by a ring of iron-containing granules

choices.label: D
choices.text: A nucleus with only two lobes, or a single unlobed nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: A nucleus with six or more distinct lobes

explanation.summary: Hyposegmentation means the neutrophil nucleus has too few lobes, appearing as two lobes instead of the typical three or four, or as a single unlobed nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils in the peripheral blood of MDS patients may show hyposegmentation and/or hypogranularity. Hyposegmentation of the nucleus can appear as simply two lobes instead of the typical three or four, or it can appear as a single, unlobed nucleus, which looks very strange in a neutrophil.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoplasmic vacuolization displacing the nucleus is a red cell precursor change, not hyposegmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tiny nuclear fragments within a large cell are described in red blood cell precursors, not as neutrophil hyposegmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A ring of iron granules around the nucleus defines a ring sideroblast, a red cell precursor finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Six or more lobes is hypersegmentation, the opposite change, classically seen with B12 or folate deficiency.

questions.stem: The neutrophils on a peripheral smear from a patient with a myelodysplastic neoplasm appear to have very light grey, almost clear cytoplasm. Which of the following best explains this appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of primary granules producing deep cytoplasmic basophilia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of iron granules in a ring around the neutrophil nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fusion of granules into needle-shaped rods within the cytoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lack of the secondary granules characteristic of normal neutrophils

choices.label: E
choices.text: Precipitation of denatured hemoglobin along the cell membrane

explanation.summary: Hypogranularity in MDS neutrophils reflects a lack of the secondary granules normally present in neutrophil cytoplasm, leaving very light grey or clear cytoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypogranularity refers to the lack of secondary granules that are characteristic of normal neutrophil cytoplasm. In MDS, the neutrophils therefore appear to have very light grey or even clear cytoplasm, as illustrated by the hypogranulated neutrophil on the smear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accumulated granules would darken the cytoplasm, the opposite of the pale appearance described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Perinuclear iron granules define ring sideroblasts, which are red blood cell precursors in the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Needle-shaped granule fusion describes Auer rods in blasts, not loss of granules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Denatured hemoglobin precipitates are Heinz bodies, a red blood cell finding in oxidative injury.

questions.stem: A hematology resident is asked to describe the platelet findings on the peripheral smear of a patient with a myelodysplastic neoplasm. Which of the following best describes the expected platelet changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are consistently absent from the peripheral smear entirely

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are invariably normal in both size and granulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are uniformly small and hypogranular in essentially every patient

choices.label: D
choices.text: They characteristically contain needle-shaped rods in their cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: They may be hypergranular or hypogranular and may be larger than normal

explanation.summary: Platelet changes in MDS are variable: platelets may be hypergranular or hypogranular, and they may be larger than normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the peripheral blood changes in MDS, platelet changes are specifically described as variable. Platelets may appear hypergranular or hypogranular, or they may be larger in size than normal, in addition to being reduced in number.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Platelets are decreased in number but are not absent from the smear.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Normal size and granulation would not reflect the dysplasia that characterizes MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The changes are variable rather than uniform, and platelets may be larger than normal rather than small.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Needle-shaped cytoplasmic rods are Auer rods in myeloid blasts, not a platelet finding.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman with a myelodysplastic neoplasm has a bone marrow biopsy showing a hypercellular marrow packed with dysplastic cells, yet her complete blood count shows anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Which of the following best explains the discrepancy between the crowded marrow and the low peripheral counts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An expanded plasma volume dilutes otherwise normal cell counts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blasts occupy more than 20% of the marrow and suppress mature cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circulating cells are destroyed by autoantibodies within the spleen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Precursor cells fail to mature in the marrow and do not enter the circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The marrow space is replaced by fibrous tissue that crowds out precursors

explanation.summary: The cytopenias of MDS reflect ineffective hematopoiesis: precursors do not mature in the marrow and never reach the circulation, despite a cellular marrow.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike the bone marrow, which is packed full of dysplastic cells, the peripheral blood in MDS shows cytopenias. This is because the precursor cells do not mature in the bone marrow and do not enter the circulation, which is the ineffective hematopoiesis that defines the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dilution by plasma volume does not explain true dysplasia and tri-lineage cytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A blast count of 20% or more would reclassify the disease as acute myeloid leukemia rather than MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Splenic antibody-mediated destruction describes immune cytopenias, not the ineffective hematopoiesis of MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Marrow replacement by fibrous tissue describes primary myelofibrosis, which gives a fibrotic rather than hypercellular dysplastic marrow.

questions.stem: A myelodysplastic neoplasm is usually first suspected when a complete blood count shows one or more cytopenias. Which of the following cytopenias is most commonly found on the complete blood count in these patients?

explanation.summary: Anemia is the most common cytopenia found on the complete blood count in patients with MDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myelodysplastic neoplasms are usually suspected when a complete blood count shows one or more cytopenias in the peripheral blood, with anemia being the most common. This is also why fatigue due to anemia is the major symptom driving treatment in many patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphopenia is not the characteristic cytopenia of this myeloid disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytopenia is not the cytopenia typically identified at presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutropenia occurs in MDS and raises infection risk, but it is not the most common cytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombocytopenia occurs and can cause bleeding, but anemia is more frequent.

questions.stem: A bone marrow aspirate from a patient with suspected myelodysplastic neoplasm is sent to the laboratory specifically to detect chromosomal abnormalities such as a deletion on chromosome 5. Which of the following studies is used for this purpose?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prussian blue staining of the aspirate smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum vitamin B12 and folate levels

explanation.summary: FISH and karyotype analysis of marrow or peripheral blood identify the chromosomal abnormalities of MDS, such as del(5q).
explanation.whyCorrect: In the workup of MDS, bone marrow aspirate or peripheral blood specimens are sent for FISH and karyotype to identify chromosomal abnormalities. Molecular gene sequencing panels are sent separately to identify characteristic gene mutations.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Flow cytometry is an ancillary study of cell surface markers and does not display chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gene sequencing panels identify characteristic point mutations rather than whole-chromosome deletions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prussian blue is an iron stain used to demonstrate ring sideroblasts, not chromosomal deletions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: B12 and folate levels are ordered to exclude nutritional causes of dysplasia, not to find del(5q).

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man who works in a metal smelting plant is found to have cytopenias with dysplastic cells on his smear. Before a myelodysplastic neoplasm can be diagnosed, his physician wants to exclude a toxic exposure that can produce overlapping dysplasia. Which of the following exposures should be investigated?

explanation.summary: Heavy metal exposure, specifically arsenic, lead, and zinc, must be excluded before diagnosing MDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: MDS is a diagnosis of exclusion because other conditions can demonstrate overlapping morphologic dysplasia. The exclusion list includes nutritional deficiency (vitamin B12, folate, copper), alcohol abuse, heavy metal exposure with arsenic, lead, and zinc, certain drugs and biologic agents, and infections such as HIV.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbon monoxide impairs oxygen delivery but does not cause dysplastic marrow morphology.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chlorinated solvents are not among the exposures that must be excluded before diagnosing MDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitrogen dioxide is a respiratory irritant and is not on the exclusion list.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ultraviolet radiation damages skin rather than producing marrow dysplasia.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman being evaluated for cytopenias with dysplastic marrow changes takes several medications. Her physician notes that one of them can itself produce dysplasia and must be excluded as a cause before a myelodysplastic neoplasm is diagnosed. Which of the following medications is the physician referring to?

explanation.summary: Drugs and biologic agents such as chemotherapy, isoniazid, and tacrolimus can cause dysplasia and must be excluded before diagnosing MDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because MDS is a diagnosis of exclusion, drugs and biologic agents are one of the categories that must be ruled out. The agents named are chemotherapy, isoniazid, and tacrolimus, so a patient taking isoniazid requires that this cause be excluded first.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker with no association with dysplastic hematopoiesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atorvastatin is not among the drugs listed as causes of dysplasia requiring exclusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone and does not produce marrow dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Omeprazole is not one of the drugs that must be excluded in the MDS workup.

questions.stem: A physician is counseling a patient with symptomatic low-risk myelodysplastic neoplasm before starting lenalidomide. Which of the following is a black box warning for this medication?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teratogenicity if the drug is used during pregnancy

explanation.summary: Lenalidomide carries black box warnings as a teratogen if used during pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lenalidomide is an immune-modulating drug with a wide range of effects, and its adverse effect concerns include severe neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity, and risk of thrombosis. It also carries black box warnings as a teratogen if used during pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemorrhagic cystitis is associated with other agents, not with lenalidomide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Irreversible cardiomyopathy is characteristic of anthracyclines such as daunorubicin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is not a described toxicity of this drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary fibrosis is not among the adverse effects attributed to lenalidomide.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with low-risk myelodysplastic neoplasm has been receiving azacitidine. Which of the following adverse effect patterns should be anticipated with this agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cholestatic jaundice with pruritus and pale stools

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dry cough with pulmonary fibrosis and digital clubbing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertension with peripheral edema and hirsutism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mucositis with nausea, vomiting, and myelosuppression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral neuropathy with hearing loss and tinnitus

explanation.summary: Azacitidine shares the toxicity profile of the pyrimidine nucleoside analogs: nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, skin reactions, and myelosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Azacitidine, like decitabine, is a pyrimidine nucleoside analog. As with the other pyrimidine analogs, its adverse effects include nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, mucositis, skin rashes and redness, and myelosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholestatic jaundice is not the characteristic toxicity pattern of this agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pulmonary fibrosis with clubbing is not a described adverse effect of azacitidine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertension, edema, and hirsutism are not part of the pyrimidine analog toxicity profile.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuropathy with ototoxicity belongs to other chemotherapy classes, not to azacitidine.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with high-risk, treatment-naive myelodysplastic neoplasm is started on azacitidine combined with a second agent that has cytotoxic activity in tumor cells overexpressing BCL-2. Which of the following is this second agent, and what does it do?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daunorubicin, an anthracycline that damages tumor cell DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythropoietin, which stimulates the marrow to make red blood cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Imatinib, which inhibits the BCR-ABL fusion tyrosine kinase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lenalidomide, which lowers TNF-alpha and stimulates some T-cell subsets

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venetoclax, which selectively inhibits the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2

explanation.summary: For high-risk, treatment-naive MDS, azacitidine may be combined with venetoclax, which selectively inhibits the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: For high-risk treatment-naive patients, a newer combination may be considered that includes azacitidine with venetoclax. Venetoclax has cytotoxic activity in tumor cells that overexpress BCL-2 because it selectively inhibits this anti-apoptotic protein, which is overexpressed in some cancer cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Daunorubicin is an anthracycline given with cytarabine as high-potency chemotherapy, not a BCL-2 inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythropoietin is a hormone used for anemia-related fatigue and has no cytotoxic activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imatinib targets the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase of chronic myeloid leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lenalidomide is an immune-modulating drug and does not act on BCL-2.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old patient with high-risk myelodysplastic neoplasm is considered for the high-potency chemotherapy regimen most often encountered in this disease, daunorubicin-cytarabine. Which of the following correctly classifies these two agents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both drugs are immune-modulating agents that lower TNF-alpha levels in the marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both drugs are pyrimidine nucleoside analogs that block DNA synthesis

choices.label: C
